title: Three modalities used by the BOD in its "scheme" to capture foreign  currency  deposits, according to lawsuit
text:
Affected parties of the BOD's foreign banks allege in the lawsuit filed before the TSJ that most of the foreign currency deposits of their clients were converted into investments in public debt bonds of the Republic or in securities of PDVSA. That is why -they argue- that the problems of the Venezuelan entity began when the government had difficulties to honor its commitments with the bondholders and fell into default or non-payment.

The case of Grupo Financiero BOD has gained relevance in the last few weeks due to the actions taken by the lawyers of the affected parties, who are seeking the return of their deposits or justice. They state that it is no longer only an issue of responsibility towards the depositors who have sued the bank, but that it extends to other dimensions such as the affectation of human rights.

Recently, the lawyers of 200 clients of the BOD who lost their savings with the liquidation and intervention of the banks abroad, went to the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (UNHCHR), Volker Türk, to denounce the Venezuelan State for denial of justice. They consider that there is a clear violation of fundamental rights such as access to justice, due to the delay of the Supreme Court of Justice (TSJ) in admitting or rejecting the lawsuit filed in October 2022.

Several reports have been made on what happened with the deposits of Venezuelan clients of the BOD to whom the resources were transferred to offshore banks such as Banco Orinoco NV of Curaçao, BOI Bank of Antigua and Barbuda, All Bank Corp of Panama and Bancamérica of the Dominican Republic. While executives of the Venezuelan financial group have not given explanations to the public opinion, about what their clients allege, except for the press conference that the president of BOD, Víctor Vargas Irausquin gave in 2019 when the financial authorities intervened the entity and its subsidiaries abroad.

What is known so far about the case are the allegations contained in the lawsuit before the TSJ against the Venezuelan financial group by its clients, who denounce that they have not been able to have access to their foreign currency deposits, which has generated significant losses for them and their families.

The lawyers in the case, Carlos Calderón and Roberto Hung, consider that they are before "one of the most important legal cases in Venezuela, that of the lawsuit for collective rights by depositors of the banks that make up the BPD Financial Group who see their assets at risk".

The following are the allegations and the most important points contained in the lawsuit filed before the TSJ against the BOD:

-Cartera de Inversiones Venezolanas C.A. is the figure that represents and leads the holding company that constitutes the BOD Financial Group, made up of insurance, stock market and banking entities, in addition to four entities of foreign nationality: Banco del Orinoco N.V. of Curaçao, BOI Bank Corporation of Antigua and Barbuda, All Bank Corp of Panama and Banco Múltiple de las Américas (Bancamerica) of the Dominican Republic.

-The operations of each one of these entities are fully linked to each other, with crossed and recurrent operations that imply the transfer of funds between them, taking advantage of the facilities allowed by the offshore banking condition and the restricted banking supervision applied in the different territories where they are domiciled. They had a common international correspondent bank (Novo Banco S.A.) of Portuguese nationality, which facilitated international transfer operations, precisely because it was integrated into a single financial group.

-In practice, the five entities of the BOD Financial Group are related, especially taking into account that three of the banking entities BOD, BDO and BOI, serve portfolios of Venezuelan clients almost entirely, and the remaining two, AllBank and Bancamerica, also have Venezuelan and foreign clients.

-The BOD Financial Group activated from both its physical and human structures, the opening of accounts and transfer of foreign currency to the Group's foreign entities; that is to say, from Venezuela, there was the attraction of Venezuelan customers that make up the deposits in foreign banks, as well as the processing of the opening of accounts, transfer of funds, including those originally made in bolivars in the BOD Venezuela; granting of credits in bolivars with guarantees and backing in foreign currency deposits constituted in the Group's foreign banks and many more binding operations.

"In fact, the great majority of us and of those affected in general, never went to the headquarters or agencies of those banks outside Venezuela, everything was done from here, in the offices of BOD Venezuela", refers the lawsuit.

-Different modalities were used by the BOD under the exchange control regime that came into effect in 2003, to capture funds from Venezuelan citizens and companies with the purpose of transferring them to the different banking entities of the group abroad.

-It also highlights a modality they used to capture foreign currency, which had its origin in 2010 until 2013, which was based on the mechanism established by the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) called System of Transactions with Foreign Currency Securities (Sitme) that allowed individuals and legal entities to acquire foreign currency through duly authorized banking entities (authorized operator as was the BOD), in auctions programmed by the BCV.

"It was through this mechanism that some of us who subscribed here obtained from the BOD foreign currency that was subsequently transferred to the Group's international banks. It is then when the BOD, established as a condition to serve as processing bank and subsequent custodian of the funds in dollars through any of its international banks, that the foreign currency be received by the international entities of the Group where a Fixed Term Deposit (DPF) had to be constituted for a minimum period of one (1) year, a process that was otherwise channeled from Venezuela by the bank's executives", it is stated in the lawsuit.

Once the imposed term of the security had elapsed, that is to say, once the one-year term of the security issued had expired, the DPF was automatically renewed despite the timely notice of the beneficiaries to terminate the investment.

-From 2015 onwards, the funding mechanism of international banks with deposits from Venezuelan citizens and companies was through loan operations and subsequent exchange in foreign currency carried out in the Group's exchange houses. The BOD granted commercial loans in bolivars with collateral on the DPFs that the clients had in the foreign banks, forced in the international banks. Part of the proceeds of these commercial loans in local currency was used for new exchange operations whose proceeds funded the accounts of these clients of the BOD Financial Group in the international banks through foreign currency purchase operations in the exchange houses that are also part of the holding company.

-Another outstanding modality used by the BOD as a mechanism to capture funds in Venezuela and transfer them to its "sister" institutions located in the Caribbean, was the issuance of a guaranteed Credit Card (TDC). It consisted of issuing a TDC backed by BOI Bank with a guarantee deposit equivalent to 150% of its credit limit. This means that the customer had to deposit, for example, $15,000 to receive a TDC with a $10,000 limit.

-The immense liabilities collected from Venezuelan depositors, estimated at a little more than one billion dollars, were used by all the offshore banking entities that make up the Group, "in high risk investments for the time". The vast majority of the foreign currency deposits were converted into investments in public debt bonds of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela or in securities of state-owned companies, specifically in bonds issued by Petróleos de Venezuela , denominated in the US currency and generating interest payable in the same currency, taking advantage of the accelerated trend of public indebtedness of the country since 2007.

"In November 2017 the wheel got stuck. Venezuela could not withstand the fall of its oil revenues and was unable to pay its debts, which resulted in the consideration by the main world financial risk rating agencies of the existence of a state of selective default (selective default) of its public debt securities. It is then that the problems of the entities in the Caribbean that make up the BOD Financial Group dominated by the holding company Cartera de Inversiones Venezolanas C.A. appear; one by one they begin to show liquidity and insolvency problems, from defaulting among themselves the return of deposits and securities in custody", it was indicated in the lawsuit.

-In September 2019, successive legal and administrative processes began in each of the entities of the Financial Group, including that of the BOD in Venezuela, which generated situations of intervention and/or bank liquidation.

title: BOD victims turn to UN human rights system for denial of justice
text:
Legal representatives of 200 clients affected by the intervention and liquidation of four banks abroad owned by Grupo Financiero BOD, continue executing procedures in accordance with the provisions of the UN Human Rights Protection System. The group of people demanding the banker Victor Vargas to return their money is mostly made up of senior citizens from the states of Zulia, Aragua and Carabobo. Others died without having obtained a response to their claim from the TSJ and the Venezuelan State.

Mr. Leal died in 2020 due to problems associated with covid-19. At the time he became ill he did not have sufficient resources for adequate treatment and hospitalization. Since 2017 he lost all the money deposited in one of the four off shore banks of the BOD, owned by Victor Vargas, which were intervened and closed by the banking and financial authorities in 2020.

Precisely in 2017 he and his family realized for the first time that they could not transfer from one account to another, part of the deposits they had in Banco Orinoco NV in Curaçao, so a host of worries began. This uncertainty never calmed down given the answers of the bank employees that went from "they were changing from one correspondent bank to another" and that they should not worry "because the situation was going to be solved". But it never happened.

"We did not have money, at that time of Covid-19, we could hear that people with insurance or wealthy people could be hospitalized in a private clinic, but we had money in Banco Orinoco so that they could take care of him, we could never have access to it. We had to go to several clinics by ambulance and they would not receive him. Thank God we had the help of a doctor friend who offered to help us financially, but his health was already very delicate and in the 15 days he was hospitalized he could not survive", said a relative of Mr. Leal who asked not to be identified.

Mr. Leal's case is one of the 12,000 clients of Banco Occidental de Descuento (BOD) who are still waiting for the delivery of their money deposited in Banco Orinoco NV in Curaçao, BOI Bank in Antigua and Barbuda, All Bank Corp in Panama and Bancamérica (Banca Múltiple de las Américas) in the Dominican Republic.

Many of those affected are individuals who opened accounts at the BOD headquarters in Venezuela, but part of their funds were sent to banks abroad belonging to the holding company Cartera de Inversiones Venezuela C.A., 99.57% owned by banker Victor Vargas Irausquin. The promise of higher returns for their investment in foreign currency in his banks outside the country was the argument to convince the clients; although others were neither consulted nor asked for authorization for the transfer of the funds.

Mr. Leal was a businessman of European descent and decided to distribute his inheritance during his lifetime to his children, who had the misfortune of making a decision whose consequence they never imagined: one of them decided to leave the money deposited in Banco Orinoco and the second in All Bank.

"We and a group of people decided in the first place to file a complaint with Sudeban with the help of Anauco and the lawyer Roberto León Parilli. Now today my family is facing problems, it is costing us a lot to keep what little we have left. I have friends who have helped me with the payment of my children's school fees and all this, without any need, since we have money to which we do not have access and which could solve many of our problems", said one of the members of the Leal family consulted by TalCual.

An unanswered case Lawyers Carlos Calderón and Roberto Hung, representing approximately 200 people, filed in October 2022 a lawsuit for collective and diffuse interests before the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court of Justice (TSJ) against the BOD, as well as against its owner Víctor Vargas and the holding company Cartera de Inversiones de Venezuela C.A.

The group of people demanding that the banker Víctor Vargas return their money is mostly made up of senior citizens, customers from the states of Zulia, Aragua and Carabobo, in the capital city of Caracas, as well as retirees and former employees of the entity itself .

After this legal action, six months passed while waiting for a response from the Constitutional Chamber presided by Gladys Gutiérrez, who is also the president of the TSJ. To date, only the administrative act has been admitted and it has not been decided whether to admit or reject the class action against the BOD. Due to the delay in the response of the highest court of the country within a maximum period of seven days, the case was referred to international courts.

At the beginning of May 2023, the lawyers went to the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (UNHCHR), Volker Türk (who was in Venezuela at the time), to denounce the Venezuelan State for denial of justice. They consider that there is a clear violation of fundamental rights such as access to justice and effective judicial protection.

"We have exhausted the legal channels in accordance with the regulations and the National Constitution. This situation reached its peak and this peak does not allow us to take a peaceful and legal path to resolve a conflict that involves a large number of people. The failure of the TSJ to make a pronouncement led us to go up a step and turn to the human rights protection system to which Venezuela is a party", stated Carlos Calderón.

By going to international human rights instances, the Venezuelan State is responsible, because it has caused a patrimonial damage and has not responded to this cause. The objective is also to take action for the protection of the user and the consumer.

"The articles of the Declaration of Human Rights of the United Nations Organization, which dates back to 1948 and refers to the right of every citizen to have access to justice in a neutral and independent court, are being violated; but the right to property is also being violated. In the face of all this, the Venezuelan legal system has not pronounced itself. There is absolute silence on the case, not even Victor Vargas has gone to court to deny the facts for which he is being sued," said Calderon.

Last Monday, June 26, a new document was sent to the Coordinator of the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights in Venezuela, to the members of the Working Group on the issue of human rights and transnational corporations and other business enterprises, to the Special Rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers and to the UN Special Rapporteur on the promotion of truth, justice, reparation and guarantees of non-repetition.

Lawyer Roberto Hung, specialist in Constitutional Procedural Law, explained that according to the special mechanisms of the Commission on Human Rights, the organization is empowered to send questionnaires to the judicial and financial authorities of Venezuela and of the other countries in which the subsidiary banks of the BOD operated.

The bodies mentioned in the document to which information is requested in Venezuela are the TSJ, Sudeban, the Attorney General's Office, the Autonomous Service of Registries and Notaries (Saren) and the National Bank of Credit; and abroad, the Superintendencies of Banks of Panama and the Dominican Republic, the Central Bank of the Eastern Caribbean, the Central Bank of Curacao and Saint Marten. Likewise, to the Court of First Instance of Curaçao that heard the bankruptcy of Banco del Orinoco and to its liquidator and bankruptcy trustee Michiel Gorsira; as well as to the Central Bank of Uruguay and the Central Bank of Holland.

"In this additional brief that we submitted to the United Nations Human Rights Commission, we added new data related to the custodians of the assets of the subsidiary banks of the BOD, and we asked them to request information from these custodians as well. Three and a half years after what happened, it has not been possible to have access to the investment portfolio held by these custodians", highlighted Hung.

According to the information gathered for the lawsuit, it was learned that there are several custodians related to the BOD, one of them is Welden Securities de Uruguay Agente de Valores S.A., which in October 2020, that is, one year after the bankruptcy of the Venezuelan financial entity and two more years have passed to date, was sanctioned by the Superintendence of Financial Services of the Central Bank of Uruguay for having incurred in irregularities regarding information safekeeping measures according to the regulations applicable in that nation.

After Welden Securities was terminated as a securities broker, it was authorized to withdraw the amounts deposited as collateral and to cancel the pledges and proceed with the corresponding returns.

Regarding the securities custodian agent Vistra International S.A. of Panama, the letter sent to the UN Human Rights Commission states that this company is not recognized as a Vistra International Investment firm, with global presence and operations, "but corresponds to a regular trading company registered in Panama, of which it is not known if it is registered in any financial authority, for which verification tasks are being carried out".

Meanwhile, Farringdon Asset Management, also mentioned as custodian of the securities of the BOD's subsidiary banks, is located in Singapore.

Calderón also indicated that in another of the actions carried out in this case, the lifting of the corporate veil of Cartera de Inversiones de Venezuela, owner of the BOD and its banks abroad, was requested. This figure would allow the company or its shareholders to respond with their patrimony.

"We have been unprotected". On September 19, 2020, the intervention of the banks located in the Caribbean occurred and four days later in Venezuela, the Superintendence of Banks and Other Financial Institutions (Sudeban) intervened the BOD because the patrimony of the Venezuelan entity was affected. Seven days later, another administrative action of intervention took place for violating anti-money laundering regulations, which lasted two and a half years. This process was then lifted to give way to the sale of the entity owned by Victor Vargas to the Banco Nacional de Crédito (BNC).

All this was happening before the eyes of those affected by the BOD, who had the hope that with the negotiation with the BNC, there would be a resolution in their favor, which was nothing more than the return of their lost or withheld deposits. Several of them -by the way- stated that their problems with this bank are of long standing.

Giuseppe Tirrito, whose Italian family arrived in Venezuela and settled in Zulia State, pointed out that his parents opened an account in Banco Maracaibo, which years later was bought and merged by Victor Vargas' BOD. At the same time they kept part of their deposits in the US bank International Bank located in Miami (United States), which belonged to the Venezuelan group. In 1999 they found out that their deposits had been transferred to BOI Bank without having been consulted.

"The only arguments they gave when we demanded an answer as to why they were moving the money without having asked for authorization was that BOI Bank was a better bank and that they were going to give us a better return. They tricked my mother by telling her that they were going to give her a debit card, checkbooks and they never gave her anything", he said.

Tirrito pointed out that despite the fact that they have gone to Venezuelan governmental entities to solve the case, "because they are the ones who protect the citizen and it turns out that this has not been the case, because only Victor Vargas and the BOD have been protected. We have denounced before Sudeban, before the Attorney General's Office. We have been left unprotected".

Approximately 50 people in Maracaibo have adhered to the lawsuit filed before the TSJ. "We never traveled abroad to open an account in this bank, none of those affected by the BOD personally opened an account in the countries where these banks were located", said Tirrito.

In the lawsuit filed before the TSJ, it is stated that it has been known that the BOD has delivered part of the deposits to several of its clients, by negotiating with them a payment in money and/or property, but many of them are companies or legal entities.

William, is another of those affected who lives in the city of Maracay in Aragua State and works as a merchant. He told that after years of being clients of the BOD and when in 2014 they were offered to deposit their money in Banco Orinoco, they never imagined finding themselves in a situation of this type.

"We had a good relationship with the bank and with the bank's managers. In 2017 everything started to go wrong, because when we needed the money we could not access the resources. They told us that they were going to help us and it was all a lie, so in 2019 we sent a communication to the Central Bank of Curaçao and they never gave us an answer," said William, who is a representative of the Asian Community of Maracay-Valencia.

He pointed out that at that time, he and a group of 10 people also in the same situation decided to meet and evaluate the steps to follow. "Several of my countrymen are in this situation.Three of us went to Curaçao to the bank and what they told us was that why ¨jurungar' (review) this issue and, that we had to wait".

The cases of those affected by the BOD have different stories. William commented that one of his acquaintances decided to withdraw his money that he had in a bank in Germany to deposit it in one of Vargas Irausquín's entities and, "he was never able to recover it and that person died. What we see is a lot of liveliness, they are using our money and we don't know where they took it. This is unethical. We want justice. It is a bank that can make its investments, but they should protect their clients' money".

For the lawyer Roberto Hung "we are facing an important case in financial matters, of operations initiated in Venezuela. It is already something systematic, it is not just one person or a group of 100 affected".

He recalled that Venezuela does not currently have a large banking sector, but it is very striking that an entity such as the BOD, located in the stratum of large banks in the country, has carried out actions that affected a large number of customers and that no responsibilities have been established.

Among those affected are also former employees and retirees of the BOD who had a collective contract with insurance plans; as well as shareholders or minority partners.

"As an employee of the bank through an incentive plan that had been developed in the financial institution, we received those incentives in foreign currency. When I left the BOD I was left with practically all of the money held back since 2017, without being able to have any kind of access or from the web page, while the cards were suspended," recounted a former employee of the Venezuelan bank who asked not to be identified.

In his opinion, the case already borders on the affectation of human rights, since he was diagnosed with an illness that kept him in a delicate situation and he could not count on his savings to pay for his treatment.

"It was a very complicated situation and, I lived and knew of other stories of families affected by this case, many also sick with cancer, others who lost their homes and vehicles, merchants who lost lines of credit they had outside the country, foundations that were also customers, in short, various situations. This has been a complex story and unfortunately no one from the bank has shown their face and whether the money exists or not. There is absolute silence".

The former BOD worker stressed that the "issue became a mystery and there is no possibility of calling anyone to ask for information", after the sale of the entity to the BNC, which, by the way, was left with only the assets and "healthy liabilities", that is to say, without the portfolio of the banks abroad. "How did a case of this magnitude come to be in this situation? We are talking about some $1.2 billion. Although the banks where those resources were located were in banks abroad, the holding company or owner is the BOD. All these affected clients are Venezuelan and they arrived there because they were clients of the BOD. It has already been a long time, everything is in limbo, it is as if those banks had never existed".

title: Will the BCV be able to contain the dollar increase? This is what two economists explain
text:
The quotations of the official and parallel dollar once again show an upward trend, passing the 26 and 28 bolivars barrier, respectively.

In the last months -April and May-, the exchange rate had remained stable, due to the banking interventions carried out by the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV), through the use of international reserves. A policy that has been criticized by economists on several occasions.

Economists Tamara Herrera and José Guerra asserted that, despite the efforts of the national Executive to contain the price of the dollar, it is "inevitable" that the trend will continue to rise.

"The national Executive is trying to use less foreign currency and that is why the emphasis is rather on containing (public) spending, administering at its discretion the increases in bonuses and labor bonuses", said Herrera, chief economist of Síntesis Financiera.

This would even be the reason why Maduro did not increase the minimum wage on May 1st. "It is so as not to have turbulent episodes, out of control in July and at the end of the year", he added.

For the economist, "the rise of the dollar is inevitable". However, he considers that what the government is trying to do is to keep the exchange rate "under control, because it is the only way it has to decelerate inflation".

In addition, "the government is using other restrictive instruments to avoid a rise in the exchange rate and to use less foreign currency, but little by little, in spite of the economic slowdown, there are signs of a certain revival in the demand for foreign currency. It may be because of some economic activity or because of some expectation of concern in the market", pointed out Herrera.

Bank intervention of almost $95 million In this sense, the economist and member of the Venezuelan Finance Observatory (OVF), José Guerra pointed out that last Monday the BCV made a bank intervention of almost $95 million, with the purpose of keeping the exchange rate stable.

This would be "the highest figure so far this year in one day and that says a lot about their intention to contain the rise of the dollar", but "my thesis has always been that it is not possible to sustain the stability of the exchange rate for a long time for a very simple reason: the Central Bank does not have the dollars to do so", argued Guerra.

He pointed out that the BCV has resorted to a "mixture of very strong policies", which is based on containing public expenditure and bank reserve requirements, which "prevents the effect of bank credit and obviously the increase of monetary liquidity, but I do not see that it is possible to sustain (the dollar) for a long time and I have been warning about it", he added.

Guerra warned that the instability in the exchange rate will have an effect on inflation in the coming months.

"To stabilize the exchange rate we need resources, dollars, because this is not a problem of bolivars but of dollars. And if it had not been for Chevron and the dollars it is selling, the exchange rate would be close to 40 bolivars per dollar, I calculate, it is difficult to know the level, but clearly it would have depreciated much more", he affirmed.

The economist emphasized that the Executive "is having cash flow problems, despite the fact that it is exporting more barrels of oil. The price of oil has decreased and this reduces its cash flow. They do not have an economic stabilization fund, they did not save in the time of abundance and now they do not have enough foreign currency".

The BCV will continue "squeezing" the international reserves. Both economists agreed that the BCV will continue to squeeze international reserves to curb the rise of the dollar.

"Given how restrictive (the government) is being in fiscal matters -I am referring to spending and taxes- it is looking to spend less foreign currency, allocate less international reserves to that. In fact, we think that 2.8 billion dollars would be enough for the year, which is less than the 3.7 billion dollars allocated last year" in banking interventions, said Herrera.

He clarified that one thing is the amount of foreign currency allocated by the BCV to the national banks and another what the banks manage to sell.

"There has been a lot of bank liquidity and that has required less injection of foreign currency after the strong bank injection made last February, which in a single week was 280 million dollars. After that they dried up the market and with that there are less foreign currency requirements", asserted Herrera.

According to Síntesis Financiera's estimates, so far in 2023, net sales of foreign currency amount to approximately US$ 610 million.

"According to our calculation that US$ 2,800 million would be required, there would still be US$ 2,000 million to intervene, unless they can become much more severe and recessive in fiscal matters", the economist pointed out.

For his part, José Guerra affirmed that the Maduro administration has two ways to control the BCV exchange rate.

"One, they use the international reserves, which is what they have been doing. And two, the dollars that are in Venezuela and the international credit cards, which fall in an account of each bank and then go to the BCV on Mondays to be sold", he explained.

However, in his opinion, none of this is enough if Venezuelans do not recover their confidence in the bolivar, since they continue "repudiating" the national currency, as a result of the economic instability, inflation, devaluation and depreciation.

"Dollar they put in the market, dollar the market swallows", expressed Guerra, who calculated that at least 160 million dollars have been destined to bank intervention so far in May.

How much would the dollar close at in May? Regarding the projections of the amount at which the exchange rate of the official and parallel dollar could close by the end of May, Herrera does not believe that it will reach 30 bolivars per dollar.

"We see that rate at the end of June, assuming that there is a certain normality in the rate of exchange intervention by the Central Bank. Even, depending on how successful this maintenance of such strong bank illiquidity may be, June may pass without passing that barrier (of 30 bolivars per dollar)", he warned.

He explained that the above scenario is in the event that no event occurs that generates "uncertainty or nervousness" in the current economic scenario of the country. Otherwise, "demand will be exacerbated and the price will get out of control", added Tamara Herrera.

Guerra preferred to reserve his estimates, but made it clear that for the rest of the year the trend will be that the depreciation of the national currency will continue.

"I do not dare to say it, I do not have elements and I do not believe that anyone has them to accurately project, but the trend clearly is the depreciation of the bolivar for the remainder of the year. There is no doubt about that", stated the OVF member.

title: Venezuela today: dollarization and a mock "perestroika".
text:
It's boiling in the afternoon in La Candelaria, in downtown Caracas, where a handful of people are crowding to eat. They don't seem to mind the heat of the long black griddle of the cachapas stand (something like a corn flour pancake), nor the prices in dollars hanging on an advertisement on the dusty awning of the cart. It is the current portrait of the proud Bolivarian Revolution.

Venezuela has entered the 21st century, no doubt about it. Gone are the revolutionary political voluntarism (that which in his book on the 20th century Alain Badiou compared to taking a beast by the horns) and its Cuban mirages.

The marks of his absence can be perceived throughout Caracas: Hugo Chávez's eyes no longer spy the destiny of the country from above, nor does red stain bodies and minds as if it were a bloody uniform. And other emblematic projects of the Revolution, such as socialist areperas, Librerías del Sur and abastos Bicentenario, today yield their space to more discreet and profitable businesses, such as restaurants, luxury hardware stores and above all bodegones (that is to say, sales of imported delicatessen).

Venezuela went from being a Cuba with money to a ruined Russia. Where McDonald's closes, an imported supermarket opens.

The model of a gargantuan and irresponsible country that Chavismo built during a decade and a half now looks abandoned, half-built and half-destroyed, since a sad alternative is already emerging from its entrails, like the creature from Alien.

It is the model of contemporary autocracies, whose oligarchies flourish under the blind weight of international sanctions, maintained by a client State. As a fellow writer put it during my visit to Caracas: "Venezuela went from being a Cuba with money, to a ruined Russia".

The metaphor is not fortuitous. In a sort of perestroika, the government of Nicolás Maduro has proposed to make the country's collapse profitable through a double doctrine of uncontrolled imports (that which was called pax bodegónica, that is, to palliate the shortage with products mostly brought from Miami) and capture the spaces of the impoverished middle class, whose flight in recent years has ceded the commercial terrain to new and more ruthless actors.

But the forms change and the spirit remains: where a McDonald's closes, an imported supermarket opens. All within the framework of a gradual de-ideologization of life, from which even the vociferous harangues of the autocrat in Miraflores do not escape.

The elderly, the sick and almost 80% of the country's registered poor are facing the total collapse of the public system on their own.

The green waveThe general mood is one of learned helplessness, of turning the page, of better talking about something else. Faith in the role of politics has been lost. And although there are not a few who observe the present with paradoxical relief, facing the memory of the so-called "hunger years" between 2016 and 2018, it is difficult to know if things are really better.

Far from the slogan that swarms on social networks ("Venezuela got fixed"), the immediate context of the country evidences a brutal economic adjustment.

The elderly, the sick and almost 80% of the country's registered poor (ENCOVI 2022) are facing on their own the total collapse of the public system (hours without electricity, days without water, years without internet) and the micro-privatizations that are offered as the only solution: international health insurance, purchase of water tanks, private satellite services.

Even so, in his Labor Day speech, last May 1st, Maduro asks to "resist" with a minimum wage of 5 dollars a month (130 Bolivars) to an inter-annual inflation of around 500% (Venezuelan Observatory of Finance), and in exchange he promises bonuses calculated in dollars: 20 for the "war bonus" and 40 for the food ticket, laughable figures in a country whose basic food basket was around 480 dollars in February (Cendas-FVM). The crowd, indignant in front of the podium, opposes, booing him. Nothing happens. The silver thread that linked the impoverished masses to the Revolution has become thinner than ever.

In everyday life, meanwhile, the pragmatism of the dollar reigns, which circulates daily alongside the local currency of two different monetary cones, indistinguishable from each other to such an extent that people recognize the current bills by looking at the date of issue of each one.

The old one million bill is worth one; the five hundred thousand, zero fifty. The exchange control and its law of exchange crimes, which prohibited the purchase and sale of foreign currency, are a thing of the distant past: the official dollar rate, which oscillates around 25 bolivars, is announced daily through the Central Bank and is replicated on posters and blackboards next to the cash registers of supermarkets and bakeries.

All products are offered in dollars, even if a patriotic modesty leads to hide such name with euphemisms such as "reference", "ref." or whatever sign they deem appropriate. The Bolivar, in its third reincarnation and with fourteen zeros less than it had in 2000, serves only as a substitute for the cents of the dollar.

Bank cards offer a loan of a few bolivars, that is, a subway or bus ride. The same goes for traditional insurance, medical and funeral, which cover at most a few hundred dollars.

Vintage countryIn this context, consumption is governed by rather suspicious rules. On the same street you can see desolate businesses and the announcement of new ventures, despite the fact that credit is almost non-existent in Venezuela: bank cards offer a loan of a few bolivars, that is, a subway or bus ride. The same happens with traditional insurance, medical and funeral insurance, which cover at most a few hundred dollars.

The price dynamics, however, still wounded by past hyperinflationary spirals -the maximum peak was in 2018 with 130,060% year-on-year (IMF-WB)-, is shown to be more in line with the free market precepts of certain flamboyant "libertarians" swarming in social networks than with the old designs of 20th century developmentalism.

Perhaps that is why the nineteenth-century zeal of Chavismo, its patriotic ruralism and its determination to re-found the pro-independence procerato have become a kind of agonizing trademark. Its faded monigots on murals and avenues, its solemn busts in front of a recent baseball stadium, all of it already exudes the nostalgic whiff of vintage, of the obsolete and outdated.

In the shadows, however, the old trenches of our civil war by installments make peace: the defenders of the public and those of the private shake hands, while the militancy of both sides pretends to be distracted.

Shameless privatizations and discreet state interventions are possible in the Venezuela of the 21st century, as long as the clarion call of the parties is silenced and the new owners of the country are not questioned.

The government itself will take care of that when it is convenient for it, because as the saying goes, firemen don't step on each other's hoses, and the new oligarchy, born in the heat of the revolutionary anvil, has no time to lose: a country hungry for consumption is lining up in front of its cash register and the money in its anxious hands is starting to dwindle again.

The authorGabriel Payares (40) has a BA in Literature, a Masters in Latin American Literature and Creative Writing.

Born in London where his parents did their PhDs, he grew up in Caracas, where he lived until he emigrated to Buenos Aires in 2014.

Winner of several literary awards, author of the books Cuando bajaron las aguas and Hotel, he published in Argentina Lo irreparable (Corregidor), an exquisite volume of short stories.

title: The silversmith who sold BCV to the banks in its 18th  intervention
text:
Meridiano Editorial Staff

The Central Bank of Venezuela(BCV) sold 63 million dollars to banks in its eighteenth exchange intervention this Monday, May 8, 1 million more than in the previous week in anticipation of greater pressures on the market, due to the possible advance payment of the increase of the cestaticket, to the equivalent in bolivars to 40 dollars.

This bet of the issuing entity is to maintain the exchange rate stability, according to the data on the evolution of prices published on Monday, May 8 by the Venezuelan Finance Observatory, and works as a determining factor in the control of inflation.

Read also: Oh Dad! This is the amount that pensioned grandparents will be able to collect once registered in the Patria System.

The price established for this intervention is 27.59 bolivars per euro(EUR), equivalent to 25.06 bolivars per dollar(USD), an increase of 0.99% compared to the quotation of the previous week.

So far this year, the monetary authority has raised 54.88% the value of the American currency it has placed in the banking system, while the official exchange rate has climbed 43.28%, with very contained variations since mid-February.

Read also: Mr. Beast raffles 50 thousand dollars, find out the steps to win them (+DETAILS)

In the first two weeks of May, the Venezuelan Central Bank has intervened in the exchange market with 125 million dollars, 18 million less than in the same period of April. An accumulated so far this year and that stands at 1,470 million dollars, a decrease of 12 million dollars or 0.84% compared to the same period of 2022.

Now, in this 2023, the average amount per intervention is US$59 million, 25.6% lower than the average of US$74 million recorded in the same period of 2022, a situation that is explained by the fact that this year there are fewer extensions and weekly sales were lower in the first month and a half.

title: Economist Luis Oliveros forecasts "couple of months of low inflation".
text:
In the last few weeks, the official exchange rate seems to have stagnated around 24 bolivars per dollar, after the BCVintervened in the exchange market for about $180 million in a single day, last February 13. The stability of the dollar has reduced inflation, as the prices of goods and services tied to foreign currency do not increase as frequently.

Venezuelans could have a break from the incessant increase in prices that has plagued the economy in the last months, since in March there was a deceleration in the monthly variation of inflation, according to studies of the Venezuelan Observatory of Finance (OVF).

With an inflation variation of only 4% for March, economist Luis Oliveros considers that Venezuela could expect a couple of months of low inflation, depending on the context and the incentives that the exchange market may have.

The key, for Oliveros, is for the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) to maintain its foreign exchange intervention policy to keep the foreign exchange market under control, although he warns that it will depend on the amount of money they can inject.

"Inflation in March, according to the Venezuelan Finance Observatory, was a little over 4%, something expected due to, among other things, the minimal variation of the exchange rate. It seems that we have a couple of months of low inflation ahead of us. The key will be whether the BCV has enough foreign currency to inject into the market", he argued.

In the last few weeks the official exchange rate seems to have stagnated at around 24 bolivars per dollar, after months of spontaneous price increases that caused chaos in the national commerce and destroyed the already very low minimum wages in force in the country for the last year.

The stability of the exchange rate has caused the prices of goods and services anchored to the dollar to maintain a certain stability, although the national economy has experienced price increases even in foreign currency.

By the time the price of the dollar began to stagnate, in mid-February, it was reported that the BCV applied the largest sale of foreign currency in the exchange market it has made so far, with .

However, with the scarce foreign currency available to the Government, it seems difficult for them to maintain the constant injection of dollars to the exchange market.

Furthermore, experts have warned that this is a superficial measure, since when the tap of dollars ends, the demand for foreign currency in the market will be much higher than the supply, which will cause an abrupt increase in the price of the exchange rate.

title: BCV narrows the gap between the official dollar and the parallel dollar through bank  interventions  exceeding $540 million
text:
The Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) carried out last Monday, February 13, the largest foreign exchange intervention so far in 2023, with a sale of 180 million dollars to the banking system, according to the calculations of the firm Síntesis Financiera. A measure that continues reducing the gap in the exchange rate of the official dollar compared to the parallel dollar.

According to figures from the consulting firm, last week it was reduced to 1.7% versus 3.9% of the previous week. In part, this is due to the strong exchange intervention carried out by the issuing entity.

"It was a product of the more intense acceleration in the official exchange rate. For the fifth consecutive week, the difference between both markers (BCV vs Parallel Rate) has been reduced", the firm detailed in its Twitter account. In this sense, how much has the BCV injected to the market so far in February, and is the government able to continue sustaining this rhythm? And, what can be foreseen, at least, in the first quarter of 2023?

Tamara Herrera, economist and head of Síntesis Financiera, commented that with the last exchange intervention made by the BCV, it surpassed the allocation it made in the whole of 2022.

"The BCV had been injecting a slightly lower amount than last year, but on Monday 13 (February) it suddenly tripled the allocation and with that it reaches 540 million dollars and exceeds the allocation of 2022 (460 million dollars)", she said.

The economist assured that with this increase the BCV sought three effects: "a) To quickly dry up the bank surpluses available for credit; b) To take advantage of the Carnival week, usually of very low exchange activity and 3) To change the negative expectations by giving some sign of financial strength".

In his opinion, "it is most likely that, given the relative scarcity of bolivars in the economy, the public will not have the capacity to absorb this allocation in the same week".

Furthermore, Herrera reminded that Venezuela is in its usual "tax payment cycle, which generates that relative shortage of bolivars to pay the annual tax liquidation that concludes on March 31. After that date, it will be seen if oil revenues improve enough, after the intervention of PDVSA, to keep the exchange rate moderately contained for the rest of the year".

Economist Herrera warned that "the challenge is not small, because the Asian market is very competitive and because the clean-up of the gigantic corruption that has taken place in PDVSA under the protection of the sanctions will be short-lived if there is no transparency and accountability in the industry".

BCV surpassed US$ 150 million in February The economist and member of the Venezuelan Finance Observatory (OVF), José Guerra, ratified that "Monday 13 was the intervention record", but so far in February the issuing entity surpassed 150 million dollars in foreign exchange intervention.

"This with the purpose of mitigating and moderating the depreciation trend that the Central Bank itself has imposed on the dollar, with the objective of bringing it closer to the parallel", he added.

However, the economist highlighted that so far in 2023, "the Central Bank of Venezuela has lost 273 million dollars of its international reserves. It is the biggest loss in a month and a half in a long time, in fact, last year in the first two months the Central Bank did not lose a single dollar of its reserves, simply because it did not make important interventions", he pointed out.

When asked about the capacity of Nicolás Maduro's administration to continue sustaining the rhythm of exchange interventions and, therefore, maintain the price of the dollar, Guerra was clear: "It is very difficult".

For the economist, "this will basically depend on two things: 1) On the entry of dollars that will have improved and increased due to the exports being made by Chevron, which is already exporting more than 50,000 barrels per day, half of which are being collected, and 2) Most Venezuelans do not want bolivars, so the dollars that enter the market, dollars that disappear, because all those who have bolivars go out to buy dollars, precisely because of the inflation that is accelerating", he said.

In this sense, he insisted that it is very difficult for the BCV to continue sustaining the rhythm of bank intervention. "To lose 270 million dollars in a month and a half is to lose almost 2 billion dollars in the year, a very substantial figure for Venezuela. So, I don't see it as possible", he pointed out.

Furthermore, he considers that if the Government accelerates spending in bolivars, "those bolivars go against the dollar, so it is not easy to stabilize the exchange rate at this time".

For the first quarter of 2023, Guerra calculates that "there will be no stabilization of the exchange rate as long as there is not an abundant supply of dollars", so inflation expectations are very high.

"The enemy of exchange rate stability is not having reserves, that people do not want bolivars, and precisely the high inflation", concluded the economist.

title: BCV sold a record $180 million to banks this #13Feb.
text:
So far this year 2023, the amount of the BCV's foreign exchange interventions has already reached US$ 569 million, i.e., US$ 68 million above the amount sold as of the same date in 2022

The Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) carried out the largest foreign exchange intervention with a sale of US$ 180 million to the banks' foreign exchange desks on Monday, February 13. The purpose is to increase the supply of foreign currency in view of a possible greater injection of liquidity in bolivars to the market, due, among other factors, to the increase in bonds paid through the Sistema Patria.

So far this year, the price of interventions rose 8.46% in a total of 15 foreign currency placements in the banking system, including interventions and their extensions, reported the portal Banca y Negocios.

"The BCV has been making more frequent sales, with the objective of maintaining an adequate level of supply to counteract, by that means, an even greater depreciation of the bolivar", the news portal pointed out.

So far in February, the monetary authority sold 269 million dollars to banks, which allows projecting an important increase compared to the approximately 300 million dollars it placed in January.

In fact, with the record sale of this February 13, the intervention expenditure already reaches 569 million dollars in 2023, 68 million above the figure sold on the same date in 2022.

The intervention strategy seems to be achieving a core objective of the exchange rate plan, which is to keep the official exchange rate competitive, since the gap in favor of the parallel exchange rate was, at the opening of this Monday, February 13, at a meager 2.36%.

The issuing entity increased in 21% the number of foreign currency sale operations to banks, but increased in 252% the amount of foreign exchange interventions in 2022, closing at $5,400 million, an average of $450 million per month, and which reflected a variation of 251.7% compared to the $1,535 million it sold to banks in 2021.

This BCV policy is executed at the expense of its low international reserves and thanks to a timid increase in oil revenues and a significant variation in the price of a barrel of Venezuelan crude oil. According to official figures, the agency's resources ended 2022 at $9,946 million, i.e., below the $10,937 million of the beginning of the year.

According to calculations of local consultants, a good part of the foreign currency resources offered in the official market come directly from the cash of Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA).

The BCV made 52 foreign exchange interventions in 2022, but if extensions are counted, the number of foreign currency sales to banks rises to 82, the highest annual volume since this policy was implemented in May 2019. Despite the BCV's strong intervention, the bolivar depreciated 74% against the dollar in 2022, being considered one of the periods of the highest devaluation of the currency.

title: Why did Sudeban authorize lending 30% of deposits in dollars?
text:
Through Circular No. 00335, dated January 18, the National Superintendence of Banking Sector Institutions (Sudeban) officially authorized banks to grant credits in bolivars on 30% of the portfolio of freely convertible deposits, according to the balance existing in these instruments as of December 31, 2007.

The mechanism established by the regulatory authority determines that "the Banking Institutions may grant credits in local currency to their clients with the resources coming from the fund raising in foreign currency, up to a maximum of resources equivalent to thirty percent (30%) of such fund raising, in such sense the foreign currency corresponding to the referred percentage must be offered in the Exchange Market System (SMC) for subsequent settlement under the different credit modalities foreseen in the Law and the complementary regulations".

Now, what are the reasons behind this measure. The economist and head of the firm Síntesis Financiera, Tamara Herrera, commented that it has several purposes, among them, to increase bank financing without reducing the legal reserve and to relieve the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) of the burden of its cash interventions.Furthermore, according to her, "it seeks to promote the private supply of foreign currency in the exchange bureaus, since the banks that decide to grant the credits must sell the dollars from those deposits".

However, Herrera indicated that the Superintendence of Banking Sector Institutions (Sudeban) has not yet announced or explained "how it will solve the mismatch that the measure may cause in the balance sheets of the banks, which up to now have been quite cautious. In fact, as Executive Vice-President Delcy Rodriguez claimed a couple of days ago, the little use was made of 10% of the deposits in dollars, precisely because the banks are aware that they must replenish those dollars to respond to their depositors", she added.

The economist pointed out that this measure is not the best way to increase the private supply of foreign currency. "We have to bear in mind the prudential rules. The banks have so far acted with this in mind".In her opinion, "it is very favorable to promote the private supply of foreign currency to attenuate eventual upward pressures on the exchange rate, but bear in mind that this supply does not take bolivars out of circulation. The only sale of foreign currency that has the power to do so is carried out by the BCV. This must be kept in mind, given that we know that public spending will have to increase soon".

Venezuelan economy needs between 8 and 9 times more in credits

Economist Luis Oliveros described as "excellent news" that Sudeban approved the granting of credits in bolivars on 30% of deposits in foreign currency, as it was previously at 10%. But, he clarified that the Venezuelan economy needs between 8 and 9 times more in credits than it currently has.

"Of course it is excellent news that credit is increasing in Venezuela. It is an issue that is needed for the financing of growth. Private enterprise advocates, asks, begs and needs financing, but here the discussion is that there is still a long way to go to meet the needs of the economy. There is still a long way to go", said Oliveros.

The economist and university professor explained that "that 20% increase should be around 300 million dollars and that is not going to come in all at once. This does not mean that tomorrow the banks will automatically lend those 300 million dollars".

Credit portfolio growth in 2022 is insufficient

The country's credit portfolio closed 2022 at 13,211 million bolivars, equivalent to 755.77 million dollars, at the official exchange rate released by the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV). An amount higher by US$441.46 million with respect to the credit portfolio of January 2022, when it reached US$314.31 million.

"2022 closed with a solid and strengthened financial system, thanks to the successful strategies of the national Government, led by our President Nicolás Maduro and Vice President Delcy Rodríguez, aimed at the total recovery and economic motorization", said the Deputy Minister of Digital Economy, Banking, Insurance and Securities, Román Maniglia, in his Twitter account.

For Maniglia, this growth represents an "unequivocal sign" that the nation is "on the right track for momentum and growth in 2023".

Despite the "successful strategies" by the Executive, for economists this amount is still insufficient to meet the demand for credit and financing needed by the oil nation to raise national production.

"If you compare with what you had at the beginning of the year, which was less than half, it is undoubtedly a significant amount. However, Venezuela needs up to 15 times that amount. So that amount is still very, very low," said Luis Oliveros, and recalled that the country had as much as $14 billion in the credit portfolio.

Currently, "Venezuela's credit portfolio is the lowest in the entire region", according to the economist, detailing that approximately two thirds of the total loans granted by the banks are commercial, while consumer credit is barely 3%.

Along the same lines, Tamara Herrera explained that when the State reports that the credit portfolio practically doubled in 2022, "of course it sounds like an extraordinary activity, that the percentage element is precisely extraordinary because of the very low level at which it is compared".

However, "being "dazzled" by that figure, for Herrera is not the right thing to do, due to the fact that it continues to be "insignificant" for the national economy.

"Even when the balance quoted is equivalent to 756 million dollars, that is little less than 1% or 2% of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP). The economies that are duly financed by their banking systems at their efficiency, the least one can aspire to is that this coefficient is in the order of 15%, while what is normal in countries where there is an important dynamic and where this streamlining is facilitated, is that you can be on the scale of 20% of the Gross Domestic Product", the economist pointed out.

The head of Síntesis Financiera highlighted that the "biggest headache" of the country's businessmen is the lack of access to financing from the banks and the State, besides waiting for the authorization of foreign currency financing in the local banking market.

"That figure is so insufficient. That percentage increase is so misleading, that even when you see at the end of the year that the growth of the amount of money in circulation in the economy was less than that of the monetary base, which is the result of multiplying the monetary base by the credit multiplier. The credit multiplier fell and that is the only thing that explains why the monetary mass has decelerated and has grown less than the monetary base itself that leaves the Central Bank of Venezuela", explained Herrera.

He added that this represents a weakening of the function of bank credit in the Venezuelan economy and "where there is no credit, there is no production".

Herrera emphasized that the economic team of the BCV "is very afraid of reducing the legal reserve to allow a greater increase in the acceleration of credit for fear that it will lead to a demand for foreign currency and put upward pressure on the exchange rate".

This is the reason why the government of Nicolás Maduro has been restricting the credit portfolio of the national banks for four years, as explained by Herrera.

In his opinion, it is extremely important for the State to promote an "active and much more agile program for the reduction of the legal reserve, so that the banks can make and create more spaces for the facilitation of production".

Otherwise, the economic activity, "whether it is an empanada stand, a bakery, a store or a small, medium or large industrial company, if it does not have financing, everything it has to do to buy inventories, supplies, repairs, expansion of production lines is delayed because they must wait to sell what they have and this is not only subject to the rate of sales, but also to the rate of collection".

title: Maduro again asked the U.S. to lift sanctions against Venezuela
text:
In the midst of a growing social unrest, which since last Monday has included protests in the streets of Caracas and the main cities of the country due to the incessant increase in the cost of living, President Nicolás Maduro described as "dramatic" the figures of the Venezuelan economy and once again asked the U.S. government to lift the sanctions against the country.

The President made special reference to public revenues, which have fallen sharply since Washington and its European allies decreed the embargo on the country's oil exports. "National income fell to dramatic numbers, but it was not that it fell three years ago, today it is in dramatic numbers", insisted Maduro during his annual message to the National Assembly, the Venezuelan parliament.

According to what he stated before the legislators, Venezuela only received 1% of the money that should have entered the country without sanctions. "At this hour that I am speaking to you here, only 1% of what should or should have entered the country entered the country," said the president, a situation he attributed to what he described as a "war" of the governments of the United States and its allies who, as he interpreted it, "sought to establish a foreign intervention" in the country.

Maduro said that since 2015, Venezuela stopped receiving tax revenues for the equivalent of 3,995 million barrels of oil, which he valued at about US$ 232 billion, occasion on which he added that "imperialism and its allies stripped" the country of US$ 400 million dollars a day in that period. "The real war has been waged against the oil industry to try to generate a total collapse and the conditions for a coup d'état and a change of regime", he affirmed.

The head of the Miraflores palace detailed that of the sanctions applied to the country, 42% were directed to government agencies; 18.7% to the oil industry; 17% to the economy and finance sector; and 7% to the private sector. Addressing the US government, Maduro exclaimed: "We do not want more sanctions, lift the criminal sanctions on the Venezuelan people, enough of criminal sanctions".

Maduro gave his account rendering to the parliament in the midst of the massive street protests that started last Monday in Caracas and extended to other cities of the country when workers of several unions, as well as retirees, came out to demand salary increases in the context of an economy that closed 2022 with a retail inflation that climbed to 305.7% measured in bolivars, the national currency, and 53.6% in dollars; according to the Venezuelan Observatory of Finance (OVF) and the firm Ecoanalítica, respectively.

According to the Center for Documentation and Social Analysis of the Venezuelan Federation of Teachers (Cendas-FVM), the total basic food basket, which includes food as well as non-food goods and services, stood at a floor of US$ 474.87 last November for a family composed of two adults and two minors, in the face of a minimum salary of 130 bolivars, equivalent at the beginning of this week to about US$ 7.4, according to the exchange rate of the Central Bank.

"Venezuela has had a growth in 2022 above 15% of the Gross Domestic Product, the highest growth in Latin America and the Caribbean", said Maduro, a dynamic that he explained by the "impact of the diversification of the economy", while he asked public and private banks to grant 30% of their portfolio in dollars to "expand foreign currency financing" to "sectors that produce goods, wealth and jobs".

According to private analysts and the World Bank (WB), in coincidence with the studies of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), the country's economic activity began to fall in 2014, amid the collapse of foreign sales of hydrocarbons and a pressing domestic crisis that worsened after the imposition of a battery of international sanctions in 2019 as part of the crusade led by Washington to seek the fall of the president, after disavowing his reelection in 2018.

With an informal dollarization and the relaxation of exchange controls, the economy had a respite and, after years of recession and hyperinflation that pulverized the purchasing power of Venezuelans, recorded five consecutive quarters of growth between 2021 and 2022. "We are going step by step, it is the real economy that is going and must go better and better," Maduro said, despite the fact that many economists have warned that the recovery is likely to reach a ceiling in the absence of deeper measures.

Maduro, who did not offer data on poverty and indigence, affirmed that the open unemployment rate dropped from 8.9% to 7.8% between 2021 and 2022. In addition, he acknowledged "some disturbances" registered at the end of 2021 which, he said, "destabilized" domestic prices, although he did not detail figures. The latest official data on inflation published by the Central Bank is from October, with a year-on-year rate of 155.8%, half of the approximately 300% measured by private consulting firms, which warn about the possibility of the country returning to the hyperinflationary cycle it left behind in 2021.

title: Alberto Fernández's dispute between federalism and centralism and the challenges for 2023
text:
(By Daniel Scarímbolo) The year of President Alberto Fernández's administration concludes with the ruling of the Supreme Court that issued an injunction for the national Government to allocate 2.95% of the volume of co-participable taxes to the city of Buenos Aires, which reopened the unfinished and constitutive discussion in Argentine history between federalism and Buenos Aires centralism. This ruling is not only detrimental to the fulfillment of the Budget 2023, approved last November in the Congress, but also to the President himself, due to the criminal charges and the request for impeachment by some sectors of the opposition, after the President decided to recuse the members of the Court and to file a request for the revocation "in extremis" of the precautionary resolution issued.

 Beyond this episode, Fernandez worked this year on the post-pandemic agenda, which included changes in the cabinet, with the incorporation of Sergio Massa in the Ministry of Economy; the reconversion of social plans for genuine employment; and the challenges for the last year of government, based especially on the fight against inflation and the recovery of salaries. Massa, who took office last August 3, raised in November the idea of lowering inflation to around 3% by April, at a rate of a decrease of half a point per month. Last month, Fernandez held a bilateral meeting with her Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, within the framework of the G20 Summit in Bali, where she obtained the authorization of the "Asian giant" for Argentina to dispose of US$ 5 billion as part of the Swap mechanism for any kind of commercial use, which will go to the Central Bank reserves to strengthen the currency, essential to reorder the economy in this fight against inflation. During this tour, the President also obtained the endorsement of the Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Kristalina Georgieva, who told him that it is very important for Argentina to maintain the economic course "as it has successfully done" during the last months, and the need to continue working on lowering inflation. Directly related to inflation is the wage recovery. In fact, according to the latest available data from the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (Indec), the wage index registered an increase of 6.7% in September, five tenths above the 6.2% inflation of that month. And on the 22nd of last month, the Minimum, Vital and Mobile Wage Council, made up of the General Labor Confederation (CGT), the Argentine Workers' Central (CTA) and the business chambers, determined a 20% increase in four tranches to reach a year-on-year increase of 110% in March. This will have an impact on pensions, the Universal Child Allowance (AUH) and all those variables that, by different laws, are tied to the minimum wage. In addition to Massa, on October 10, Victoria Tolosa Paz joined the cabinet as Minister of Social Development; Ayelén Mazzina as Minister of Women, Gender and Diversity; and Raquel "Kelly" Kismer de Olmos as Minister of Labor. Tolosa Paz replaced Juan Zabaleta, who returned to the mayor's office of Hurlingham; Mazzina replaced Elizabeth Gómez Alcorta, who resigned after questioning the operation of federal forces carried out by court order for the eviction of the Mapuche community Lafken Winkul Mapu from the land they occupied in Villa Mascardi, where seven women were arrested; and Olmos succeeded Claudio Moroni, who left the position due to personal issues. On November 1, Santiago Maggiotti took over the Territorial Development and Habitat, replacing Jorge Ferraresi, who resigned and returned to the Avellaneda City Hall. And on the 30th of the same month, Diego Giuliano took over in Transportation to replace Alexis Guerrera, who resigned due to health problems. As regards social plans, last November 3, the President signed a decree to advance in the process of linking such assistance with genuine employment, and as from the entry into force of this measure no new registrations were granted in the programs Potenciar Trabajo, Potenciar Inclusión Joven, Nexo and Plus Esencial. The decree "puts a ceiling on the number of Potenciar Trabajo beneficiaries", which is 1,350,000, as indicated by Tolosa Paz in the announcement, and anticipated that there will be about 10,000 monthly withdrawals, whose amounts will go to "the acquisition of machines and tools for the production of goods and services" for the recipients of the plan, or also for the "educational offer and job training". Fernández was also this year president pro tempore of the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (Celac), which on January 24 will hold its Leaders' Summit in Buenos Aires and will meet at the San Martín Palace of the Foreign Ministry. There, the President will deliver the balance of his year in office and will finish his term of office, and "he is not working on his re-election", government sources told Télam. "In any case, it will have to be decided how and who will lead Celac during 2023", they added. As president pro tempore of that organization, he had an interesting intervention in the so-called "Meeting on Venezuela" with his peers from France, Emmanuel Macron; and Colombia, Gustavo Petro; in the framework of the 5th Paris Peace Forum, held on November 11 and 12 in the French capital. There, the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela agreed to return to the political dialogue between the government and the opposition, after the support of Fernández, Macron and Petro, in order to reach a solution in that country, "without intervening" but "bringing Venezuelans closer to finding a way out", according to the Argentine president himself at that time. Negotiations of this type in Venezuela will continue in 2023. As a counterpart to her possible departure from Celac, Fernández assumed in Montevideo, last December 6, the Pro Tempore Presidency of Mercosur, until June 2023, with the challenge of promoting the development of fair and secure supply chains for the productive and economic complementarity of the countries of the bloc, according to sources from the Foreign Ministry. From this position, Argentina will focus on the importance of incorporating science and technology and adding value to exportable products. In addition, it will propose an internal and an external agenda: the first is based on issues such as the customs union, a proactive green program, border integration, migration issues, health and education, among others. The second is based on finding solutions to pending issues with the European Union and negotiations already underway in Canada and Indonesia, in addition to deepening integration in Central America and the Caribbean, and then moving on to Africa. (Télam)

title: Bcvv to  intervene  with a significant amount in the exchange market to contain the rise of the dollar
text: Caracas - The Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) will intervene in the foreign exchange market tomorrow, Friday, for the fourth time during the week, now with the largest amount registered during the last weeks due to the increase in the quotation of the US dollar (USD) against the bolivar (Bs).According to information, the Venezuelan monetary authority will intervene with a very important amount until next week, with the purpose of containing the exchange rate.On Thursday afternoon, the official dollar rate stood at 15.57 bolivars according to the rate of the Venezuelan Central Bank. The rate represents an increase of Bs 0.34 with respect to the previous day when it closed at Bs 15.23.

title: Síntesis Financiera: BCV to increase  intervention  this week to about $160 million but will only mitigate exchange rate rise
text:
Síntesis Financiera calculates that the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) will increase its intervention in the foreign exchange market this week to about US$ 160 million, as opposed to US$ 80 million last week. However, he warns that "it will only be enough to mitigate the increase in the exchange rate".

"Possibly dose it throughout the week. The impact of these allocations is uncertain. The exhaustion of the stabilization scheme has raised uncertainty as to what measures the government may take in the middle of the Christmas season, or at the beginning of 2023," it states in its Twitter account.

The firm recalls that last week the dollar rose 32%, the highest variation of the year, surpassing the record of 27% of the third week of August. So far this month, as of December 9, the price of the dollar has risen 38%.

"The dollar's rise was in crescendo throughout the week, with a BCV lagging behind the exchange market, allocating foreign currency in amounts lower than the market instability claims. It will be difficult to change the course of the exchange rate for the remainder of 2022, given the loss of effectiveness of the instruments used to contain it", assures Síntesis Financiera.

The firm considers that "the official rhetoric, with its usual load of political interpretations to an economic phenomenon, has awakened fears of a return to rigid controls or the deepening of deterrents to the holding of dollars".

Therefore, he concludes that "the only effective way to contain the depreciation of the bolivar is to strengthen the demand for money. The reluctance to hold bolivars is what persistently leads to seek refuge in solid assets, either inventories or dollars, which is almost the same thing given the high imported component of the goods that serve as refuge".

title: Unchecked inflation: Venezuelan  currency  devaluates 17% against the dollar in less than a week
text:
The Venezuelan bolivar recorded a 17% devaluation against the dollar in the last week, whose price has increased rapidly both in the official and parallel markets, where it surpassed 14 and 18 bolivars, respectively, this Friday.

In seven days, the price of the currency in the official market increased 20 %, rising from 11.69 bolivars to 14.12 bolivars, according to the reports of the Central Bank (BCV), which reports daily the average quotation resulting from the operations of the exchange desks of the banking institutions.

In the parallel market, on the other hand, the increase in the price of the U.S. currency, used in most commercial transactions in the country, has been greater, soaring from 13.78 bolivars to 18.26 bolivars, an increase of 32% in one week, according to the Monitor Dólar Venezuela portal, which offers the daily quotation taking into account several markers.

Thus, the bolivar devalued 24% against the dollar quoted in the unofficial market.

Wages and pensions

The minimum wage and pensions, fixed at 130 bolivars last March, have since lost 69% of their value, as a result of the devaluation of the bolivar.

These incomes, at the official exchange rate, went from US$ 29.68 to US$ 9.20, thus sinking the salary and pensions even further, below the extreme poverty threshold per income range established by the World Bank, of US$ 1.90 per day, at US$ 0.30 per day.

Venezuelan economist and associate professor at IE University in Madrid José Manuel Puente told EFE that the Caribbean country's impoverishment "has been overwhelming, a consequence of the government's very poor economic policy management," even in the midst of rising oil prices.

"Venezuela is in the midst of an oil boom, a consequence of the Russia-Ukraine war, in which Venezuelan oil prices, which reached 92 dollars, today are in the order of 70 dollars, but it is still an extraordinary price for Venezuela to be experiencing these terrible exchange imbalances with terrible impacts on wages", he explained.

The strategy

The Madurist dictatorship has been applying a strategy to contain the exchange rate which consists of controlling the demand for dollars, reducing the issuance of bolivars -necessary to buy foreign currency- through the reduction of public expenditure and the restriction of financing.

However, in the last months, the Venezuelan regime increased spending with several payments to public workers, at the same time that it has been releasing credits, which increased 123 % in the last year.

For his part, economist and university professor Ronald Balza Guanipa told EFE that the Central Bank has increased "the issuance of bolivars for government spending" in "activities it is carrying out at the moment" that are unknown, in addition to the payment of Christmas bonuses to public sector employees.

At the same time, he pointed out that the BCV has also reduced the sale of foreign currency with which it had been feeding the supply to contain the exchange rate.

However, according to Balza Guanipa, it is difficult to know what the supply of foreign currency is due to the fact that it is not known how many dollars are circulating or how many are entering the nation from the sale of oil and other exports due to the lack of official data.
