title: Inflation in Venezuela Reached 21.9 % in November, Says Independent Entity
text:
Inflation in Venezuela in November was 21.9%, 7.4 percentage points higher than in October, according to data released Monday by the Venezuelan Finance Observatory (OVF), an independent entity outside the country’s Central Bank.

The accumulated inflation for the first 11 months of the year rose to 195.7%.

The OVF stated that this acceleration of inflation occurred in a context of a “significant” depreciation of the bolivar, estimated at 43%, and a “loss of reserves of 1,154 million dollars” between November 2021 and 2022.

“This suggests that the BCV’s (Central Bank of Venezuela) policy of interventions in the exchange market to stabilize the exchange rate has lost effectiveness and fails to contain the rise in prices, while at the same time generating a drain on the BCV’s reserves,” he added on Venezuela’s inflation.

The sectors with the highest increases in November were leisure at 30.4 %; goods and services at 27.9 %; education at 29.4 %; and clothing and footwear at 27.5 %.

Likewise, the OVF indicated that the cost of the food basket, calculated for a family of five, was 366 dollars, while the “minimum salary remains at 130 bolivares (11.62 dollars)”.

“The existing salary gap has been impacted by the increase in the exchange rate. Thus, while the average payment in the Metropolitan Area of Caracas stands at 120 dollars per month for the private sector, in the public sector it reaches only 11 dollars per month,” added the entity, made up of former congress members and economic experts.

Venezuela emerged last December from hyperinflation which started in 2017 and went on for four years to reduce the value of the bolivar, the official currency, as well as citizens’ trust in it, so they unofficially adopted the dollar in an attempt to protect their income.

title: The Venezuelan economy in 2023 "hangs on a license".
text:
The decision of the US Treasury Department to relax Chevron's license will decide the fate of the Venezuelan economy for next year, and not only because of the impact on oil production but also on inflation, devaluation and consumption. Projections by Síntesis Financiera and Ecoanalítica coincidentally point to a growth for 2023 of 4% without the license and a maximum of 12% with the approval of OFAC announced on Saturday 26th.

Analysts pointed out that in order to estimate the behavior of the Venezuelan economy in 2023, it was necessary to wait for a decision from the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), a body that depends on the U.S. Treasury Department, involving a relaxation of the oil sanctions against PDVSA or at least a new license to Chevron with extensions to operate.

And no wonder. Oil production has been the main engine of the country's economic activity, so after the debacle of Petróleos de Venezuela due to years of disinvestment and diversion of resources, the country was plunged into an eight-year recession, which deepened with the U.S. sanctions against the industry.

This is how the government of the U.S. company Chevron Corporation to expand its operations in Venezuela, as early as Saturday, November 26, when a new round of dialogue between the administration of Nicolás Maduro and the Venezuelan opposition began. This Thursday, December 1, Chevron's General License 8 expires, so expectations on the subject were increasing.

This measure of the Treasury Department will decide the fate of the Venezuelan economy by 2023, not only in terms of oil production, but also in terms of inflation, devaluation and consumption.

The director of the consulting firm, pointed out that the expansion of Chevron's operations in the country would obviously contribute to increase production, but she does not expect it to be a significant figure. Nevertheless, it could lead the Venezuelan economy to an expansion of 8.7% for next year. He maintained that if the license to the North American oil company was not approved, the growth would be 3.5%. These figures, however, are still modest if one takes into account that the country lost 80% of its size in a period of eight years.

"With the license extension, the increase in oil production will be slow and moderate. But we believe that the barrels of Venezuelan crude exported by Chevron will be made without discount," he said in a speech given at a forum of the Venezuelan Real Estate Chamber.

The report highlights a 14% result for the local oil sector after the OFAC measure, an average production of 785,000 barrels per day (b/d) and an oil export of 586,000 b/d, for a total amount of income of US$ 11.4 billion at a price of US$ 53 per barrel.

Síntesis Financiera's projections are in line with estimates that pointed to 2023 growth of 4% without a license and a maximum of 12% with OFAC approval. "We believe that in the event that the United States grants a license to oil companies that allows them to expand their operations in the country, Venezuela can grow between 10% to 12%. A slowdown will occur if no measures are taken and no agreements are reached regarding the country's oil situation", said recently Asdrúbal Oliveros, director of the local consulting firm.

Tamara Herrera recalled that Chevron's resources obtained from its crude oil exports will very possibly amount to $3.2 billion at a rate of approximately $78 dollars per barrel.

If the license had not been approved with new guidelines, the figures would change drastically. In this sense, production would continue the decline it has had in recent years, to 677,000 b/d on average for all of 2023, as well as an export of 516,000 b/d and an income of $9 billion to a barrel heavily punished by the discount at $48.

"By extending the license to Chevron, greater transparency and better prices in the volume exported by this company will be observed, but also possible positive externalities in the Venezuelan oil industry and, consequently, a recovery of expectations and a sequel of licenses to other companies", stated Herrera.

On the other hand, he maintained that if the license had not been granted, "the country's economic activity would slow down or would depend only on the anomalous impulses of the so-called black economy".

In his opinion, the national oil industry "has not been able to take advantage" of the current world energy crisis, which has generated high fuel prices.

The Venezuelan economy stopped falling from the end of 2021 and in 2022 it has maintained positive rates, however, for Herrera this year has been a period in which "the set of positive factors that generated the recovery was exhausted and metabolized". Among these factors he points out, the end of the pandemic, the pragmatic easing of the economic policy in practical but not legal terms.

"The positive effect of the dollarization process, for example, was halted because the government itself at the beginning of the second quarter introduced the reform of the Large Financial Transaction Tax, which," he said.

No license for hyperinflation The global economic environment will also have an effect on Venezuela in 2023. The director of Síntesis Financiera pointed out that the global recession will have an impact on remittances, which have been a determining factor for Venezuelans' income. For next year, this factor of remittances together with the persistent inflation in the local economy, will generate a lower consumption among Venezuelans.

"The rhythm in the volume of remittances to Venezuela has been slowing down due to several aspects: the terrible conditions in which many migrants are currently, many families have reunited outside the country and therefore the needs of remittances are different and the recession is affecting everyone".

On the other hand, he emphasized that another important element that is changing is the speed with which the speed of salary increases in the private sector is losing strength, and therefore "consumption, which is the engine that allows to dynamize the economy, is also slowing down".

He maintained that a lower income in foreign currency for the country and a political environment that demands more public spending, will accentuate the monetary financing of the deficit, which is largely responsible for the hyperinflation process experienced by the Venezuelan population. He considers that oil revenues continue to decline and therefore the key tool that has been the foreign exchange intervention has been weakened due to the decline in revenues.

"In 2023, the intervention of the BCV (Central Bank of Venezuela) will be the mainstay of the exchange rate policy, but there are concerns about its sustainability. If the pressure on the exchange rate continues, we would enter a scenario close to hyperinflation", said Herrera.

He explained that the anti-inflationary policy of Nicolás Maduro's administration has exhausted its effectiveness, due to the fact that decelerating public expenditure "has become unfeasible", while tax collection in real terms is growing, but is insufficient. On the other hand, he said that the BCV's open market operations (Currency Hedging Securities) have not yielded positive results and "indexation creates a dilemma for the issuing entity itself".

The positive aspect of the license for the exchange market is that by expanding its operations in the country, Chevron will have to sell part of its foreign currency obtained from exports to meet its commitments in bolivars, which will alleviate the pressure on the US currency. However, it must be remembered that the process of recovery of the oil fields in which the company manages together with Pdvsa will be slow, it will also have to deduct from the income from exports what is owed by its partner and the Treasury will not receive royalties or taxes corresponding to the oil activity.

title: How much will the price of the dollar reach by the end of 2022? This is the opinion of economists
text:
So far in 2022, the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) has injected around 150 million dollars to banks, with the aim of containing the rise of the official dollar, but how feasible and lasting can these exchange interventions be in view of the fall of international reserves and the decrease in oil production.

Economists consulted by HispanoPost agree that the lack of official data from the government of Nicolás Maduro makes it increasingly difficult to make estimates. However, they calculate that the dollar could close by the end of the year, between 10 and 15 bolivars.

"How much the dollar will close at in 2022, nobody knows, not even the Central Bank itself knows. I have seen many estimates that speak of between 10 and 12 bolivars, but this is speculation. What is clear to me is that it will go up in the remaining months, because the Central Bank of Venezuela cannot sustain the intervention indefinitely, because it has lost a lot of reserves", said economist José Guerra, member of the Venezuelan Finance Observatory.

Even, for economist Manuel Sutherland, it is probable that the dollar rate could double. "It could reach 15 or 16 bolivars, depending on the difficulties that the government has to finish paying bonds and important labor commitments, as well as suppliers for the end of the year".

The distortions in the exchange market make economist and director of Ecoanalítica, Alejandro Grisanti, question whether the BCV will be able to maintain the exchange rate until December: "It seems that it will devaluate, that it should close in a range of 10 and 13 bolivars per dollar for this year and it will depend on to what extent they will really unleash in the economy".

"That is to say, the lower it closes, which is closer to 10 bolivars, we are talking that the exchange rate is going to have greater expressions and greater probabilities of devaluation in the first quarter of next year and to the extent that it closes closer to 13 bolivars, it would go very much in line with what we are expecting in inflation", added Grisanti.

Likewise, university professor, economist and member of the National Academy of Economic Sciences, Leonardo Vera, recalled that in Venezuela there is no statistical basis of how the real economic activity has evolved, because the Central Bank of Venezuela stopped publishing this data since the first quarter of 2019.

"It is difficult to make projections, due to the fact that volatility is much higher. Today we are seeing a quotation between 8 and 9 bolivars per dollar in the informal markets and it would not have any time that at the end of the year this could be in 10 and 12 dollars, if there is no special event", commented Vera.

Christmas bonus payments: will the dollar have an impact? The devaluation of the bolivar has caused Venezuelans to lose confidence in the national currency and seek refuge in the dollar. Last August the exchange rate, both official and parallel, soared partly due to the amount of bolivars in circulation, following the payment of the holiday bonus due by law to the country's teachers.

This led us to ask economic experts whether the payment of Christmas bonuses to be paid by the Maduro government to public employees could generate a new impact on the price of the dollar.

Leonardo Vera explained that the measure taken by the State to pay Christmas bonuses to public administration workers in four parts "will perhaps help it to lighten the pressure on the exchange market, because let's say that it gradually reduces the pressure that the excess of liquidity may generate in the exchange market".

However, for José Guerra, the payment of the Christmas bonuses will have an effect regardless of whether they are paid in installments or in full. "They are doing this at the cost of an impressive loss of international reserves, between December last year and October 14, 2022, they have lost more than 920 million dollars, which is the highest figure in the last three years".

Guerra added that "on the one hand, it increases the demand for products and, on the other hand, it also puts pressure on the exchange rate, because when the pensioner spends, commerce wants to replenish inventories and, obviously, this translates into an expression of the demand for goods and dollars. I do not think it will be much, because the Christmas bonuses are not a significant amount and, in addition, they are being paid in a fractioned manner".

Alejandro Grisanti also estimates that this pressure of bolivars that will be seen in the payment of Christmas bonuses in the Venezuelan economy could have an impact on the exchange rate of the dollar.

"In order to maintain this exchange rate stability, which is not desired, but it seems that the government needs it, it is going to have to sell foreign currency for some 600 million dollars in November alone and an additional 400 million dollars in December. But, once again, the question here is whether this is the most efficient use of foreign currency or whether it should be used and spent in other areas that may be more important than burning dollars to maintain an artificially low exchange rate", the economist reflected.

Sutherland emphasized that "it is evident that there is a very large fiscal gap. In addition, the State does not have enough income and what it does is to issue money without backing, artificial money, which when it enters the national stream, causes inflation because it is a monetary injection without real value, but purely artificial".

The economist emphasized that "the economy is extremely small and the amount of bolivars circulating in the economy is extremely low. The entire monetary mass could be equivalent, more or less, to some 1,500 million dollars or a little less than that".

For Sutherland "the problem is that this exchange rate, artificially low, creates very big distortions in prices and makes the prices in foreign currency go up, reduces the competitiveness of the industry and national production, prevents the export of anything other than oil, makes oil exports yield much less than they should in Venezuela and only benefits a caste of importers who live off this differential".

Are international reserves at risk? Economists warn that the financial policy managed by the government of Nicolás Maduro to maintain the price of the dollar is not enough to alleviate the financial crisis that the country is going through and puts the international reserves at risk.

Guerra assured that "the government has a very limited capacity because the liquid reserves of the Central Bank are very low, of 4.8 billion dollars, because it is worth remembering that they report that they have 9.9 billion dollars, but we have to subtract 5.1 billion dollars which are special drawing rights assigned by the International Monetary Fund, which are not reserves because they are not liquid. They are not available and a good part of the liquidity is gold".

Grisanti described that what has happened in the last three years, where inflation has been much higher than the devaluation, "what you end up having is an increase in the cost of living, an increase in the price in dollars and a lower purchasing power".

Vera ratified that as long as oil revenues and foreign currency revenues maintained by the Venezuelan State do not increase significantly and the liquid reserves held by the BCV remain at such low levels, the economic instability in the country will continue.

"This scenario could only change substantially, if and only if, for example, Venezuela obtains the 5,000 million that are trapped in the International Monetary Fund, by way of special drawing rights and that should, under normal conditions, have been distributed to Venezuela, just as they were distributed to the different member countries of the fund many months ago. This would help to feed the international reserves and with this the Central Bank could become very creative when intervening in the exchange market", said Vera.

Manuel Sutherland emphasized that "we are at the historical minimum, without a doubt, in terms of total reserves and import capacity", for which he qualified as an "error that the BCV adds the special drawing rights, which are in the International Monetary Fund, as if they were its own international reserves".

Economic growth projected for Venezuela Despite the financial circumstances the country is going through, economists project that Venezuela's annual economic growth could be around 7%, as estimated by the International Monetary Fund and the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC).

"There are some indications that the growth rate of the first semester could be a little higher than the second semester, because the oil activity has not advanced much more in the second semester of this year and it seems that the advances registered at the beginning of 2022 compared to the beginning of 2021 augured a more or less good recovery of the oil sector and already towards the second semester of this year that is not what is being seen", said Vera.

In this sense, Sutherland pointed out that "most of the estimates say that it is quite probable that the Venezuelan economy will grow between 10 and 12 percent. I believe it could be a little less, due to the inflationary rebound, the drop in oil production, among other factors. The economy could close 2022 with a growth between 7 and 9 percent".

title: The parallel dollar fell on Friday to 8.56 bolivares
text:
