title: Plataforma Unitaria blamed Maduro for the devaluation: "it continues to impoverish Venezuelans".
text:
The Unitary Platform blamed this Wednesday the regime of Nicolás Maduro for the devaluation of the bolivar registered in the last few days, which "continues to impoverish the Venezuelan family".

Economist José Guerra, member of the Governance Agreement Commission of the Unitary Platform, assured that the devaluation of the bolivar is due to the lack of confidence Venezuelans have in this currency.

Guerra specified that, in view of the accelerated inflation, citizens acquire goods or foreign currency to protect their income. "When a currency is devaluating, it is because the public wants to get out of it", he stated.

"The policy followed by Maduro's Central Bank of Venezuela of interventions in the exchange bank has resulted in a loss of more than 750 million dollars between January of this year and August 19. The Central Bank has no way to withstand the demand for dollars because it simply has no supply of dollars", he explained.

He added that this is a unique case in the world of an oil country that is not accumulating international reserves in the form of dollars but rather is losing them.

Guerra pointed out that the problem does not reside in the fact that the payment of bonuses and salaries to workers is pressuring the exchange market, but that the devaluation is due to the "loss of confidence in the national currency; first due to the hyperinflation experienced up to January of this year and then due to the inflation which is still high".

Guerra pointed out that the solution to the Venezuelan crisis must be a political change and an economic change, stressing that new policies must be generated to generate confidence in investors, which in turn will reestablish the purchasing power of Venezuelan workers and that employment will flourish.

Finally, he suggested that "together with this, a program must be designed to increase oil production. Currently 650 thousand barrels per day are being produced; Venezuela can produce in the medium term close to one million five hundred thousand barrels of oil, increase incentives for agriculture and cattle raising, and above all that the Central Bank does not continue to issue inorganic money".

title: Parallel dollar continues to rise, reaching Bs 6.42 and experts predict more inflation
text:
As a result of the exchange intervention policy implemented by the Government to influence the price of the parallel dollar, the country's international reserves have fallen by more than $500 million since December 2021.

The relative stability that the exchange rate has maintained during the last year seems to be about to be broken, since in the last quarter there has been again a galloping depreciation of the bolivar against the US dollar, which this Wednesday, August 17, reached the price of Bs 6.42.

During the last quarter there was an increase in the parallel exchange rate, which went from being valued at Bs 4.62 to Bs 6.42 per dollar, according to publications of the Venezuelan Central Bank. This translates into a 28% increase in only three months.

In contrast, in the first six months of the year there was no increase. In fact, there was a slight appreciation of the bolivar against the U.S. currency, falling from Bs 4.71 to Bs 4.62 per dollar.

This increase of the parallel dollar causes an ever greater disparity against the official exchange rate, since the Central Bank of Venezuela establishes it at Bs 5.97 per dollar. This means that the Monitor Dólar Venezuela marker is 7.5% higher.

In other words, to pay a $100 bill, Bs 597 would be needed if the merchant charges at the official rate, but Bs 642 if the parallel rate is applied. That is a difference of Bs 45 between both payments.

Economist José Guerra, founder of the Venezuelan Finance Observatory (OVF) and deputy to the National Assembly in 2015, warns that inflation will continue its course, so it is likely to observe a greater movement of the parallel rate in the coming months.

During the last year, Guerra and other economists have warned that the strategy applied by the BCV to try to contain the exchange rate was unsustainable, since they injected money from international reserves into the exchange market to increase the supply and maintain the price.

As a result of this policy, since December 2021 there have been losses of more than $500 million of the international reserves, which have fallen from $5,886 million to $5,330 million (discounting the $5,000 million added by the BCV that actually correspond to the Special Drawing Rights that the International Monetary Fund has pending to be assigned to Venezuela).

"The strategy of the BCV and the Government to intervene (the exchange market) by selling dollars was exhausted due to the sharp fall of the BCV's international reserves, as seen in the chart. It was only a matter of time", reasoned Guerra.

The economist added that a second element adds pressure on the exchange rate. He referred to the fall in oil prices and exports, which translates into less money for Venezuela and therefore a lower capacity to inject dollars into the exchange market. "Inflation is going to increase", he asserted.

According to estimates by economists such as Asdrúbal Oliveros, director of the consulting firm Ecoanalítica, the equilibrium exchange rate -which does not take into account the distortion of supply and demand- is around Bs 22, almost four times the official exchange rate.

title: The government does not  intervene  in sales to  Venezuela  and there are no risks: mincomercio
text:
Mauricio Galindo - Economics Editor @galmauGermán Umaña, one of the ministers of the new government, is beginning to move forward with an agenda as rich as the name of his portfolio: Trade, Industry and Tourism. In this conversation, the new minister explains several aspects of these tasks, among which stand out the idea of reviewing trade agreements and recovering the voluminous trade that took place in the past with Venezuela. Umaña explains the points in which there may be unequal conditions in trade agreements and the possible ways to try to correct those situations in which it is not possible to compete on equal terms with the producers of Colombia's partner countries. He also refers to tourism and how to maintain the momentum of these activities, after the tax reform project contemplates removing the existing tax incentives. In your campaign you proposed to seek changes in the FTA with the U.S. What is the way forward?

 We are evaluating the results of internationalization in Colombia. We have to look at it over the last 30 years. Since the opening in the 90's; then came the need for certain countries to propose bilateral negotiations. This negotiation methodology began as a World Trade Organization Plus, in which there are at least three major agreements: the first one Colombia signed was what was called the G3, which later became the G2, with Mexico. Then, with the United States, and later, the association agreement with the European Union. Where would this evaluation lead to? The result is asymmetrical because with subsidies, domestic support and other measures of equivalent effect that Mexico, the European Union and the United States kept alive and apply, there is an imbalance. If one has subsidies and the other does not, there is no price competitiveness. We import millions of tons of food, which is neither bad nor good, but what they cannot tell us is that we are not competitive because it turns out that it is not a problem of competitiveness, but of subsidies. Once these imbalances have been gauged, what is the way forward? We have to analyze what we are going to do, not tariffs, that is not true. That will go to inflation. We are seriously analyzing how to recover a minimum of food sovereignty; how to apply the rules of international trade and its limits in order to put the agricultural sector under equivalent conditions. To strike a balance between imports and domestic production needs under competitive conditions. And that has two components, some internal measures, in consultancy, technical assistance, seeds... and a talk on how we can balance the injustice, with the European Union, with the United States and even with Mexico, although it is not so dramatic. Apart from agriculture, where else are there imbalances? In services, because only those that are the product of the fourth industrial revolution, of transportation, are liberalized. And why is there no liberalization of professional and business services? They should be liberalized because that is our offer. Why have the fundamental rights to education and health remained in these agreements as goods and not as fundamental rights? Everything that has to do with arbitration tribunals, such as the International Center for Dispute Settlement. It cannot be that we are about to be condemned because we denied the environmental license. They first gave the mining license to exploit Santurbán. In these agreements it is possible to put the exploitation of coal above environmental rights. They are not going to call you a protectionist. They are not going to tell you that you are against the free market. On the contrary, what I am saying is that there are market failures derived from these agreements. How does the assessment you are making affect new agreements? They were negotiating with the United Arab Emirates and, whatever it was, they were going to close it. But despite the fact that Colombia, but especially President Duque, whom I esteem and respect very much, wanted to sign that agreement, the Emirates did not want to sign it. It was an imperfect agreement, with problems especially in the origin. We will have to see how the agreement is, how far they have advanced, and see if it is worthwhile for them and for us to continue with that negotiation. As President Duque said at the time -although he denied it with the Arab Emirates, I don't know why-, no more free trade agreements will be signed until that evaluation is made. What is coming for tourism? We are playing with perfecting and fulfilling the peace agreements. A dream that can become a reality in spite of what has happened in the last four years. And those peace agreements are fundamental in the most forgotten but most promising areas of the country. In the Amazon, in Guaviare, in Vichada, everything is tied to the possibility that these peace agreements are supported by investment, by crop substitution, by the development of infrastructure, and to be able to combat drug trafficking. One kilometer that we recover from the roads or 100 square kilometers of crop substitution are a thousand square kilometers of territories for sustainable tourism for the indigenous communities, for the black communities, for the peasants. To convert tourism, little by little, in the substitution of many of the foreign currencies generated by the extractive sector. How does the end of tax incentives for certain tourist activities influence? Look, possibly there will be things to improve, but it is not the hotel business that is important. What is important is that the progressiveness of the tax reform will contribute to eliminate exemptions in many sectors that are not allowing inequality to decrease. The tax reform is to be able to respond to social, infrastructure and security needs in conflict zones. All the resources of the ministry, which are not large resources, but are important because of their multiplying effects, are going to be dedicated in the area of tourism to large projects in the peace zones and in the areas with more difficulties. The ministry is going to promote, develop and make clear policies, but not to build big hotels or to give exemptions, but for the development of sustainable tourism. What are your expectations regarding trade with Venezuela, which reached 8,000 million dollars? Of course, we had a trade of US$ 8 billion. In 2020, legal trade dropped to 220 million. Legal trade this year (if the border is not opened, which it will be) will be $650 million. Once the border is opened, we will replace illegal trade with legal trade. Without any problem we can say that this year with Venezuela we will have minimum 800 million dollars in bilateral trade, that is still 10 percent of the best time, but do not forget that the Venezuelan gross domestic product fell between 2015 and 2020 by about 75 percent. In 2021 that gross domestic product recovered, and this year they are going to have growth of 20 percent. To the extent that the demand in Venezuela recovers and we also demand Venezuelan products to balance the trade balance, trade is going to grow and we think, from the analysis we have done, that we are talking for the year 2023 about 2 billion dollars and at the end of the government of our President Petro we are going to reach levels of 4.5 billion dollars, 60 percent of what was the best time, but we really have to be clear that this depends on the recovery and balance of the economy. And at the moment, how are the payment mechanisms for exporters? In the payment mechanisms there is no influence of the government, of the Central Bank, because there are sanctions to the Central Bank. What there is is a supply and demand in dollars through the exchange bureaus and there the daily exchange rate is fixed. Seventy-five percent of those dollars go to the domestic market, because the Venezuelan economy has a high degree of dollarization, but 25 percent is for export payments. From the point of view of exchange control it no longer exists, and there are mechanisms for payment, especially those of the banks, in the money desks that they send to their sister banks. It is usually sold in advance, and there is no risk. Of course, entities such as the Colombian-Venezuelan Chamber do due diligence. Now, what is bought and what is sold is fluid.

title: BCV significantly lowered foreign  currency  sales to protect international reserves
text:
The BCV slowed down its rate of foreign currency sales to banking exchange desks in order to safeguard the already depleted international reserves. In spite of the foreign exchange intervention, the price of the dollar continues to rise and remains at the new ceiling of 6 bolivars.

The foreign exchange intervention policy of the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) continues to have limitations. Despite the increase in foreign currency inflows to the country, due to the rebound in oil prices, the international reserves are not enough to keep the exchange rate at bay.

The BCV considerably reduced its sale of foreign currency to the banks' foreign exchange desks, going from 100 million dollars per week to 60 million dollars, but it also divided the delivery of foreign currency in two parts.

The consultant's data indicates that on Monday, August 1st, the Central Bank allocated a little more than $45 million and on Wednesday, August 3rd, it complemented with $15 million, achieving small reversals in the exchange rate in those two days of 0.3% and 0.1%, respectively.

In spite of the fact that the price of the currency has had a lower growth rate since last year, due to the monetary policy implemented by the issuing entity to restrict liquidity, its quotation in the exchange system reached the 6 bolivars ceiling. While the BCV's exchange rate has not reached this ceiling, it always follows in its footsteps.

Since January 29, 2019, the BCV started its exchange intervention plan with the purpose of "achieving stability in exchange and monetary matters and stopping hyperinflation".

The measure is based on the fact that the agency injects foreign currency and withdraws the necessary bolivars to the banking entities, in order to maintain the defined exchange rate target. Since the beginning of the exchange interventions, it was decided that they would be weekly,

Economist José Guerra recently recalled that the inconsistency of the economic policy based on a fiscal expansion and an expansion of inorganic money by the issuing entity, in a context of exchange control with a fixed preferential rate since 2007, was depleting the international reserves and giving way to the economic collapse of the country.

In addition to this, he warned that the BCV has "excessively burned reserves" in a clearly wrong policy to contain devaluation and inflation.

"If the Central Bank perceives that this inflation is a transitory phenomenon, that the currency is depreciating due to a circumstantial factor, the correct thing to do is to intervene and sell foreign currency to stabilize this inflation. But if the trend is permanent, because the exchange rate is depreciating due to the fact that people do not want the local currency, the right thing to do is not to intervene because, if you intervene, you start to deplete the reserves," Guerra said .

Tamara Herrera, director of Síntesis Financiera, explained that central banks have instruments to control the monetary mass and in the case of Venezuela, the availability of bolivars in the money market; but they do not have instruments in dollars because they do not issue in that foreign currency. "The difference is in how they do it", he said.

With this statement he hints that if positive results are not obtained in the execution of the monetary and exchange policy, people will continue to look for foreign currency for the protection of their resources.

"Everyone, whether a company or an individual, every time they have a surplus in bolivars, they continue to look for hard currency and the reason is merely transactional, because the propensity and the need for imports continues to increase. Also for hedging purposes, until it is not convinced or the very slow stabilization that is being sought is not achieved", stated Herrera.

Guerra reiterated that for any nation, not having sufficient reserves "is a very serious problem", since it cannot meet its foreign debt commitments and for the payment of imports.

"Why is it that even though the price of oil is at an all-time high, the BCV, instead of gaining and accumulating international reserves, is losing them? Something does not add up, where are the reals, asked the economist.

According to figures from the consulting firm Ecoanalítica, the administration of Nicolás Maduro has 154% more income in foreign currency in the year 2022. In addition to an inter-annual increase of 104.5% of the equivalent tax collection in dollars.

In its report, Síntesis Financiera pointed out that the agency did not intervene in the exchange market when the increases were more intense: 0.9% and 0.4% on Thursday, August 4 and Friday, August 5.

"In short, it tolerated an acceleration of the rate of depreciation to 1.3% in the week, compared to 1.1% in the previous week and 0.6% in the week before that," the consulting firm pointed out.

The BCV's international reserves have remained at around US$10 billion. According to the last figure shown in its web page of August 8, they closed at $10.3 billion. This amount means a drop of $620 million with respect to the beginning of 2022 and of $981 million compared to the $11,281 million of a year ago.

Síntesis Financiera considers -however- that the foreign exchange intervention will increase in the next days, but at most to $80 million and could repeat the behavior of the previous week, splitting the sale of foreign currency in two portions.

"The BCV doses its foreign exchange intervention to save reserves for weeks of greater monetary pressure", explained the consultant in the report.

title: Monthly inflation accelerates again to 10.1% in May
text:
Economist José Guerra stresses that the economic policy employed by Chavismo must change, since not even with all the reforms implemented is inflation being effectively contained.

The shadow of inflation looms over the Venezuelan economy months after believing to have controlled it, since for the second time this year a double digit figure is registered, after surpassing a 2021 with single digit percentages.

According to the figures of the Venezuelan Finance Observatory (OVF), inflation during the month of May stood at 10.1%, almost tripling the 3.6% recorded during April.

This increase is reminiscent of the 10.5% that the OVF reported in April, which now does not seem to be indicative of an isolated case but of a pattern of accelerating inflation, despite the fact that it is far from reaching the levels of hyperinflation that the country suffered between 2018 and 2020.

The economist and founder of the OVF, José Guerra, warned that this is a considerably high figure compared to the monthly records evidenced in 2021, since with it Venezuela maintains the path towards a three-digit annual inflation.

"Inflation is not totally defeated as we had assumed. We are back to double digits, which is a considerably high figure. We had been in single digits for several times. Now there is an inflationary rebound," he highlighted in the presentation of the monthly inflationary report via Zoom.

With this update, cumulative inflation from January to May is already 34.4%. In addition, the year-on-year variation from May 2021 to May 2022 stands at 151%, still a three-digit figure.

"Although we are not at hyperinflation levels, one of 10% per month still marks a triple-digit inflationary course. Although it is evidently lower than those we have seen in hyperinflation processes, it is still worrying", insisted Guerra.

The report also highlights the list of items with the highest increases during the month. This month presented the particularity of presenting a considerable price increase in the education sector, due to the adjustment of tuition fees for the next academic year. The list of increases presents the following items:

Education: 54.9%. Miscellaneous goods and services: 24.8%. Recreation: 16%. Clothing and footwear: 18.6%. Housing rentals: 13.2% Food: 11.9% Housingrentals: 13.2% Housingrentals: 13.2% Housingrentals: 13.2% Housingrentals: 13.2% Housingrentals Food: 11.9%Food: 11.9% Transportation Transport: 11.5%Transportation: 11.5% Causes behind the accelerated inflation Causes behind the accelerated inflation For Guerra, there are multiple reasons that explain this acceleration of inflation and much has to do with the intervention of the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) in the exchange market, as it failed to control the dollar exchange rate.

"The BCV was unable to stabilize the exchange rate during the month that concluded. In fact, the exchange rate increased 14.8%. That increase is passed on to the prices of goods, not only tradable goods, but also non-tradable goods such as services or student fees because the dollar is used as a reference for the price increase", he reasoned.

The issuing entity used $158 million to intervene in the exchange market in April, one of the highest amounts it has injected from the international reserves, which continue to deteriorate due to this policy.

Guerra warns that if such huge injections continue throughout the year, the international reserves will be emptied. For this same reason, the OVF notes that in June the trend has not been the same and the BCV is injecting fewer dollars.

Another crucial aspect is international inflation. Thanks to the international trade crisis unleashed by the covid-19 pandemic and now Russia's conflict with Ukraine, inflation soared globally. Goods imported into Venezuela have a higher price and this is also reflected in the inflation figures.

Regardless of the reasons, Guerra stresses that the economic policy employed by Chavismo must change, since not even with all the reforms implemented is inflation being effectively contained.

"An economy blocked by credit, with strong foreign exchange intervention and still the inflation rate is 10%. That means that something is not working," he stressed.

Food did not increase too much The family food basket measured by the OVF barely increased $1, going from $381 in April to $382 in May. Although the increase was tiny, it still remains the highest price it has been since the observatory has been measuring the prices of basic food goods.

This figure means that the majority of the country cannot have access to a food basket that satisfies the basic food needs of a Venezuelan family, since the minimum wages averaged in the private sector barely support a third of the basket, while the minimum wage of the public administration can only buy 10% of the products.

Those most affected by this disparity between salaries and the price of goods are pensioners. The elderly population is a victim of the inequality gaps that are becoming more and more accentuated in the new Venezuelan economy.

"They are leaving out of the scope of consumption important sectors of the Venezuelan population with an income of $30 of the minimum wage. We are talking about 3.2 million pensioners and close to 700,000 employees of the public administration", says Guerra.

title: The high cost of reducing inflation in Venezuela
text:
In the last few weeks, a large part of the opposition and economists with a neoliberal bias in the country went from using Venezuela as the worst possible scenario to which Argentina would be heading to, to taking it as a model of "war won" against inflation. The Venezuelan economy, after four years of hyperinflation and two monetary reconversions, managed to get below the "hyper" threshold and even showed lower price increases than those shown in Argentina today. But it did so at a very high cost.

The praise received by Venezuela from the economic establishment is not only for the results but mainly for the extremely contractionary policy applied to achieve them. These adjustment measures are intended for Argentina, even though this has generated in Venezuela the impoverishment of the purchasing power of household income, a collapse of the Gross Domestic Product and has deepened the emigration of around six million inhabitants.

"The government recognized in facts that its policy of controlling the economy had failed and now they have gone to the other extreme: extreme neoliberalism. There is no price control, no taxes are paid on exports, there is a massive import bubble even with products that are produced in the country and the dollar went from a situation in which it was illegal to one in which it is the only reference. At the same time, the government is receiving more dollars: a small recovery of oil, remittances from the millions of Venezuelans who left the country and the export of gold. Between this and the sale of reserves, the relationship between the bolivar and the dollar remains stable, it has even dropped a little", explained to El Destape the sociologist Edgardo Lander, professor emeritus of Social Sciences at the Central University of Venezuela in Caracas, one of the Venezuelan intellectuals chosen by the late President Hugo Chávez to negotiate the No to the FTAA and a referent of a citizen platform that for years has been seeking to propose an opposition not aligned with the United States.

The prelude to the hyperThe massive exodus of Venezuelans began in 2015 and three years later, when the number of emigrants traveling the region by plane, bus and on foot already exceeded three million, the UN included Venezuela among the countries with humanitarian crises requiring urgent assistance. The government of Nicolás Maduro rejected this qualification and then, in 2019, when the suffocating U.S. sanctions against state-owned companies and the financial system against the South American country arrived, they began to blame the "U.S. blockade", equating it with the one suffered by Cuba for more than half a century. The truth is that although the sanctions decreed by Donald Trump were not the cause of the economic crisis, they did deepen it to unprecedented levels for the country.

It was the time of the empty supermarkets, of the giant wads of money worth so little that they were thrown in the streets as a sign of protest, of the denunciations of hoarding and the raids that uncovered warehouses full of products, which businessmen refused to sell due to controlled prices that, according to their arguments, did not allow them to make profits or to guarantee new imports.

Maduro's government tried to control the situation with the Local Supply and Production Committees (CLAP) boxes that distributed basic foodstuffs imported by the State to friendly countries that allowed circumventing sanctions, constant increases in the minimum wage and a policy of ever greater intervention in the economy. However, he was unable to stop the shortages, the deterioration of the State and of the public services under his charge -health, education, transportation, fixed telephones-, the collapse of oil production, the main source of foreign currency, and hyperinflation.

Maduro was also unable to curb another effect of this economic crisis, the loss of support from the most vulnerable sectors, the backbone of Chavism's electoral base since its origin. "Since five or six years ago, we see a sustained decline of the electoral base of Chavismo. In last year's gubernatorial elections, the opposition candidates as a whole got considerably more votes than those of the ruling party. But the government kept most of the governorships because we are facing a divided opposition, which says that its priority is to defeat Chavismo, but then each force presents its own candidate and they do not reach agreements", Lander pointed out.

The Venezuelan strategy Venezuela managed to get out of the hyperinflation cycle it had been in since 2017. Inflation was 9585 percent in 2019 and 2294 percent in the first five months of 2020. To try to reduce the inflationary impact of monetary expansions, the Central Bank of Venezuela increased the required legal reserve (part of the deposits tied up in the monetary authority) and retracted the growth rates of monetary aggregates (circulating and demand accounts) in 2019 and in the first months of 2020. However, and as part of the plan to mitigate the effects of the pandemic, since March 2020 this policy was relaxed and the pace of issuance accelerated that year. According to the Central Bank of Venezuela, the National Consumer Price Index reached twelve months with a monthly variation below 50 percent, considered by analysts as the threshold of hyperinflation, while accumulating four consecutive months with a single-digit monthly variation. According to the Bolivarian monetary authority, last year closed with an annual inflation of 686.4 percent. This is not all good news.

The question is how that result was achieved and which of all the measures had an effect. "The process of deceleration of inflation occurs due to the stability maintained by the price of the dollar, due to the recurrent interventions made by the Central Bank of Venezuela by burning international reserves to maintain the exchange rate without significant oscillations," Martín Epstein, political scientist and economic analyst of CEPA (Center of Political Economy of Argentina), told this newspaper.

"There was a very strong economic contraction, of 88.6 percent of GDP from November 2014 to August 2020, and a rebound 10 percentage points taking from November 2020 to December 2021. At the beginning of March, workers' base salary is equivalent to 29 dollars. There had been no revision for a year", Epstein explained. As a reference, the value of the food basket in February 2022 reached $365; that is, the minimum wage does not even cover 10 percent of the necessary food intake.

According to figures from the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean(ECLAC)Economic Commission for Latin America and the CaribbeanEconomic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean(ECLAC), the frequent revisions of the minimum wage did not allow compensating the growth of prices, so that said wage contracted 37.4 percent in real terms between December 2018 and December 2019, and 30 percent in the first six months of 2020 with respect to the end of 2019.

"The process of dollarization of the economy and the strong restriction and recession seem to be determinants for the inflationary deceleration," Epstein pointed out, even though that has increased social inequalities between those who receive income in domestic currency with respect to those who do so in foreign currency. Ninety-nine percent of prices are dollarized and only 49 percent of payments in the main urban centers are made in bolivars. Grocery stores, supermarkets and clothing stores now mark their prices in dollars.

The image today is different from that of just a few years ago. In Caracas, one can again see the gondolas full, the highways full of cars, many of them new imports, and the restaurants, especially in the wealthier areas, full. "Now merchants are selling because they have the capacity to do so in dollars and buy with their dollars, without asking permission from the government", explained Lander. But that image of recovery is partial, according to the sociologist. "The shortage now is of a different type. It is no longer that of a State that tries to control things and the business community decides not to sell; now it is of a capitalist type. Before, everyone felt the shortage, now it is felt by those who have nothing to pay for it," he said.

"The humanitarian crisis has been half compensated by the remittances of six and a half million migrants. In many families the parents left and left the children with the grandparents, or the father left alone...it is a migration in which the relationship with those who stay here is very fluid. It is a cushion that has allowed many people to survive," added the sociologist.

The deficit adjustment was in line with the fall in activity. By 2017, the public deficit exceeded 20 percent of the Product, the highest in Latin America, and private estimates currently place it at around 7 percent. Other measures implemented to deepen the adjustment were to eliminate the gasoline subsidy, relax price controls and open the exchange market, which was subject to tight state control for more than 16 years.

"The strong contraction of the economy had an impact on the hyperinflationary spiral, but it attenuates the inflationary process by reaching such a significant reduction of the Venezuelan economy", added the CEPA analyst. In short, it seems that the logic that is trying to be imposed in Venezuela and that some analysts intend to copy in Argentina, is to carry out a brutal contraction of the GDP, dollarize the economy, strongly adjust public spending, consumption and salaries; and thus, lower inflation.

But even at this high cost, inflation is not a problem of the past in Venezuela.

On the one hand, it depends on its capacity to continue controlling the price of the dollar by selling reserves -limited by US and European sanctions-, expanding its oil production capacity -also limited by sanctions, the deterioration of its infrastructure and its massive indebtedness with China, with which it has an oil-for-debt agreement- and on a flow of remittances, which will undoubtedly be affected by the crises that the economies of the countries of the region are going through. For this reason, Maduro's government has been making concrete and clear political gestures for some time now to reinsert itself in the international community -led by the United States- and become attractive to receive foreign investments.

And on the other hand, for Lander, the effect of the war in Ukraine will also be strongly felt in Venezuela. "In energy, oil and gasoline, not so much because they are highly subsidized. But in food there will be an impact because there is still a very high imported component in this area. Our country does not produce wheat, imports 100% of its flour and is no longer self-sufficient in milk, coffee and sugar", he said.

title: The recipe behind Venezuela's leap to economic recovery
text:
ana rodríguez brazón - el tiempo correspondent - caracas@anarodriguez_bThe hyperinflation nightmare is over for Venezuela. In theory, the country has had a year with monthly inflation figures below 50 percent, bidding farewell to a stretch of 37 hard months. Now the path of a recovery is emerging, still viewed with caution. During the last few years, Venezuela recorded an 80 percent drop in GDP. Its main income -oil- was also affected and went from receiving 100 dollars to 34 dollars per barrel. In 2014, a few months after Nicolás Maduro came to power, the situation began to deteriorate and in 2017, with the economic sanctions imposed by the United States, the pit was reached. Still in memory are those days when one had to wait in line for one or two kilos of corn flour, the brawls outside supermarkets and the images of people dying of heart attacks in the lines waiting for their turn to buy.

 Although this has been overcome, there are still lines to get gasoline, as well as people looking for food in the garbage. However, this 2022 is expected to grow 8.6 percent compared to 2021. This data is provided by the report of the Instituto de Investigaciones Económicas y Sociales de la Universidad Católica Andrés Bello (IIES Ucab), which estimates a better year for the country, despite the fact that extreme poverty closed above 90 percent, according to figures of this same institution. The economic progress is focused on estimating that oil production could reach 950,000 barrels per day. Thus, the oil GDP would grow 39 percent with a five percent increase. Henkel García, director of the firm Econométrica, explains to this newspaper that everything started from 2018, when there was a change in the position of the National Government by starting to lower the harassment to entrepreneurship and all its policy of controls. Although for García this is not enough, at this moment there is evidence of a deceleration of inflation and containment of the exchange rate. "If this trend of fiscal and monetary discipline that the Government has had continues, we could end up with a double digit inflation in 2022", he said. The study of the Catholic University coincides with the appreciations of García, who participated in the forum 'Analysis of the current situation of Venezuela and perspectives for the year 2022', organized by the web portal La gran aldea. The document details that the measures implemented by Nicolás Maduro's regime, such as the "monetary and fiscal stabilization" carried out by the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV), have had positive effects. Researchers believe that inflation would reach 225 percent annually, below the 686 percent it had in 2021, and even lower compared to the 2,960 percent in 2020 and the 9,586 percent in 2019. However, that 225 percent rate is still inflationary. According to analysts, this recovery formally started in the second half of 2021 was also obtained by the increase in oil production and exports to Asian markets, managing to evade sanctions. In this sense, the exchange rate stabilization allowed certain freedom in the foreign exchange market, reducing the legal reserve from 85 to 73 %. In addition, tax collection has increased and the fiscal deficit has decreased. If this context remains unchanged, the path will continue to improve. Another aspect highlighted by the research is that remittances sent by migrants, estimated at US$ 2.7 billion in 2021, by 2022 would be US$ 3.5 billion, which represents an increase of 26.1 percent in 2021 and 30 percent in 2022. Recovery without the IMF "Venezuela was adapting to the US sanctions and found new markets to orient its exports. This allows us to affirm that the Venezuelan economy is beginning to recover," economist Francisco Rodríguez told EL TIEMPO. However, Rodríguez warned that living standards will continue to be low compared to the past. The also founder of Oil for Venezuela, when asked whether or not the intervention of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is necessary taking into account that the Caribbean country did not execute this procedure, the expert highlights that with the IMF "everything would have been easier". "If a loan had been obtained in this way, it would not have been necessary to resort to private parties". "It would have been positive for the country to have had the support of the IMF because it would have prevented the contraction of imports from being so strong", emphasizes Rodríguez. For him, the outlook is worse because although there is no debt with the IMF, there is debt with private companies, amounting to US$ 170 billion. This implies that although this debt is in default for reasons related to the sanctions, when the nation becomes part of the world economy and the sanctions end, it will have to solve the problem of debt restructuring. "They are creditors who are willing to sue Venezuela, to take assets from it, to seize payments for oil effects and the debt will accumulate faster", warns Rodriguez. Hence, everyone agrees that these Venezuelan signs of recovery are comparable to a person suffering from a serious illness, who, although showing signs of recovery, is left with after-effects that are not so easy to heal. Uneven with these data and improvements, the purchasing power of the common citizen continues to be a nightmare. However, on Thursday, Nicolás Maduro announced that the minimum wage will be set at half a Petro (digital currency created by the Government), which is equivalent to 126 bolívares (28 dollars), plus a proposed 45 bolívares in food bonus, which would be about 10 dollars. If this is implemented, as the President did not indicate when it would come into effect, Venezuela would be talking about 40 dollars in salary, which represents an increase of 1,700 percent with respect to the 10 bolivars currently paid to workers. For García it is important to take into account that if the economic contraction was of 80 percent, in order to recover the level the country had, a 400 percent growth would be needed. Hence, people do not fully feel the improvements that Maduro himself has talked about. "Trade is recovering much more than production in areas such as manufacturing, for example. In that uneven growth we see very depressed wages," says Garcia. The humanitarian emergency still persists. For Susana Raffalli, a public nutritionist, Venezuela is still among the countries with the most intense emergency. In the region, it is accompanied by Guatemala and Colombia, the latter with an increased risk precisely because of Venezuelan migration. And despite the fact that the regime tries to avoid them, the sanctions have also weighed heavily. "Today, 14'000,000 Venezuelans have humanitarian needs. According to the UN, 7.8 million Venezuelans are undernourished," Raffalli noted. Analysts agree that, in addition to the measures already adopted, it would be beneficial to improve basic services, expand bank credit, increase oil production and exports. "If the law of fair prices is repealed, that would give an institutional floor to the economic opening we are seeing", said García, who also agrees with the need to relax sanctions. Everything points to the fact that the Venezuelan economy will continue to be based on oil revenues added to tax collection. With those 950,000 barrels per day that production would reach, there would be a 75 percent growth in the country's main industry, which currently does not exceed 543,000 barrels per day. "In addition, exports could reach 760,000 barrels per day," says the Ucab report. For now, the great beneficiary is Maduro, who will have to demonstrate that he has found a way to one of his weakest points: economic stability. Something that would mean political stability. If this progression is maintained, at least until 2024, when the presidential elections will take place, the current administration will find a longed-for stability.

title: Maduro denounces before the UN the use of the migratory crisis to "justify an invasion" of Venezuela
text:
MADRID (EUROPA PRESS)-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro denounced on Monday before the United Nations Human Rights Council the use of the migration crisis to "justify an invasion" of Venezuelan territory.

Maduro has thus defended that Venezuela is known for being "historically" a recipient of migrants. "More than 12 million migrants live here, most of them coming from Colombia," he has pointed out during the 49th regular session of the council.

"There are some six million Colombians fleeing war, misery, drug trafficking and paramilitarism in Colombia. Today they are resorting to the expedient of the campaign against migrants to justify an intervention against Venezuela", he asserted before forcefully rejecting "the perverse campaign".

Likewise, he denounced the "kidnapping" of Venezuelan gold and capital by foreign banks. "I want to denounce that the Bank of England, with the support of the Government of the United Kingdom, is keeping 31 tons of gold of our country, belonging to the historical legal reserves of Venezuela," he lamented.

"I must also denounce that the Novo Banco de Portugal has sequestered in the modality of freezing more than one billion dollars (about 893 million euros) of Venezuela, that Citibank transferred 342 million dollars (305 million euros) from the Central Bank of Venezuela belonging to the country, to an account of the US Treasury in an illegal manner. With this money they pay operations of international criminal organizations", he said in a telematic session.

Maduro has stated that the financial institutions have denied the Caribbean country the "right to use these resources to buy vaccines, medicines, food or supplies in the fight against the coronavirus pandemic". "The misnamed sanctions have deprived our country of 99 percent of foreign exchange income from exports," he has stressed.

Furthermore, he has insisted that these resources are used by other countries to finance criminal actions against Venezuela. "With this money they pay for the operations of the international criminal organization (...) that attacks our country", he has reiterated.

In this sense, he has pointed out that there are currently more than 500 coercive measures to "damage the Venezuelan economy". "Venezuela has been the target of 502 unilateral coercive measures and other criminal and illegal, direct and indirect measures to destroy our economy, destabilize our democracy and put an end to the inclusive social model built by the Bolivarian revolution," he explained.

Shortly before, Maduro emphasized that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has refused to give Venezuela 5 billion dollars (about 4.4 billion euros) as part of the "special drawing rights" to face the pandemic.

In March 2020, the IMF rejected the Venezuelan government's request for financial assistance of 5 billion dollars to address the pandemic after considering that the "fund was not in a position to consider such request".

title: Academics consider that reform of tsj law reinforces lack of judicial independence
text:
Caracas - The Academy of Political and Social Sciences of Venezuela rejected the reform to the Organic Law of the Supreme Court of Justice (TSJ) that reduces the number of magistrates, as well as the way in which they are elected by the national Parliament, because they consider that the respective public consultations were not carried out and "the absence of independence" of justice in the country is reinforced. In a communiqué, issued on Friday 28 and published on its website, the Academy sets out its position on the reform of the Organic Law of the Supreme Court of Justice (LOTSJ), published on January 19, 2022, in Official Gazette No.

 6.684, Extraordinary, with the sole purpose of modifying the current composition of the highest court of Justice by reducing the number of its members and the appointment of new Magistrates and intervening in its organization and operation."Justice in Venezuela lacks independence since magistrates, judges and prosecutors do not have stability and are subject to external pressures. This lack of independence is a guarantee of impunity for crime, especially for serious human rights violations including crimes against humanity, and at the same time, it is used for the political persecution of opponents of the regime", they write in the document.Communiqué of the Academy of Political and Social Sciences of Venezuela"This Academy has repeatedly insisted on the defense and the necessary validity of the values and principles that inspire the Venezuelan constitutional system and the necessary independence and suitability of the Judiciary as a guarantee of the fundamental elements of the Rule of Law. Likewise, it has held that the basis and foundation of the administration of justice is compliance with the constitutional rules on the appointment and election of judges and magistrates, in which transparency and broad participation of society is an element of its legitimacy as a Public Power. The Supreme Court of Justice must enjoy independence and autonomy as guarantor of the supremacy and effectiveness of the constitutional norms and principles; it is also responsible for the direction, government and administration of the Judicial Power, the inspection and supervision of the courts and the public defender's offices (art. 267, Constitution). Only a Supreme Court of Justice and courts composed of competent, independent and impartial judges can comply with the constitutional and international standards established in the treaties and other instruments in force. In this regard, it is necessary to recall that according to the UN Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary, persons selected for judicial office shall be "persons of integrity and ability and shall have appropriate legal training or qualifications", that, "No method used for the selection of judicial personnel shall ensure that they are not appointed for improper motives" and finally, that in the selection of judges "no discrimination shall be made", including on the grounds of political or other opinion (Art. 10).).According to international rulings, as well as the decisions and opinions of international bodies, justice in Venezuela lacks independence since magistrates, judges and prosecutors lack stability and are subject to external pressures. This lack of independence is a guarantee of impunity for crime, especially for serious human rights violations including crimes against humanity, and at the same time, it is used for the political persecution of opponents of the regime. For the Academy it has been an ethical priority to defend the Rule of Law and the primacy of the 1999 Constitution, hence publicly through its communiqués and meetings it has referred to the outrages committed by the Supreme Court of Justice through its sentences, which rather than interpreting the Constitution has arbitrarily changed its norms, creating defenselessness, lack of protection and legal insecurity. For the aforementioned reasons, in view of the promulgation of the reform of the Organic Law of the Supreme Court of Justice, the Academy of Political and Social Sciences is obliged to pronounce itself, rejecting its text for the following legal reasons:1. The National Assembly did not make the respective consultations on this legislative reform to the other organs of the State, to the citizens, especially to the independent experts in the matter and to the organized civil society, in accordance with the provisions of Article 211 of the Constitution of the Republic. 2. The change of Article 8 of said Law, by which the number of judges of the Constitutional Chamber is reduced to five and the judges of the remaining Chambers to three, was carried out without having accredited the technical, material and substantive reasons for such modification of the Supreme Court of Justice, in accordance with the provisions of Articles 204 of the Constitution, which is applicable to all of the modified articles.3. The amendment of Article 25 adds a clause incorporating the constitutional mechanism of inter-institutional dialogue between the Constitutional Chamber and the National Assembly, which will prevent the Constitutional Chamber not only from exercising the so-called normative jurisdiction, but also from issuing favorable rulings, which constitutes a legislative overreach, all the more serious insofar as it omits the fact that the other Chambers, such as the Civil Cassation Chamber, have also been unconstitutionally modifying several laws (annulling legal norms and changing their legal meaning), in the illegitimate and abusive exercise of a misunderstood diffuse control of constitutionality. 4. In accordance with the provisions of Article 270 of the Constitution, the Judicial Nominations Committee, as a means of citizen participation in the management of public affairs, and especially in the election of judges of the Supreme Court of Justice, is composed of representatives of the different sectors of society, in accordance with the provisions of the law, and therefore, cannot have deputies as members. In other words, the Judicial Nominations Committee is not an organ of the National Assembly, nor of the Citizen Power. Notwithstanding the clear constitutional provision, the reform of Articles 65 and 69 of the LOTSJ modify the correlation of members of the Judicial Nominations Committee, in favor of deputies to the detriment of civil society, going from 54.54% to 47.61%. Likewise, an absolute majority is established as a quorum for constitution and a simple majority as a quorum for deliberation, all in favor of the political control of the judiciary by the parliamentary majority established in Article 65.5. Article 64 of the Reform imposes the incorporation of the Judicial Nominations Committee as an advisory body in the selection of Magistrates of the Supreme Court of Justice, the Inspector General of Courts and the Director of the National School of the Magistracy, as well as of the Judicial Electoral Colleges for the election of judges of disciplinary competence, without it being known what were the technical, material and substantive reasons for its incorporation in this task, other than the parliamentary political control of the judiciary. Pursuant to Article 270, as stated, the Judicial Nominations Committee cannot have deputies as members. This, in short, denaturalizes and politicizes the Committee; and also constitutes a usurpation of constitutional functions since, by incorporating deputies to the Nominating Committee, which is only responsible for selecting the list of candidates for the position, then those same deputies are incorporated to the National Assembly to elect the Magistrates from that same list.6. The reform of Articles 81 and 83 establishes that both the Inspector General of Courts and the Director of the National School of Magistrates will be appointed by the National Assembly, based on the same procedure established for the appointment of the Magistrates of the Supreme Court of Justice, which entails a severe political interference of the Legislative Power in the independence, autonomy and functioning of the Judicial Power (art. 267, Constitution).7. Article 38 of the LOTSJ, as amended, maintains with a different wording, the definitive selection of the magistrates by a simple majority of the members of the National Assembly, if the latter does not achieve, after three consecutive sessions without an agreement for the appointment, the favorable vote of two thirds (2/3) of its members. This rule, in addition to violating the constitutional principle of the appointment of all high authorities of the State with the favorable vote of two thirds (2/3) of the members of the National Assembly, which is even expressly ratified for the removal of the judges of the TSJ (art.265).8. Regarding the incorporation of the second final provision (art. 13), the reform states that the appointment of the twenty new magistrates and their alternates will proceed, adding that the magistrates "who by the date of entry into force of this Law have not completed the term for which they were appointed and designated, may run again for these positions". Consequently, it would be producing for certain magistrates, the possibility of spending more years in the Supreme Court than the fixed 12 years that they can remain in their positions. This is contrary to the express provisions of the Constitution (art. 264) regarding the total duration of the term of office or period of office of the justices: "(...) they shall be elected for a single term of twelve years". Thus, magistrates can only be elected for a single term, the maximum duration of which, in any case, is twelve years.9. The reform that replaces the Unidad Tributaria (Tax Unit) as the reference value for the determination of jurisdiction and the fines provided for in Articles 26, 81, 121, 122 and 123, with the official exchange rate of the highest value currency established by the Central Bank of Venezuela, generates serious doubts as to its constitutionality. In view of the content of the Law of partial reform of the LOTSJ, it is necessary to conclude that it deepens the political dependence of the appointment of the magistrates of said Court and other instances of the justice system in Venezuela, and therefore, with effects on the operation of all the organs of justice. By virtue of this, it is concluded that this Law reinforces the absence of independence of justice in Venezuela, as it is openly contrary to the standards of due process, appointment and stability of judges, contained in international instruments on human rights and the Rome Statute, as well as in the jurisprudence of the courts and other international bodies, especially the International Criminal Court and the organs and agencies of the United Nations". Julio Rodríguez Berrizbeitia, President.Cecilia Sosa Gómez, Secretary.

title: Opposition congressman demanded quarterly adjustment for Venezuelan pensioners
text:
The opposition deputy of the Parliament of Venezuela José Gregorio Correa requested Monday to the regime of Nicolás Maduro to increase and adjust quarterly pensions collected by retired public workers, in proportion to inflation.

"Pensions should be adjusted and increased quarterly, according to inflation figures for a better living of our young (seniors) third and fourth age," said the parliamentarian in a press release.

Correa recalled that these are people "who gave their best years and do not receive adequate remuneration" and who deserve to age "with dignity and respect".

He assured that, from the Parliament, he will work so that pensioners and retirees "have the claims they deserve".

In recent days, the deputy asked his colleagues in the National Assembly (NA, Parliament) to think of this group as one of the priorities for the legislative agenda of the year that has just begun.

"We have to have a new year where retirees are also a priority (...) and that the State has the obligation to take care of each one of those Venezuelans who served to make, for many years, the public administration what it is," said the deputy on that occasion.

Correa also asked that the budget approved for 2022, which amounts to more than 13.457 billion dollars, include improvements for the country's retirees, including a benefit that allows them to "live with dignity".

Last month, the Venezuelan Observatory of Finance (OVF) indicated that monthly inflation in Venezuela was 6% in November, year-on-year inflation stood at 769%, and cumulative inflation was 616.9%.

"The items with the highest increases during the month in reference were health with 18.6%, goods and services with 16.5%, food 11.5% and footwear 9.8%," the organization said in a statement.

The OVF said that, as in previous months, the behavior of prices responds to the "stability" that has maintained the exchange rate in the Caribbean country, where "recorded an increase of 5.7%, in line with the rise in prices," a percentage much lower than usual, linking months with double digits.

However, the observatory said that this policy of stability resulted in the fall of international reserves.

"This policy of exchange rate stability was expressed in a drop of US$171 million in the liquid international reserves of the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV), as a result of sustained intervention by the central bank in the foreign exchange market by offering dollars in cash," the NGO explained.

title: Venezuela close to leaving hyperinflation behind, but not its aftermath
text:
In one of the countries with the worst economic prospects in the world, the exit from the hyperinflationary cycle after more than four years looks like a light at the end of the tunnel. Venezuela -according to economists and what the Central Bank of Venezuela itself has announced this week- will reach in the first quarter of 2022 more than 12 months with monthly inflations below 50%, which would technically indicate its exit from hyperinflation. The aftermath of this cycle, however, will still remain a lead in the wing for the economic recovery that the government promises every year.

Nicolás Maduro belatedly acknowledged hyperinflation, a word rarely uttered officially, although it has been one of the problems that has most afflicted Venezuelans in recent years. Venezuela and Zimbabwe have been the only countries with hyperinflation during the 21st century. The Caribbean nation is also one of the rare cases of oil-producing countries that have experienced this economic disease. And Venezuela will be the only country that has gone through hyperinflation and a pandemic, says Marino González, a researcher at Simón Bolívar University in Venezuela and La Rioja University in Spain.

For the academic, who has dedicated himself to studying hyperinflation and its approaches, the Venezuelan hyperinflation has not been an exclusively monetary phenomenon like most of the cases recorded in history. "Unlike other Latin American countries like Brazil and Argentina, here it manifests itself after a great loss of productive capacity experienced by 15 years of controls. The destructive effect of hyperinflation adds to the previous and now pandemic."

Looking at some indicators between 2017, when the hyperinflationary fire started, and 2021 shows its effects. From 87% poverty, the country went to 96%, according to the annual Encovi survey. There is another more dramatic data: at the close of 2017 only 1.4 million Venezuelans had left the country, today there are six million out, according to United Nations figures, moved mostly by the impossibility of sustaining themselves economically in the country. "The human capital lost during this time will be difficult to replace," says economist and university professor Hermes Pérez.

Pérez points out that Venezuela suffers from the three most serious diseases of an economy: consecutive economic contraction for eight years, hyperinflation and unemployment, which this year reaches half of the active population. "Of course it's good news to get out of hyperinflation, but in 2022 Venezuela will undoubtedly continue to have the highest inflation in the world, even now when all countries are fighting it.

Inflation destroys the functions of money, Pérez explains. One scar left by hyperinflation in Venezuela is the virtual disappearance of the bolívar, which has even changed its face in the one-bolívar currency (which has been stripped of 14 zeros after three reconversions). The so-called Barre bolivar, after Albert Barre, the engraver of the Paris Mint who was commissioned in 1873 to engrave the profile of the Venezuelan hero facing to the left, persisted on the coins until a few months ago. Those that came out in October, with the third monetary reconversion, have the face that Chavismo reconstructed after the exhumation of the remains of the Liberator, ordered by Hugo Chávez in 2010, stirring up the historical conspiracy that he was assassinated by his enemies. It is the one repeated on all banknotes since 2018 and, since this year, on coins, with a wider, rounder nose, bushy eyebrows and square jaw, "the mulatto Bolivar," as Chávez, who once joked about his resemblance, called him. In any case, today it is the most devalued bolivar.

Today, dollars account for 70% of transactions in the country. They are in the hands of informal vendors or at the cash register of any establishment. The de facto dollarization allowed by the Government from 2019, after the repeal of the illicit exchange rates, is the natural response in any process of hyperinflation, but in Venezuela it has ended up throwing confidence in the national currency, which will be a problem for the future. "Not having confidence in the monetary sign does not help economic recovery," Pérez stresses, and González points out, as another peculiarity of the Venezuelan process, that none of the hyperinflations that have occurred in Latin America have ended with dollarization.

But for Maduro - and for the country - it has been an escape valve, as he has recently acknowledged, and it is one of the factors that has helped to get out of hyperinflation, four years later just before surpassing the five-year record that Nicaragua experienced between 1986 and 1991, in the first decade of Sandinismo.

"The exit from hyperinflation is happening by spontaneous generation, not by joint economic measures to combat it," Pérez responds. In his opinion, in addition to dollarization, other situations have had a greater impact on ending the hyperinflationary cycle in an economy that is a fifth of what it was a decade ago. The destruction of the demand for money, in part because of the six million Venezuelans who are not in Venezuela, the liberalization of prices, the government's intervention in the market with injections of dollars to artificially contain the exchange rate - because despite the sanctions it now benefits from the rise in oil prices - and, the most costly of the measures, according to Pérez, the exaggerated legal reserve imposed on banks to totally restrict commercial and personal credit.

Lowering inflation is just one of the conditions for the economy to take off. Different economic firms forecast a moderate contraction by the end of 2021, after falls of up to 39% in a single year, and even some growth for 2022 driven mainly by the private sector. The haze, however, remains over whether these easings will be sustainable and lead to a real economic turnaround. title: The Venezuelan Observatory of Finance reported cumulative inflation of 616% through November
text:
Monthly inflation in Venezuela was 6 % last November, reported Tuesday the Venezuelan Observatory of Finance (OVF), an independent entity that brings together several economic analysts, who detailed that the year-on-year stood at 769 %, and at 616.9 % the accumulated one.

"The items with the highest increases during the month in reference were health with 18.6%, goods and miscellaneous services with 16.5%, food 11.5% and footwear 9.8%," the organization said in a statement.

The OVF said that, as in previous months, the behavior of prices responds to the "stability" that has maintained the exchange rate in the Caribbean country, where "recorded an increase of 5.7%, in line with the rise in prices," a percentage much lower than usual, to link months with double digits.

However, the observatory said that this policy of stability resulted in the fall of international reserves.

"This policy of exchange rate stability was expressed in a drop of 171 million dollars in the liquid international reserves of the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV), as a result of the sustained intervention of the issuing institution in the exchange market by offering dollars in cash," the NGO explained.

The organization explained that this stabilization in the exchange rate also contributed to the slower pace of expansion of the regime's spending, which resulted in a 5% increase in the monetary base during November, and generated that the prices of goods produced in Venezuela are "relatively expensive, compared to imported goods".

"When comparing the annualized inflation rate observed in November 2021 of 769 %, with the annualized exchange rate variation rate of 340 %, it is notorious that the price increase far exceeds the depreciation of the bolivar, which suggests that the currency is becoming dangerously overvalued in real terms," the observatory said.

Finally, it pointed out that this situation is causing sectors such as the agri-food and manufacturing industries to lag significantly behind commercial activities in terms of dynamism.

(With information from EFE)

title: Venezuela's inflation was 8.1% in October, independent agency says
text:
Caracas, Nov 8 (EFE) - Venezuela's monthly inflation was 8.1% last October, reported Monday the Venezuelan Observatory of Finance (OVF), an independent entity that brings together several economic analysts, who added that the year-on-year was 1,258% and the cumulative was 576.3%. The OVF maintained that the deceleration of inflation is due to the stability that the price of the dollar has maintained, due to the "recurrent interventions" made by the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) "burning the international reserves to maintain without significant oscillations of the exchange rate". "The item that showed the greatest variation was recreation with 19.2%, followed by education with 11.8% due to the return to on-site classes, transportation with 11.3% and alcoholic beverages with 10.5%," he added.

 As an effect of the monetary reconversion that came into effect in early October, with the elimination of six zeros to the currency, the observatory indicated that there was also an increase in dollars in the prices of products and services. It also noted that the price of the food basket in foreign currency reached a historic high of $343.75 for a family of five, with a variation of 12.77% over the previous month, when it stood at $304.83."Thus, access to the food basket according to the minimum wage was 0.69%, while the minimum wage remained at 7 bolivars ($1.5)," he added. The observatory pointed out that these figures are estimated at the same time that it is declared the flexibilization of the measures by the pandemic of covid-19, the return to presential classes and the proximity of the regional and local elections of next November 21.

title: OVF: October Food Basket Reaches All-Time High of $343.75
text:
The Venezuelan Finance Observatory (OVF) reported that monthly inflation for the month of October was 8.1%, while inter-annual inflation stood at 1,258% and accumulated inflation at 576.3%.

The item that showed the highest variation was recreation with 19.2%, followed by education with 11.8% due to the return to on-site classes, transportation with 11.3% and alcoholic beverages with 10.5%.

An increase in dollars was evidenced in products and services, as an effect of the last monetary reconversion, which came into effect on October 1.

On the other hand, the price of the food basket in foreign currency reached its historical maximum of 343.75 dollars for a family of 5 members, with a variation of 12.77% compared to the previous month, located at 304.83 dollars. Thus, access to the food basket according to the minimum wage was 0.69%, while the minimum wage remained at Bs. 7.00.

This deceleration of inflation occurs due to the stability that the price of the dollar has maintained, due to the recurrent interventions made by the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) by burning international reserves to maintain the exchange rate without significant oscillations.

Such figures are estimated at a time when the government has declared the flexibilization from November 1 to January 1, 2022, a return to classes with scarce conditions and attendance, and in view of the elections of governors, state legislators, mayors and councilors on November 21, 2021.

title: IMF's US$5 billion that Venezuela doesn't receive and for which the government and opposition are negotiating
text:
US$5 billion is a lot of money.

Especially for a country like Venezuela, which has been in the throes of a serious economic and social crisis for years.

That's the amount that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is supposed to give the country as part of the special drawing rights that the Fund will allocate to developing countries to help them alleviate the economic blow of the covid pandemic.

But Venezuela is for the moment excluded from that distribution.

At least, as long as the opposition and the government, negotiating in Mexico to end the country's long-running political crisis, do not agree on how to handle that money and other Venezuelan state assets under litigation abroad since January 2019, when opposition leader Juan Guaidó proclaimed himself interim president of the country and won the recognition of the United States and most European and Latin American countries.

Nicolas Maduro made clear his demands for the government to participate in the new dialogue process. REUTERSWhatare

Special DrawingRightsSpecial Drawing Rights are a system created in 1969 by the IMF to provide liquidity to world economies and to be able to provide additional reserves to member countries in case of difficulty

.Manuel Sutherland, director of the Caracas-based Centro de Investigación e Información Obrera (CIFO), told BBC Mundo that it was "an anchor in a basket of currencies that could be used or exchanged as a reserve fund in situations of economic difficulty".

When the 2008 crisis erupted they were used to keep the world economy afloat and in 2020 the Fund again resorted to this mechanism to counter the effects of the coronavirus on the global economy.

The IMF has not yet released the corresponding funds to Venezuela. GETTYIMAGESWhy the money is not coming to VenezuelaVenezuela

should be one of the countries most benefiting from this possibility of financing on very advantageous terms, which other countries will begin to receive imminently, but the international dispute over who is its legitimate president, the poor relations of successive Chavista governments with the Fund and the breaches of the transparency requirements it demands by the government of Nicolás Maduro prevent it from receiving the funds

.The IMF agreed this time to release about $650 billion, the largest amount in its history.

The refusal of member countries like the United States that do not recognize Maduro is blocking the disbursement of Venezuela's share of that huge pie.

Sutherland also notes that "there is also a lot of mistrust from sectors within the country that do not want the Maduro government to directly manage that money.

The Venezuelan opposition has insisted for years that Venezuela is living under "a dictatorship" and Guaidó's so-called "interim government" has sought ways to wrest control of Venezuelan assets abroad from Maduro.

Guaidó claims it is about "protecting" the wealth of Venezuelans, but Maduro's government considers it "an operation to plunder and steal the national patrimony."

Both parties maintain open litigation regarding Venezuelan strategic assets abroad, such as Citgo, a subsidiary in the United States of the state-owned Petróleos de Venezuela; the company Monómeros, recently intervened by the Colombian authorities; or the nearly US$2 billion of Venezuelan gold retained by the Bank of England and still pending a final resolution by the British courts.

Government and opposition negotiate again in Mexico, but for the moment they are still far from an agreement. HECTOR VIVAS / GETTYAlreadyin March 2020, at the start of the pandemic, the IMF rejected the government's request for a US$5 billion emergency loan. "There is no clarity" on international recognition of Maduro, the Fund said in a statement at the time.

But the Venezuelan government's friction with the IMF goes back a long way.

The late President Hugo Chávez frequently criticized the Fund, which he considered "an instrument of colonialism" and even promoted alternative international organizations with the support of allied governments in the region.

The Venezuelan government also forced IMF technicians out of the country and closed the door to advisory and collaboration missions.

Usually, the Fund requests the development of reform plans and the supervision of their execution from the countries to which it grants loans, but, as Sutherland recalls, "Chavismo has refused to cede what it calls economic sovereignty and to make the economic changes demanded by the IMF and a large part of civil society".

Most experts agree that years of statist economic interventionism, corruption and waste led Venezuela to its current situation, which has been aggravated by U.S. sanctions and has driven 5.4 million people to leave the country, according to U.N. figures.

What could be done with that money in Venezuela

Economist Sutherland said "US$5 billion would seem small for an oil economy like Venezuela's, which once had US$80 billion in average annual export revenue.

But the drop in Venezuela's oil exports, its main source of foreign currency income, has drastically reduced its international reserves, now just over US$6.3 billion, according to the Central Bank of Venezuela.

Given that figure, Sutherland estimates the corresponding drawing rights could represent up to ten times the total liquidity the country now has.

The aid could serve to alleviate the suffering of Venezuelans when one in three suffers from food insecurity, according to the UN World Food Programme, and the National Survey of Living Conditions carried out by experts from Venezuela's main universities calculates that eight out of ten households live in poverty.

GETTY IMAGESSutherlandpoints out that "an agreement at the dialogue table in Mexico "could facilitate obtaining those resources that are so urgently needed"

.However, the negotiations appear to be stalled.

4 keys to Venezuela's new dialogue between government and opposition in MexicoJorge Rodríguez, head of the Chavista delegation, announced that he will include Alex Saab, a Colombian businessman imprisoned in Cape Verde awaiting extradition to the United States, where he is wanted on money laundering charges.

An investigation by the website Armando.info attributed Saab as the mastermind of a massive corruption scheme linked to the government-subsidized food delivery program.

Venezuelan analyst Luis Vicente León believes that the attempt to include the controversial Saab as an accredited diplomat reflects "the government's decision to freeze the negotiation process".

Requesting the incorporation of Alex Saab to the negotiating team in Mexico is part of the official decision to release him. But given the low probability of it happening, this seems a clear message of the government's decision to freeze the negotiation process.

But, like many other observers, Sutherland views them with skepticism: "They're arguing among political party leaders with very little national rootedness, and they've forgotten about the most urgent issues, like the humanitarian and social crisis."
