title: Interview / Juan Guaidó / 'The opposition is central'
text:
The loss of democracy begins with the attack on the free press, warned the president of the Venezuelan Parliament, who confirmed that Mexico is among the possible venues for a dialogue with the Government of Maduro

What was Venezuela like before Chavismo?

Venezuela pre-ninety-eight, before what they called the revolution or socialism of the 21st century, was a Venezuela with inequality, with social debts, but with access to education, with a solid oil industry, with citizen security, with territorial integrity, with the exercise of sovereignty. There was a strong middle class, a relatively low public debt compared to what we have today, inflation was under control.

What is it like today?

It is a Venezuela in extreme poverty, which has generated the largest migration and refugee crisis the continent has seen in recent decades, today only comparable to Syria, a country that has years at war.

(It's) a country where not a single vaccine (against Covid-19) has come in through the COVAX system, where a nurse earns $3 a month, where children grow up dreaming of leaving the country, it's a tragedy, a humanitarian catastrophe. We are looking for alternatives to deal with the emergency, and to restore democracy.

It is a Venezuela that is in dictatorship, in autocracy, with the peculiarity that the state disappeared. Today, the Central Bank does not control the interest rate, the official currency despite being the bolivar is no longer the current currency (but) the dollar, the euro, gold. This sets up a failed state, the absence of the state with a dictatorship pretending to hijack the public powers.

The most basic thing is citizen security, somehow minting the currency, and none of that today can be done by (Nicolas) Maduro.

On the other hand (there is) a majority of citizens protesting, demanding rights, looking for alternative solutions to the conflict, looking for international allies to be able to attend to the humanitarian emergency and to be able to have free and fair elections, to solve this terrible conflict that when you put it in contrast, what it was in '98, in '99, or the first part of the 2000s , versus what we have today, we see an unprecedented catastrophe.

How did the process of institutional destruction take place? How was it tolerated? Is society complicit in what happened, the businessmen, the television companies, the radio stations, the journalists?

Democracy is based on the strength of its institutions and society, on NGOs, on the natural counterweights to the State.

Democracy is always at stake. In Venezuela, they evidently did not say, as no dictator says: 'We are going to destroy the institutions, we are going to kidnap them, we are going to seize them and we are going to weaken them in order to strengthen the one in power of the day.' In Venezuela came for the first thing, through the media, censorship, persecution of the free press, critical thinking. Then, the positioning of figures affects the dictatorship in positions of power. They always tried to co-opt the institutions.

We must be very vigilant about independence, about the autonomy of the powers that be. The National Parliament, for example, must be a guarantee of comptrollership, counterweight, denunciation and voice of minorities at all times.

What they call the dictatorship of the majorities, even by one vote, you have to be very careful, that was what (Hugo) Chávez exercised from the beginning leveraged in two things: one, yes the popularity at the time, but two, the use of state resources to generate social control to large parts of the population , is what some define populism, that which led to a dictatorship of the majority, and sometimes of the minority, because today Maduro does not have any kind of popular support.

How to remove Maduro from power?

We have tried literally everything. We have won majorities, founded parties, generated an almost unprecedented movement of civic struggle. In the last 12 years we have had thousands of demonstrations, some massive, millions in number of people, some modest, hunger strikes, citizens' protests, we took parliament from you electorally.

In Venezuela, we are facing a transnational dictatorship, with links to terrorism, to drug trafficking, to farc dissidents, to the ELN. We have suffered political assassinations, persecution, imprisonment, exile... We are resisting, from a vulnerability. The country with the largest oil reserves on the planet has no gasoline. Venezuela, today a country (the fifth or eighth) with gas reserves is now cooking with firewood, in an almost barbaric situation.

What do we have to do to achieve democracy, to achieve an orderly transition, which is what we want? What we have been doing for years: building majorities, exercising it in the streets despite the risk, making our struggle visible, seeking the articulation of the international community to accompany our demand, which is a simple one: free and fair elections.

Would you support a US military intervention in Venezuela?

The choice of international force is controversial, no one wins in a dilemma between war and peace. If you ask any citizen of the planet what they prefer, war or peace, 99 percent would say peace. What we have to evaluate right now in Venezuela is what alternatives we have to stop the suffering, the danger that Nicolás Maduro represents, not only to Venezuelans, but to the entire continent because of drug trafficking, because of terrorism, because of the migration crisis. In other words: Would you support it or not? I support the democratization of Venezuela, the holding of free and fair elections, the big issue is how to get there. And whether or not the use of force is necessary, what I believe is that it must be evaluated responsibly in order to save lives, to regain legitimacy.

We must evaluate the social cost, the cost of a dictatorship in the region, what it represents in drug trafficking and terrorism. Nicolás Maduro, by the way, with great ties to drug cartels in Mexico, which represents a great threat to the continent.

We must responsibly evaluate all the options we have to achieve an orderly transition that generates governability in Venezuela.

What is most talked about now about Venezuela is this national salvation agreement, what is it? What role is Mexico going to play?

We have called it an agreement because the agreement is the objective of a negotiation. In Venezuela there have been seven negotiation processes in the last 8 years, and none has reached an agreement.

Venezuela does not need another failed negotiation process, it needs an agreement to democratize the country, to regain confidence in Venezuela in international investment, to reactivate the productive apparatus; we went from three million barrels (of crude oil) a day to less than 500 thousand, having invested 300 billion dollars in the industry.

The possibility of an agreement is the possibility of saving Venezuela, it is to reverse the migratory flow, it is to have an independent arbitrator who can govern an electoral process and turn the electoral process into a window of solution to the conflict. It is to be able to generate confidence in the multilaterals so that they triple or increase their humanitarian participation in Venezuela. The big question is how to achieve this, understanding that in the past the dictatorship used negotiation processes to defuse international pressure and thus buy time, to mock Venezuelans and the international community.

The first thing is that there is this temptation, this risk, and we must prepare ourselves for that as well. The second thing is to use the tools we have, which is the exercise of the Constitution, the clear demand for free and fair elections, international pressure. As Juan Gonzalez (adviser to US President Joe Biden on the Western Hemisphere) said recently: if we do not succeed in a negotiation, multilateral pressure will continue.

Therefore, being clear about all these tools is going to allow us the possibility of an agreement, as we have called it, of national salvation. Today in Venezuela we need everything from vaccines, to water, to gasoline.

It is said that it will be in Mexico that this national salvation agreement will be signed. Do they require Mexico's endorsement at this juncture?

In order to form an agreement, there are many roles for the international community: facilitation, mediators, guarantors of the process.

We have recently spoken with the Kingdom of Norway, who already did so in 2019 and are aware of the Venezuelan actors and can facilitate the process. We are evaluating possible venues for the holding of a possible negotiation... it is a possible negotiation.

We are assessing Mexico, Norway, some other countries that can independently, impartially and respectfully host a possible negotiation.

What has the process been like for Mexico to host? What has been the dialogue with Mexico and how feasible is it that Mexico will be and not another place?

It could be any country, Canada, USA, Spain. The democratic alternative is welcome in any country in the world.

One of the main variables is where the two parties feel comfortable. Not many countrieswhere the dictatorship can feel comfortable, so that's one of the variables.

In 2019 it was in Barbados and Oslo, they were two venues to hold the negotiating rounds. At the moment we are in the phase of exploration, of the possibility of a negotiation, within the technical elements is the headquarters, the physical location, and a possible one is Mexico.

From the Venezuelan experience, and what you mentioned about there not many countries that Nicolas Maduro would feel comfortable in, and Mexico is one of them, what do you think of the Mexican opposition's stance that we're on our way to becoming Venezuela?

Democracy is not only elections, we saw it for many years in Venezuela, it is independence from power, it is respect for freedom of expression, it is the strength of its institutions, it is the respected counterweights, those are the variables that have to be taken care of a lot as Mexicans.

The Opposition of any country is central, respect for the Opposition in any country is fundamental. No ruler of the day should in any way be offended when what is sought is to preserve democracy.

From your experience as an ordinary Venezuelan, what do you think of the news and what is happening in Mexico?

We, at the beginning, said: We are going to become a second Cuba. And some saw us as exaggerated. For us it is very painful to be the bad example now, now we are the bad example Cuba and Venezuela, that should fill us with strength to continue fighting, to continue fighting.

What I do draw attention to as a Venezuelan is that they are attentive to the signals, to the attack on the free press, to the attack on the Opposition, to the desire to trivialize the struggle of minority sectors. These are all signs that do not help to strengthen democracy. Any democrat must accept criticism, he must open up the spaces for the alternative, for minorities, so any signal made by the opposition must be received by the government. Being a democratic government, it must not feel attacked in any way, when what you want to preserve is democracy.

The internal political dynamic, of positioning the factors, of the different parties, is a natural political dynamic of any country, it happens in Mexico, in the United States, even in dictatorship in Venezuela.

I call on both the opposition and the government of (Andrés Manuel) López Obrador, as well as Mexican society, to be attentive to the signs, sometimes the totalitarian drift gradually passes. There is the temptation of populism constantly.

I repeat, democracy is not just elections, it is not just the Executive, democracy is the system, the ecosystem, in some way, of institutions, of society, of respect for fundamental human rights, of respect for the public purse, and above all for the natural counterweights in each country.

What advice would you give mexico so that we do not follow the path of Venezuela?

To the Mexicans, to my brothers in Cuba, in Nicaragua, in Peru, in Colombia, preserving democracy is a daily and constant task, not a gift, it is not a legacy, it is a constant struggle, to preserve institutions, to denounce and be alert to the signs that can lead to democracy on the wrong path, to undermine democracy. , weakening the institutions, attacking the free press, the fundamental pillars of democracy, we must always be vigilant.

I call on young people to participate in decision-making, to participate in citizens' organisation, to participate in political parties, to be part of the constant denunciation, but also of the alternatives, to be part of associations, student movements, NGOs, decision-making places, that is fundamental.

What democracy is going to guarantee in the future is going to be the strength and strength of its social fabric, how willing we citizens are to defend our rights and to do our duties, because the populist temptation, the totalitarian temptation, is also going to be there forever. The best antidote is citizenship, institutions, mobilization, demand, protest, defense, counterweights, among others. I always put a lot of emphasis on the free press, because it was one of the first to attack in Venezuela.

title: Venezuela to introduce 1-million-bolivar bill as inflation persists
text:
CARACAS, March 5 (Reuters) - Venezuela's central bank said on Friday that it would introduce a banknote worth 1 million bolivars beginning next week, as years of incessant hyperinflation continue to batter the value of the crisis-stricken South American country's currency.

The new banknote will be worth just 52 U.S. cents at the current official exchange rate. Interannual inflation was running at 2,665% as of January, according to the central bank.

The once-prosperous OPEC nation's economy has been in a tailspin for the past seven years, spurred by a collapse in oil prices that led to a drop in imports and a gaping fiscal deficit, prompting the central bank to print more bolivars.

"These new bills will complement and optimize the current denominations, to meet the requirements of the national economy," the central bank said in a statement.

In addition to the 1-million-bolivar banknote, the central bank said it will introduce 200,000- and 500,000-bolivar banknotes to circulate alongside the 10,000-, 20,000-, and 50,000-bolivar bills currently in circulation.

Years of hyperinflation and erosion of the bolivar's value have led Venezuelans to use U.S. dollar banknotes for many everyday transactions. President Nicolas Maduro has called the informal dollarization process an "escape valve" while blaming U.S. sanctions for the economy's woes.

Critics say the root of Venezuela's economic collapse lies in the interventionist policies of Maduro and his socialist predecessor and mentor, Hugo Chavez. (Reporting by Deisy Buitrago Writing by Luc Cohen Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: The dictionary of the crisis in Venezuela: a 2020 review from A to Z
text:
2020 ended and Venezuela is facing another year of likely political startle and an economic crisis that seems hard to overcome. The long list of everyday problems that the country lives, and which was exacerbad by the coronavirus pandemic that marked the last nine months, can be reduced in a brief dictionary.

A, from Embrace: the dream word and the forbidden gesture. Something so common among family and friends became so important in 2020 that it had never been given before. With the appearance of the covid-19, the distance and veto came to affection. Venezuelans, like the rest of the world's citizens, dream of regaining that custom that has never been given so much value.

Bolivar B:the national currency lost 95.50% of its value throughout the year, which made it almost useless with no choice but to give way to the dollar. In early January, 48,709 bolivars could be exchanged for a dollar. Today, 1,066,000 bolivars are needed for the same operation.

Covid-19 C:The scourge of the year almost all over the world was (and is) in Venezuela one of the problems best controlled by the government of Nicolás Maduro. With 113,121 contagions, of which, according to official information, 95% are already recovered, and 1,025 deaths, the Caribbean country is one of the least affected by the virus.

Dollar D:The American currency, once detailed by Maduro's government, shifted the devalued bolivar and became the country's trading engine, contrary to the more optimistic expectations of the representative, who hoped that the petro - venezuelan cryptocurrency launched in 2018 - would be the life table of an impoverished nation, something that did not materialize.

Election e:Controversial legislative elections on December 6 showed that more and more citizens are moving away from chavism, which lost nearly 1,400,000 votes from the 2015 elections. It still happens to the opposition led by Juan Guaidó, who did not participate in the contest, but called a popular consultation that showed him that about 1,700,000 people withdrew his trust.

F of Fraud:the word chosen by the opposition to develop its electoral counter-campaign in the face of chavism. According to the political sector that closes ranks around Guaidó, the elections were a fraud, which is why they refused to participate and compete in the polls with their opponent.

G of Gasoline: Fuel shortages were another obstacle to be overcome. Thousands of Venezuelans were forced to queue to load their tanks, up to 6 days with their respective nights, in kilometer rows of vehicles, in order to get a few litres of gasoline.

Hyperinflation H:November closed with cumulative inflation of 3,045.92%, according to data from the National Assembly (AN), a body that provides the information in the absence of reports from the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV), an entity to which it is appropriate to give these figures. Several experts estimate 4,000% at the end of the year.

I of Pardons: At the end of August and by surprise, Maduro decided to grant measures of grace to 110 people, including 53 prisoners who were released and 57 other citizens who received dismissal of causes or lifting of punishments. For the opposition, it was a propaganda element of the election campaign.

Justice J:it remains one of the outstanding subjects in Venezuela and, in 2020, was ratified. Break-ins without a warrant, arbitrary detentions, violations of freedoms, prisoners without trial or disqualifications with dubious arguments. Quarantine served the authorities to strengthen control andRepression.

Kilometers K: a measure to which Venezuelans are very accustomed, and not only to calculate the distance of their travels. Kilometers of tail to load fuel, kilometers to find signal on the phones, to look for water, kilometers walking to leave the country clandestinely. And the difficulties that added 2020 added more kilometers in the particular account of each.

L de Leopoldo (Lopez): the escape of the opponent, who was in the residence of the Spanish ambassador to Venezuela as a guest, since April 30, 2019, copied the interventions of the president and government officials in the last week of October, and generated a wave of reactions of chavismo against Spain, where López settled after his departure from Venezuela.

M of Migration:Due to the coronavirus pandemic, thousands of people who had left Venezuela fleeing misery were forced to return because they had lost their jobs in host countries, but over the months and the laxity of the closing and confinement measures, the exodus began again.

N of Shipwreck: The desire to leave the country led hundreds of Venezuelans to venture out by sea, especially to Trinidad and Tobago, in small and improvised boats that were wrecked, causing the drowning deaths of more than a hundred people during 2020.

Or Obstacle:if there is a country in Latin America where every day becomes an obstacle course, it is Venezuela. Opening the pot and crossing your fingers to get water out is probably the first challenge to overcome. And then... will there be light? How much will the bolivar have been devalued? Will the price of flour have doubled? Will you get gas?

Parliament's P: the institution that chavism has longed for since it lost in 2015 and which it managed to recover in the December 6 elections. Legislative power was a cause for debate every day of 2020. On 5 January, the new Members will take office and Guaidó will have to make way for the new generation, although he threatens to hold on to the parliamentary presidency against the wind and tide.

Q of Perhaps:in Venezuela there is no certainty of almost anything, not even of the most common issues. Maybe there's water today. Or not. Maybe you'll get gas, or maybe you won't. The light may not go out all day, or maybe it will. You'll probably get the medicine you need at a pharmacy. Or maybe none at all.

R of Resilience: Venezuelans' ability to adapt to almost any situation is not something new, but 2020 earned them to break their own record and prove that they are prepared to assume that a pandemic is just one more stone along the way.

Sanctions S: WithJoe Biden's victory in the U.S. presidential election, he came to Venezuela in the hope that sanctions blocking Caribbean country funds and property in the American nation will be lifted, at least in part, when the elected representative takes office on January 20.

Telework T : abad idea turned into an obligation. To telework, you need at least one stable internet connection, an electrical system without constant outages and good telephone signal. None of the three is guaranteed in Venezuela, let alone if it is a private address. The telework turned 2020 into a "teletortura".

U of Usurpation: if there is something that has not changed this year in the South American country it is Guaidó's favorite word. He maintains that Maduro is a "usurpable" for holding on to the Presidency that"assures" it is up to him, even though it has not been measured in an election.

Vaccine V: two days before the end of 2020, Venezuela signed with Russia a contract for the purchase of 10 million doses of the Sputnik V vaccine to prevent covid-19 and in it are given all hopes to return to normal.

W of Wuhan:the place where it all began, where the germ of the virus that would change the world was gestized, and that would give the final lunge to a Venezuela ravaged by dozens of vicissitudes and plunged into a crisis that many craved eternally.

X of Xenophobia:the amendments introduced by the National Electoral Council (CNE) for indigenous voting, including the elimination of direct and individual suffrage, resulted in rejection by the opposition and the detractors of chavism, who crossed out the governing body and the government of xenophobes and accused them of marginalizing minorities.

And from Yulimar (Rojas): in a few things there is consensus in such a polarized country, but the athlete, double world champion of triple jump and silver at the Olympic Games in Rio de Janeiro in 2016, again achieved unanimous applause, after receiving, last week, the 'Silvestre of the Year' award for the world indoor record she won with a jump of 15.43 meters at the Mitin in Madrid.

Zoom Z: The video call app shortened distances, facilitated interviews and allowed work meetings. And it also served to make birthday toasts or family parties that made loneliness more bearable. But, like any technological element, it is far from the ideal system in Venezuela, due to the lousy functioning of the connections.

title: Dollarization squeezes Maduro's "betrayal" on his failed socialism
text:
The unstoppable rise in the dollar in Venezuela has deranged dictator Nicolás Maduro, who to halt the rise of the US currency in the country, decided to inject public money through bonds.

The "consecutive flood maelstrom weekly" of the foreign currency puts pressure on the regime, whose unpredictable behavior led to an increase of 46.6% in the last three weeks, Ecoanalytics says.

The figure shows that the market is sensitive. The firm suggests that the dollar price is going through an "uncertainty" that enhances its value.

Changes (certain or not) to the minimum wage, the regime's intention to authorize a more sustained easing of local business activity and the coming (and almost inevitable) episodes of gasoline shortages are three factors affecting currency shooting.

The "injection of resources" by tyranny into the market is the "element that alters exchange dynamics".

According to Ecoanalytics data, chavismo records "interbank transactions with ever-increasing amounts of up to $37 million and a drastic fee cut is an unequivocal sign of central bank of Venezuela (BCV) interventions in such transactions, either directly or under payment orders issued from official entities."

An instant effect Following these actions, the amount of money issued by the BCV (monetary base or primary money) increased by 22.2% in real terms becoming "the largest increase seen in the aggregate since the beginning of 2019, when the minimum wage was tripled in a month," notes the analysis of the finance firm.

Although these movements of Maduro's socialism are executed "in the absence of official information on the origin of such an injection", it is clear that the "increase comes expressly from state payments to its employees of these eras, further fueled by the forthcoming legislative electoral processes convened for the coming week."

The move is far-fetched, as "for a country to increase its monetary base and monetary liquidity by 30%, it would take 50 weeks or four years," Alejandro Castro, Operations Manager, revealed to La Prensa.

title: Argentina and Venezuela: what they agree on and what they don't
text:
The escalation of financial and political dynamics makes the comparison with Venezuela appear more and more in the consultations we receive.

Both economies were favored by the jump in commodity prices during the first decade of the '00s and both maximized short-term growth through unsofiable income distribution. Both brought public spending to GDP above 40% and both forced a wage improvement well above their productivity. Both collided when the fall in commodity prices toppled exports, much more aggressively in Venezuela.

However, there are significant differences in the functioning of the economy and politics that do not extrapolate dynamics. Nor the possibility of living for more than seven years with an exchange gap well above 100% by decoupling domestic prices of the economy as happened between 2007 and 2014. Let alone the feasibility of sustaining "governance" in the face of a drift of the economy with sustained hyperinflation that in two years added five zeros to the currency.

In relation to the economy, the productive structure is very different. Venezuela is a food-importing country, and fuel exporter, produced by the state-owned company (PDVSA). That is, the export dollars went directly to the Central Bank, and the tax was financed directly from the company's profit transfers. The resulting company's decapitalization collapsed oil production, which until 2014 was offset by 19th crude oil prices.

Fuels historically accounted for 90% of Venezuelan exports and 50% of tax revenues. In Argentina, the export structure is significantly more diversified. The state "appropriates" part of exports via withholdings and taxes, and settlement is also mandatory within certain timeframes, but production is private. This is a minor difference in answering the question regarding the viability of the exchange rate gap at levels above 100%.

In the previous trap, with an average gap of 45%, one sojero producer took half the dollar price, the other half being withholdings and gap. With the 120% exchange gap and current withholdings a sojero producer takes a third of the price in marginal dollars, one-third are withholdings and the rest is a gap. Above these levels the settlement is slowed down and the BCRA loses reserves. It's not an exchange rate competitiveness problem, it's a gap problem.    

Venezuela is an economy that has coexisted with a very rigid trap since 2003 and a exchange rate gap above 100% since 2007 when it loses the fiscal surplus (180% of the exchange rate gap in 2009 and 2010) and a decoupling of domestic price dynamics that remained until 2014.

As of 2012 inflation stood at around 20/30% per annum and in 2013 and 2014, inflation stood at 58% and 68% respectively with an exchange rate gap of 474% and 1300% respectively. It is only in 2014 that the moderate inflation regime began to become one of high inflation with a price increase rate of 184%. Three years later Venezuela enters hyperinflation

The escalation of the gap in Venezuela occurs while the official exchange rate barely moved. There was a 100% jump in the official dollar in mid-2009 with the international financial crisis (the preferential for food imports remained at 2.15 bolivars and the official increased to 4.3). There was a second jump in 2015 (food import increased 50% to 6.3 bolivars, the officer jumped 200% to 12, and there was one free without intervention that by then was quoted toalmost 1000 bolivars).

Until 2015, the Treasury took advantage of the foreign exchange gap, placing dollar debt that was exchanged for bolivars through SITME at an exchange rate 50% higher than the official one. This scheme was supplied by Central Bank dollars that held dollar debt prices.

This decoupling of inflation from the exchange rate gap observed in Venezuela came against a back of high monetization of a primary deficit that started in 2007 and stood above 7% of GDP from 2009 with a 30% peak in GDP in 2018. Also with a very high current account surplus until 2008, and it was reduced to a level between 0 and 2% until 2014. In 2015, with the collapse in the price of crude oil, exports were cut in half, and the current account went into deficit. At this point it was when the scheme collapsed and Venezuela went to hyperinflation.

In relation to politics, while Argentina has alternation, Venezuela had an authoritarian regime that, after Chávez's death, intervened at the ballot box. The regime stands with the Army behind it and an interruption of the democratic system.

It is implausible to think that a government is holding up to such an economic dynamic here. The drift in Venezuela includes a 67% fall in GDP since 2004 and a price dynamic that has been inflation of more than 50% per month for three years.

In other words, there is no room to live in Argentina with a currency gap at these levels for a long time without inflationary consequences even with current account surpluses. In the previous trap, the gap never exceeded 80% and on average remained at 45% even with external deficits, but the expectation of political change in 2015 and the feasibility of opening the capital account to recompose reserves; and fundamentally the sale of BCRA futures during 2015 allowed local prices to be decoupled.

At the same time, it is unworkable to think of a scenario of monetary disruption that lasts in time without political consequences. The problem is that politics in Argentina reacts after the fire.

This crisis was avoidable. Managing the run since 2018 by squandering reserves, non-transition after the sung outcome of THE PASO, the nine-month delay in debt settlement paying with reserves, the pandemic and the handling of an eternal quarantine in a country without credit and without currency complicated everything.

title: Tensions with US contribute to Turkey-Venezuela alliance
text:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — At first glance they look like a strange couple.

But Turkey—a power in the Mediterranean that is often irritated by what it calls Western interventionism—and Venezuela, a Caribbean nation rich in oil and gold but in perpetual crises and under U.S. sanctions, have a few things in common.

There are economic ties; the most murky aspects have attracted scrutiny from the U.S. Treasury Department. They stand in solidarity in their anti-American discourse, even though the United States is one of Turkey's main trading partners. The personal relationship between the rulers of Venezuela and Turkey is warm, forged in part by words of mutual solidarity during internal attempts to expel them from power.

This alliance was evident Tuesday with Turkish Chancellor Mevlut Cavusoglu's visit to Caracas to sign agreements and commemorate the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two nations.

"There will be no sanctions, no blockades, no situation that prevents us from further deepening our integral relationship, and our economic and trade relationship in particular," Venezuelan Chancellor Jorge Arreaza said at a joint press conference with Cavusoglu.

The Turkish diplomat, who visited the Dominican Republic and Haiti before his arrival in Caracas, said his meetings in Venezuela focused on agriculture, construction, tourism, education and medical assistance. Despite the pandemic, the volume of trade between Turkey and Venezuela tripled in the first six months of this year compared to the same period in 2019, Cavusoglu noted without mentioning specific figures.

"We must continue," the Turkish minister declared. He told Arreaza that Turkish Airlines intends to become the first airline to resume flights to Caracas "when you open your airport".

The main international airport closed passenger flights due to the pandemic, although the number of airlines operating there had declined for years as the country fell into crisis. The economy deteriorated, political conflict and human rights abuses intensified, millions fled Venezuela, and U.S. sanctions virtually crippled its iconic oil industry, which has been struggling before.

Along with Russia and China, Turkey is among the small number of countries that represent a lifeline for Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, who has repelled the attempts of opposition leader Juan Guaidó to depose him. The United States has made it increasingly difficult for these countries to do business with Venezuela, as happened last week when it confiscated the cargo of four ships allegedly transporting Iranian fuel to Venezuela. Iran said the United States had no right to confiscate shipments in international waters.

The U.S. Treasury Department has also expressed concern about the gold venezuela says it flew to Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.

From early 2018, when foreign exchange reserves ran out, Venezuela began selling gold to pay for contracts, including some for a food distribution network that was used to carry out corruption in a plot allegedly led by Maduro's close friends, the department said.

A Turkey-based company run by Alex Saab, a Colombian entrepreneur linked to Maduro's circle, "bought goods in Turkey on behalf of Venezuelan customers, raising prices before selling them back to Venezuela," the department said last year.

Saab was arrested in Junecape Verde on his way to Iran and has challenged his extradition to the United States. Maduro's government said the businessman was traveling to Iran on a "humanitarian mission" to buy food and medical supplies.

Maduro, who seasons his speeches with socialist rhetoric, claims that American pressure amounts to an attempted coup. His personal relationship with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan began when he expressed solidarity after the Turkish ruler survived an assassination coup attempt by a group of military personnel in 2016. Erdogan returned the favor when Guaidó, whose movement is currently inactive, was campaigning intensely against Maduro.

However, Turkey continues to operate within U.S. restrictions. Last year, Turkish bank Ziraat stopped working with Venezuela's central bank due to U.S. sanctions.

"Therefore, U.S. punitive measures that increase the cost of Turkey's relations with Venezuela could force Erdogan to reduce his support for Maduro," even if he continues to censor U.S. policy toward Venezuela, former Turkishiplomatic Imdat Oner wrote. In an analysis for the Washington-based Wilson Center, Oner described the relationship between Turkey and Venezuela as "an alliance of convenience."

title: The Chavista regime raised the minimum wage to 300,000 bolivars, equivalent to $15
text:
A wad of sovereign bolivars, the currency that replaced the strong bolivar last year after inflation of 1,000,000% (Yuri CORTEZ / AFP)The Venezuelan regime of Nicolás Maduro announced on Monday a 375% increase in the minimum wage, which will now be 300,000 bolivars, according to the Chavista constituent Francisco Torrealba, in a measure that is far from covering the loss of capacity employees' purchasing.

"Happy Monday, new minimum income for all Workers in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela has been established in 300 thousand Sovereign Bolivars of which 150 thousand correspond to Minimum Wage and 150 thousand to Cesta Ticket Socialista," explained Torrealba, who is also chairman of the Committee of Workers of the ultra-chavista National Constituent Assembly, whose functions are in conflict with the opposition National Assembly.

Torrealba accompanied its publication with an image of the Official Gazette announcing the increase.

This is the third recomposition of the minimum wage for the year, as Cocuyo Effect recalls, amid a brutal economic crisis with high levels of inflation, sharp falls in domestic gross product (53% between 2013 and 2018) and an uncontrolled increase in the dollar.

#FelizLunes New minimum income for all Workers in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela has been established in 300 thousand Sovereign Bolivars of which 150 thousand correspond to Minimum Wage and 150 thousand to Cesta Ticket Socialista. #ClaseObreraResteadaConMaduro pic.twitter.com/lwTe7l6mvT

— Francisco Torrealba (@torrealbaf) October 14, 2019In fact, at Monday's official exchange, the minimum wage is equivalent to $15.2 on the official market, and about $18 in parallel, according to the Central Bank of Venezuela cited by Cocuyo Effect.

According to National Assembly data, inflation for 2019 is at the moment at 3.336%, so the measure is hardly used to alleviate the situation.

Inflation reached 130,000% in 2018 according to official data, although other estimates speak of about 1,000,000%. The extreme situation led to a currency exchange in August 2018, abandoning strong bolivars to adopt sovereign bolivars, a process that included removing several zeros.

The Central Bank of Venezuela (Reuters) (Marco Bello/)In January 2019 the minimum wage increased to 18,000 sovereign bolivars, and in April it did so to 40,000 (with 25,000 food basket), a derisory figure with which it was not even possible to buy a carton of eggs, but which remained until October.

Venezuela is also in the midst of an unprecedented political crisis, with a chavista regime that has been brutally repressed by opponents and is considered illegitimate by much of the international community, and an opposition national assembly elected in 2015 that appointed the legislator Juan Guaidó as interim president, without being able to fully hold the office.

Against this backdrop, it is estimated that nearly four million people have left the country in recent years.

title: So Victor Vargas' BOD swindled Venezuelans for millions of dollars
text:
The various institutions of the Chavista banker inside and outside Venezuela have been intervened by the authorities. Photomontage: PanAm Post.The Western Discount Bank (BOD), chaired by tycoon Victor Vargas, better known as Hugo Chavez's banker, is embroiled in a million-dollar scam scandal where the bank decided to attract clients, sell them dollars and subsequently prevent or complicate them from withdrawing their money.

Among the hundreds of victims of the million-dollar scam, there are Venezuelans who in the face of the crisis in the South American country decided to invest all their savings, relying on a bank that seemed serious; and there are those who decided to accept third-party payments with dollar deposits held by the bank.

To understand the BOD environment, it should be remembered that the financial institution has subsidiaries in different countries. There is the AllBank in Panama, the BOI Bank in Antigua and Barbuda, the Banco del Orinoco in Curacao and Bancamérica in the Dominican Republic.

#Antigua Regulatory Commission imposes special measures on #boibank belonging to the #bod group after #BancodelOrinoco interventions and pic.twitter.com/IfxZlpFyL5 #AllBank

— Gil & Rosas (@GilRosas_Ve) September 21, 2019

AllBank was intervened on 12 September by the financial authorities of Panama; the Orinoco Bank in Curacao faces a judicial settlement process after the Central Bank of that country found "serious irregularities". For its part, the Financial Services Regulatory Commission of Antigua issued a number of administrative measures derogators from the BOI Bank; while Bancamérica is currently going through a difficult period after the secretary and chairman of the Audit Committee resigned.

Letter from the Central Bank of Curacao to the employees of the Bank of Orinoco (First Report)The court's judgment in the case of the Banco del Orinoco on 5 September would be linked to the above-mentioned scam against clients of that financial institution; however, the bank decided to close and decree its liquidation.

"The court's measure was given two weeks before the bank decided to close, they claimed they had no way to pay us for the sanctions," a witness victim of the millionaire scam that the bank owes at least $2 million owed the bank told PanAm Post.

"We initiated the lawsuit in Curacao and when we went to court, the court ruled in our favor and gave the bank two weeks to pay the debt; however the bank decided to close and now we have to wait and see if they are going to fulfill the payment," he said.

Venezuelan journalist Casto Ocando published on its web portal Primer Informe, a circular issued by the Central Bank of Curacao and San Maarten dated September 27 in which the financial institution addressed the employees and customers of the Bando del Orinoco to tell them in a nutshell that "there is nofunds"."Unfortunately, the Bank has so far been unable to locate any substantial good in the BDO. This means that there are currently not enough funds to satisfy BDO creditors, or to pay any salary and/or benefits for employees. As a result, the Bank does not currently have the capacity to pay any wages for this month," reads in the missive.

The journalist noted through his social networks that, in addition, the Curacao Prosecutor's Office "studies opening a criminal investigation and filing charges for alleged fraud against the directive of Banco del Orinoco NV, among them Víctor Vargas, Luis Alfonso Borbón, Santos Alonso and Joel Santos".

Sources: Fiscalía de Curazao studies to open criminal investigation and bring charges of alleged fraud against the directive of Banco del Orinoco NV, among them Víctor Vargas, Luis Alfonso Borbón, Santos Alonso and Joel Santos.

— Casto Ocando (@cocando) September 30, 2019

The modus operandi of the scamTo describe how the Western Baco Discount (BOD) operated, PanAm Post relied on direct testimonies from victims, complaints via social media and press reports. He also contacted the administrators of the "BOD Scams" Facebook page and on Twitter @estafadosbod.

The Western Discount Bank in Venezuela started the acquisition of customers 8 years ago to sell them dollars at a preferential price, either with the aim of saving or doing some commercial transactions.

The complaints, made through social networks, indicate that at least 20,000 Venezuelan customers were scammed by the bank. The sum of the blocked funds is $1 billion.

In 2018 a group of entrepreneurs reported in Caracas that the BOD kept their savings hijacked and that, when they tried to withdraw them, the bank employees informed them that they were blocked because they had been invested by the financial institution.

According to a TV News report, one of the defense lawyers for the case, José Luis Alcalá, noted that "the bank has many difficulties, because they used investors' money to buy bonds from the national government debt, bonds that plummeted market and have failed to recover," says they "lost."

The idea was for customers to buy dollars in bolivars and their currencies to be deposited into accounts of their subsidiary banks. Some would have their money in Curacao, others in Panama, Antigua or the Dominican Republic.

Some customers were offered certificates of deposits, and others were given account numbers; the offer seemed really tempting as they could have an interest rate between 4.0% and 5.5% annualized on the condition that the money be kept there for a renewable 6-month term. If he did not wish to extend the time limit, he or she must inform you in writing about 10 days before the expiration date.

Usually these clients, in the case of Banco del Orinoco for example, waited for the 6 months to request that the funds be transferred to other accounts; however, they began to notice that the financial institution began to make excuses for them by preventing each saver from making their respective transfers or withdrawals.

There he allegedly initiated the BOD strategy, in many cases when clients sent the notification, the bank ignored it and then said that time had been met to somehow unlock the funds; in other cases customers began to notice "technical failures".

TestimoniesVictims who are considered scammed by the bank tell PanAm Post that on all occasions they triedwithdraw your money or make transfers to access the dollars, the bank set about making excuses or slowing down the process.Most witnesses prefer to remain anonymous because the bank has not yet paid them their money; they hope not to retaliate when making the complaint.

"We fell into a misleading offer, deposited our savings trying to safeguard our assets because of the situation in Venezuela. They did an excellent lobby for us to turn in our funds and we did. We even sold some properties to do so," one of the scammed Venezuelans told PanAm Post that as it still expects the bank to pay it, it preferred to remain anonymous; he also claims to have received some threats and extortion to stop him from reporting.

"It was at the end of 2016 when I moved my capital and my family's for that bank, there I put my savings of 50 years of work and now we are practically with nothing waiting for the BOD to give me my money," he said.

In their testimony, the victims of the scam pointed out that at first, when it came to attracting customers, the bank was very diligent and interested in serving them; yet everything changed when they began to claim their assets.

"The first two months were when we saw a good development with the bank, but then it got complicated because we started to see technical problems at the transfer level. My money was in Curacao at The Orinoco Bank, and I stumbled upon the surprise that at least 60 people (almost 40 were Venezuelan) had the same problem," the witness said as he traveled to the island to try to get his money back.

"Our savings are hijacked, we don't know what status they're in, in my case it's a million two hundred thousand dollars that the Orinoco Bank has withheld. The first excuses were that there were problems with the Caracas Stock Exchanges, after we had to wait. The answers are short and banal," he said.

Carlos Castellanos is another Venezuelan who settled in Bogota and who agreed to give his name to the PanAm Post because the bank paid him after his complaint was made public.

'I understand that the scam started in 2012, but I in 2014 sold all the properties I had in Venezuela, at the time I had 24 million bolivars and I did not know what to do with that money or where to deposit it and the BOD offered to open a deposit account in Antigu a. They were very kind, they had immense courtesy and my son and I opened two accounts," he said.

"They sold certificates of deposits with maturity of 60 or 90 days, and if you wanted to withdraw the money at the end of that period, you had to send a notification within 10 days of the deadline, so that then the money would be transferred to a checking account and make the transfer i.e. In sending the notification, the bank responded with a "received" and said that they would soon send a form that in some cases arrived, and in another cases was late when the date had expired," he added.

"From Panama we came to live in Colombia and I had a family medical emergency and I called the bank because I needed the money and the BOD replied that what I needed it for. The form came to me two weeks later in English and with some tiny letters. Already in 2016 I decided to go to Maracaibo, the city of the bank's headquarters and there they promised me that they would make me a transfer of 30 thousand dollars and give me a visa credit card. The transfer was not made, the card was given to me at two or three months and after two months they suspended it. After making the public complaint and waiting so hard, I finally got the bank to call me and pay me," he said.

Thesituation is complicated by the name of the BOD being the banker Victor Vargas, who in addition to these allegations would be involved in dark million-dollar plots at the international level; which is why BOD whistleblowers have serious doubts that they probably won't be able to get their money back.The power of journalism. title: Hyperinflation in Venezuela: So far this year, the price index accumulates 2.674%
text:
Venezuela is going through hyperinflation as a result of the crisis (Photo by Yuri CORTEZ / AFP)Hyperinflation in Venezuela continued in August its slowdown at a year-on-year pace, stood at 135.379%,according to a report by the opposition majority Parliament presented on Thursday. However, the price index increased compared to the previous month, at 65.2%, almost twice as muchas July, said Mr Angel Alvarado,a member of the Legislative Finance Committee, at a press conference.

So far this year, cumulative inflation 2.674%,the committee detailed.

The year-on-year slowdown responds to an "incipient" monetary discipline of the Chavista regime, the decline in public spending and the monetization of the deficit through the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV), evidenced through July, explained to the Agency AFP the Economist Asdrúbal Oliveros,of the firm Ecoanalítica.

But although compared to 2018 "the inflation rate is slightly lower", the fundamental problem has not been solved,the specialist said, auguring an upward trend the rest of the year.

Dictator Nicolás Maduro launched a reform program in August that included the elimination of five zeros to the bolivar and a 96% depreciation of the currency against the dollar,while promising to end the issuance of money without support, according to analysts , the main fuel for inflation.

In the absence of official statistics, the National Assembly publishes inflation rates on a monthly basis (EFE/Rayner Peña)Today in Venezuela, immersed in the worst crisis in its recent history, "the minimum wage (...) buys only 2% of the food basket,"Ms Alvarado said.

Maduro doubled the minimum wage in April to 40,000 bolivars, which then amounted to about $8 but today is only $2. A carton of 30 eggs, for example, is sold for 70,000 bolivars ($3.5) and one kilo of meat to 50,000 bolivars (2.5).

Parliament, the only power controlled by the opposition, has since 2017 disclosed its own inflation rate, in response to a statistical silence of the BCV, which had not given data for three years until it offered it again in May, although it has not remade.

The issuing body then reported that inflation in 2018 had reached 130.060% and that the economy has halved since 2013. It still doesn't release 2019 figures.

Parliament, whose decisions are considered null and void by justice after finding it "in contempt," calculated last year's inflation at 1,698,488.2%.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) reduced its inflation forecast in 2019 from 10,000,000% to 1,000,000%.

title: Savage capitalism in Venezuela
text:
After several years of expropriation, hyperinflation, bankruptcies and financial collapse, what is left of Venezuela's private sector could be forgiven for running out of hope.

But entrepreneurs say the economic crisis in the South American country accelerated the movements of Nicolas Maduro's government to move away from the full socialism of his predecessor, Hugo Chavez, towards a freer market.

"As business people we wanted price freedom and a free flow of dollars for many years. Now prices are effectively released and you can pay with dollars," says a senior consumer goods executive. Venezuela "adopted a savage capitalism," he adds.

Ministers did not officially announce policy changes and were not available for interviews. But entrepreneurs say that in recent months, rules restricting hard currency transactions have not been enforced, many price controls were abandoned, imports were freed, and Venezuela's shocked economy was struck Quickly.

462121As a result, some products that were previously scarce or could not be re-appeared in stores, although their prices are out of reach of the vast majority of shoppers. Inflation fell from its stratospheric levels of more than 100,000% last year, to an expected level of several thousand percent this year.

462125"The economy stabilized to some extent," says Dimitris Pantoulas, an analyst and consultant in Caracas. "It was chaos, with rows everywhere and no food. But now, even though it's much more expensive, you can get whatever you want."

"There is a certain orthodoxy," said Asdrúbal Oliveros, director of Ecoanalytics. "But he came very late and in a messy manner. The controls were not lifted, they just don't apply. This is very arbitrary."

No one suggests that Venezuela's economy, paralyzed by years of mismanagement and reeling from US sanctions, is in something close to a sustainable position. Gross Domestic Product was more than halved in a few years, in what Ricardo Hausmann, a former central banker, called the greatest economic collapse in the modern era other than a war or a natural disaster.

But some business leaders welcomed the greatest economic freedom in recent months, even if the reasons for the Maduro government are far from pure.

"It was not out of conviction but by necessity that the pressure of exchange rate controls was reduced," said Carlos Larrazábal, outgoing head of Fedecámaras, the country's main trade association. "There is a deep recession in the productive sectors, consumption is falling dramatically, there is no funding.... credit is impossible."

To combat inflation, banks were forced to keep 100% of deposits as mandatory reserves at the central bank, which suspended loans. Credit card limits failed to keep pace with galloping inflation, which put a brake on consumer lending. And some of the few remaining industries that still work complain that they cannot compete in production costs with cheap, unregulated imports.

"Purchasing power plummeted, so sales fell 20% from its previous level," says the owner of a manufacturing plant. "But I still have a factory ready to produce for a much larger market. So, in the short term, this situation is no better. But in the long run, it's good because there's less state intervention."

Pantoulas compared Venezuela to a warlike economy. Only "10%of the population has access to everything they want, but the other 90% live in hardship," he says.In fact, the annual fedecámaras assembly, held this month at a university in Caracas, had a certain sense of wartime. When the speaker system did not play the national anthem during the opening session, delegates stood up and shouted of "Viva Venezuela!".

"The private sector refuses to disappear," Larrazábal said in a defiant speech to delegates. "This is not an option for us.... we are part of the solution, not part of the problem."

When the FT asked him in advance how long the private sector could resist, he painted a bleaker picture: "It's hard to predict... there used to be more than 12,000, almost 13,000 industrial establishments (in 1998), now there are no more than 3,000 left."

The Mexican exception also creates Washington's strategic need for no other exception in Argentina. title: The thousand and one ways of living without light or water in Venezuela
text:
By the time you read this, surely millions of people in Venezuela continue without hydropower for six days. The tragedy that is lived in that country is understood only, perhaps, by someone who suffers it or has lived something similar a while ago.

They are six days without light or water, in much of the country. Without Internet and without metro in Caracas, the main means of transport of the capital used by almost three million people, according to the Ministry of Transport. From Thursday until Monday morning, electric service was almost nil throughout the country. The Internet measurement observatory, Netblocks, published on Saturday that 96% of Venezuela was without this service, after the blackout.

The less fortunate saw how their relatives died, as did Elizabeth Diaz, a resident of Valencia, the third most important city in the country. Her 19-year-old daughter suffered from cerebral palsy, and weighed 10 kilos of chronic malnutrition. Díaz narrated a local journalist who, after suffering a medical emergency last Saturday, decided to take her to two public outpatient clinics, but they did not attend her for lack of electricity. Then the city police transferred them to the Central Hospital in Valencia, where the young woman died in the arms of her mother.

See more: Why did Migración Colombia not allow Maduro's cousin to enter the country?

Entire Venezuela was dark and desolate day and night for three continuous days. The oil country, in just five days, lost 26 confirmed lives, so far, due to the blackout, according to the National Survey of Hospitals. This caused, in addition, by the nonexistence of power plants in 50% of the public hospitals throughout the nation. However, Juan Guaidó, president sworn in by the National Assembly and recognized by more than 60 countries, said on Sunday that there may be between 40 and 60 fatalities, unofficially, because before the national blackout, communications in the oil nation have Been complicated and have not been able to confirm more.

For everyday life, power plants were transformed into the salvation of those who have them in their homes, but also on the right hand of the media, some private companies, telephone companies and even hotels. During those three days without electricity, there was no way to pay, in a nation where cash is scarce and the currency is devalued by more than 96%, according to the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV). Where the datáfonos, called "point of sale" in the South American country, did not work because there was almost no telephone signal. What caused that in specific areas of two of the three highways of the city, these became the meeting point of dozens of people, seeking coverage to communicate.

Given this, part of the more than 2.3 million Venezuelans abroad, according to the UN, when they heard the news about the blackout, quickly entered into despair because they could not contact their family and friends. While on the other hand, Venezuelans in that nation, around 30 million inhabitants, searched during the day to resolve their situation in the face of the crisis. Many left their homes early, for two or three days, to pharmacies and supermarkets that were open, to buy mainly non-perishable food, as well as ice and salt in order to keep their food in good condition. Before this, the dollar bills became an escape to chaos. Mainly, for those who fortunately have foreign currency.

See more: Spain offered help in Venezuela's energy crisis

However, there were more stores, supermarkets, gas stations and pharmacies that had to close,because there was no electricity. In addition to the fear of their owners before possible looting, events that occurred in a store in Caracas and in Maracaibo, Zulia state, in a shopping center and different stores. They only opened those businesses that had an electric plant.

The car and the charger to use in this became the best ally of those who have them. And, although many did not have the same luck, in their cars they could listen to some of the radio stations, which managed to be on the air. "It was hard for us to communicate. There was no access to mobile data. I could not stand this level of misinformation anymore. I did not know anything, or anyone and it was driving me crazy, "said Carlos Rodriguez, 28, from Caracas.

The reason for the electrical failure that generated such a crisis in an oil country, was partially known, about an hour and a half after almost the entire Venezuela went off last Thursday afternoon. Luis Motta Domínguez, Minister of Electric Energy and president of Corpoelec, reported that this situation was due to "sabotage", an argument that was later repeated by Jorge Rodríguez, Minister of Communication, who also added that it was the fault of the "American empire" and Marco Rubio, American senator. However, a day later Rodriguez said it was "a cyber attack by the United States."

See more: Diplomatic blackout in Venezuela?

During the day, and the partial restoration in some areas and not in others, the streets of the urbanizations and neighborhoods, neighbors were seen to go down to talk among themselves, while the younger ones carried out activities that perhaps because of the existence of the Internet and the technology have been lost in this new century. Several took advantage of their days also to read and even to play board games with the family, without knowing for almost three days what was happening specifically.

"This is for a while, we must prepare," said several citizens. Many lost food, because ice and salt were not enough. Others cooked on grills inside or outside their homes, because they do not have a gas stove, but an electric one. "On Friday night we resolved dinner with bread and cheese. The next day, the situation continued, our breakfast remained bread and cheese, fortunately we had. Then we went to buy charcoal, to use a small barbecue in the apartment to solve the cooking of meat, make arepas and coffee. We swallowed smoke, but we managed to change the menu, "said Carmen Diaz, 50.

However, the hours without light kept happening and with it the desperation increased. At night, citizens played pots in protest and shouted slogans against Nicolás Maduro. On Saturday, thousands went out to protest all over the country, due to the failures in the electric service, in a demonstration called by Juan Guaidó.

But it was on Sunday that the president of Parliament, together with deputies to the National Assembly, and the engineer José de Viana, former president of Hidrocapital (public water utility company in Caracas) and Movilnet (mobile phone company), assured that the situation was generated by an incident in the interconnection system in the high voltage networks, which transport electricity from the generating plant, to the cities located in the interior and west of Venezuela.

See more: In Venezuela years ago there was a foreign intervention

"An accident of these is terrible and therefore is avoided. There are 2000 kilometers to be maintained and taken care of (pruning and cutting) very well because it has to be without vegetation, "said De Viana. Statement that resembles sources linked to Corpoelec, who according to Guaidó, confirmed that a vegetation fire on Thursday afternoon affected thethree lines of 765 kilovolts between El Guri - the largest reservoir in Venezuela, which feeds more than 80% of the country's electricity - and the Malena and San Gerónimo B substations

Given this, in Caracas today electric service has returned almost entirely, but not in the surrounding areas. Many homes in the capital have not had electricity for six days, although in the interior of the country, the situation is more tragic. At least 12 Venezuelan states continue without these basic services, including the long lines to get gasoline throughout Venezuela.

If there is no light, there is no water During these last six days the water service has also been affected. If the Venezuelan already had daily rationing, imposed by zones, for years now, now nobody receives it.

In Caracas, after the light was partially restored after three days in much of the city, the scenes have taken a turn. Now, the situation is to search according to economic possibilities, the way to get water.

On the Boyacá avenue (cota thousand), similar to the Bogota circumvallation, the image of citizens drinking water from El Ávila, a mountain located north of the capital, is repeated daily. Entire families get off their cars with pots and containers of different sizes to make long lines and get the liquid. While others come walking, to join that group. The same thing happens on the Francisco Fajardo highway, the main road that connects the entire city, where the Guaire River is located nearby, a well-known waterway, and where people from Caracas go to get a water pipeline that flows into it.

See more: The day that Venezuela went out

In the case of people with greater purchasing power, they cancel the tank truck service, which in the face of the crisis they charge in dollars in cash. While in the interior of the country, there are images of some Venezuelans who are bathing in sewers. "In the coming hours we will be gradually reestablishing the supply of drinking water in all the big cities of the country (...) I also announce the activation of the 'Blue Tank' plan to provide water reserve tanks to all the homes of the country, "said Nicolás Maduro, on national television on Tuesday.

However, for José De Viana, an engineer and specialist in the area, he indicated that the water supply could normalize in seven days "after the Caracas metro starts operating again. When that happens they will know that the electrical system was restored, "he said.

See more: Venezuela blames the US UU of the worst blackout in its history

Meanwhile, Tarek El Aissami, attorney general, appointed by the National Constituent Assembly, announced on Tuesday that they were opening a new investigation against Juan Guaidó, for his alleged involvement in the "electrical sabotage." While Maduro also designated that day a International Commission, with the support of China, Russia and the UN, "to investigate thoroughly what happened and establish responsibilities, the world must know the full truth about the attack, high technology," he said on national television.

For their part, Venezuelans continue to be dismayed, some unbelievers, about the situation they lived for more than three days. "I never thought to live something like that. I knew that outside of Caracas these things happened, but I never thought that in the capital and for so many days, "said Laura De Freitas, 21 years old.

title: Venezuela's Maduro loosens private sector,  currency  red tape-sources
text:
CARACAS, Jan 31 (Reuters) - As Venezuela grapples with U.S. sanctions on its vital oil industry, socialist President Nicolas Maduro has made plans to lift some price and foreign exchange controls in a bid to revive the country's battered economy, sources said.

Since 2014, Maduro's government has directly imported and distributed raw material for industries like food processing and construction. But the government has now informed some companies in private meetings that they can buy their own foreign currency to import what they need, five industrial and financial industry sources said.

Until now they have had to go through the government's complex system of exchange controls to obtain scarce foreign currency.

But business leaders said the shift may have limited impact with Venezuela deep in hyperinflation after five years of recession.

TOO LATE

"This has come too late," said Jorge Botti, a former leader of Venezuela's largest industry group, Fedecamaras. "Even the most optimistic people, who for months held out for a shift in economic policy, are now betting on a change in government."

Venezuela's central bank said on Tuesday that starting in February, banks would be able to sell euros to private companies in "strategic sectors."

The banks would be assigned euros each Monday depending on how much local currency they had deposited in central bank coffers.

The change comes as Maduro is facing the boldest challenge since taking office in 2013. Opposition leader Juan Guaido has claimed the presidency, arguing that Maduro's May 2018 re-election was fraudulent. He has won support from the United States and many Latin American countries.

The United States imposed sanctions this week that will likely halt exports of crude oil from state oil company PDVSA to U.S. refineries, cutting off a key source of the OPEC nation's revenue in order to pressure Maduro into leaving office and allowing Guaido to call elections.

Years of heavy government intervention have prompted several multinational companies to abandon Venezuela. The walk back of regulations comes as the government has allowed the bolivar to depreciate to the parallel rate, after years of controls created a black market for foreign currency.

The changes come after sanctions from the United States and European Union have made it difficult for the government to move money abroad since banks are wary of dealing with it.

Venezuela's official foreign exchange system has offered very little hard currency to the private sector since 2015, after a collapse in oil prices left government coffers dry.

Maduro blames the economic crisis on private companies, which he accuses of conspiring with the domestic opposition and the United States to wage an "economic war."

One of the people with knowledge of the policy changes said companies with export capacity would be the only ones that would be able to buy euros from banks.

The government would also make its system of price controls, which are intended to contain inflation but have instead contributed to shortages of basic goods, more "flexible" to allow prices to rise in line with the bolivar's depreciation, the sources said. ($1 = 0.8740 euro) (Writing by Luc Cohen Editing by Phil Berlowitz)

title: Venezuela 's  Central Bank  to  intervene  to stabilize exchange rate
text:
CARACAS, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Venezuela's Central Bank said on Tuesday it will intervene in the foreign currency market to stabilize the exchange rate between the bolivar and the U.S. dollar with the goal of stemming hyperinflation.

In a statement on its website, the bank said it would aim to stabilize the rate at 3,300 Bolivar Soberanos (Sovereign Bolivars) to the dollar. Inflation in Venezuela is estimated to reach 10 million percent this year. (Reporting by Caracas newsroom Writing by Angus Berwick; editing by Frank Jack Daniel)
