title: Latin America "builds" a legal wall against Venezuelan migration
text:
The UN points out that there are 2.3 million Venezuelans who left their country. A figure that can increase especially after the recent economic measures that gave Maduro (EFE) The massive migration of Venezuelans became the worst migration crisis in the history of Latin America; a drama that this week went around the world, but that has been overshadowed by the same affected region.

The UN estimates that 2.3 million Venezuelans have fled their country. At this rate, they will be the largest number of displaced persons in the history of Latin America, and could even surpass those displaced by the Syrian crisis (6m). (Via @ TheEconomist)

Do we take it seriously? pic.twitter.com/yGtSqRFfcz

- Rodrigo Morales C (@Rodrigomoralesc) August 20, 2018

This Monday, August 20, the first pages of the mass media were dedicated to the great suffering that Venezuelans face today, not only in their country where Nicolás Maduro offered a series of announcements that formalize the devaluation of 95.8% of the currency - figure according to the same Central Bank of Venezuela -, but also the hardships to which they are subjected when leaving their land looking for a "better future".

From the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the big television platforms in England, France and Germany reflected the reality of a migratory crisis only comparable to that of Syria, while the rest of the media in Latin America, turned their eyes towards the new migratory measures that in the end, somehow, closes the doors to thousands of Venezuelans desperate to flee from a nation in ruins.

The crisis is such that the OAS convened an extraordinary meeting to deal with the mass migration of Venezuelans; While on Tuesday, the Government of Ecuador also convened a meeting to discuss the unusual migratory flows of Venezuelan citizens.

The Government of #Ecuador calls a meeting on September 17 and 18 in Quito to discuss the unusual migratory flows of Venezuelan citizens. Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, Costa Rica, Chile, Mexico, Peru, Paraguay, Panama, Dominican Republic, Uruguay and #Venezuela invited.

- Mariano de Alba (@marianodealba) August 21, 2018

And is that the governments of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Chile and Argentina made the decision to adjust their immigration laws to reduce the flow of Venezuelans for reasons of "security", although this announcement left thousands of Venezuelans on the verge of emotional collapse .

Despite the disparity of figures, the most recent and most stringent show that the emigration of citizens of this country, in the last two years, roughly equivalent to the population of cities such as Cartagena (Colombia), Arequipa (Peru) or a fourth part of the inhabitants of Caracas.

The UN points out that there are 2.3 million Venezuelans who left their country. A figure that can increase especially after the recent economic measures that gave Maduro in which he announced not only the devaluation of the currency, but also the increase in taxes and gasoline prices.

Between 2015 and 2017 the migration of Venezuelans to all parts of the world increased by 132%; in the case ofthose that go to countries of South America the increase was of 895%.

The "construction" of a legal wall began While the countries of the region have strongly criticized the president of the United States, Donald Trump for wanting to build a wall to prevent immigration, on the other hand the American continent begins to put obstacles against Venezuelans who flee desperate from their country. Measures that would also be causing many Venezuelan relatives can not meet under the principle of family reunification, a universal right.

Venezuelans without a passport are in the outskirts of the Ecuadorian city of Tulcán (EFE / Maria Paula Goyes) Colombia, Ecuador and Peru now demand that Venezuelans show their passports in order to enter; this, despite knowing the "impossible mission" that citizens face in order to acquire the document because the Nicolás Maduro regime paralyzed the delivery.

Getting a passport in Venezuela can cost about $ 1,000 on the black market, in a country where the salary does not exceed USD $ 2 per month.

The requirement of current passports was challenged by the Ombudsman of Ecuador, who requested precautionary measures before the courts to prevent the application of the measure. The Ombudsman, Gina Benavides, said that this requirement is not legal or constitutional, and ensures that it goes against "basic principles of humanitarian assistance."

The General Director of Migration Colombia, Christian Krüger Sarmiento, criticized Ecuador and Peru for demanding that those fleeing Venezuela present a valid passport.

"To demand passport today for Venezuelan citizens, when we know that their government is not issuing them, is to punish the people for the mistakes of their leaders, because we can not forget that Venezuelan citizens are leaving their country not for pleasure, but because of of the expulsion policy that Mr. Maduro has imposed, "said Krüger.

Venezuelan immigrants gather outside Tulcán in Ecuador (EFE / Maria Paula Goyes) To this measure of the passports, the announcement thatThe Peruvian government made the deadline for Venezuelans who enter the country before October 31 and can apply for the Temporary Permit of Permanence.

But Venezuelans who flee from the severe economic crisis, can not move through all the countries of the region with ease. Because countries like Chile or Panama also require a visa.

Last April, Chile announced the creation of the "democratic responsibility visa" for those Venezuelans who would like to work and remain temporarily in the country. A permit that can only be requested through the consulates of Chile in Venezuela.

For its part, in 2017, the government of Panama also began to demand a stamped visa for all Venezuelans who would like to visit that country for a maximum period of 30 days.

After Panama, Honduras, Nicaragua, Guatemala and El Salvador adhered to this regulation that requires a special visa for Venezuelans; while the 27 countries of the European Union require a passport with at least nine months of validity, round-trip tickets and, in some cases, even a letter of invitation and medical insurance. Venezuelans are fleeing their country with very little money in their pockets and with few belongings; Although they emigrate with the hope of achieving quality of life, they are becoming a great burden for the other nations of the region.

While that happens, many Venezuelans with dreams and illusions see how little by little they are "closing the doors" to emigrate, because we must remember that Nicolás Maduro has installed "kidnapping" as state policy, denying thousands of citizens the right to their passports; reason why the most expeditious solution was to leave the country by land and only with the identity card.

How to tell those migrants, who probably sold all their belongings, who can not reach their destinations and who have to return to a country in ruins? It is condemning thousands of Venezuelans to a state of depression without return. Above all, for those who are already in their destination country and who hope to reunite with their children and family.

Thus, while the whole world criticizes the wall that Trump plans to build between the United States and Mexico, Venezuelans are forced to face a humanitarian crisis unique in its contemporary history and also the "construction" of a legal wall to reduce its migratory flow The governments of the world refuse to be part of a military intervention in Venezuela, but they also refuse to receive the thousands of Venezuelans who seek to save their lives and those of their relatives.

title: Keys to understanding the case Banesco  Venezuela
text:
The Venezuelan bank Banesco Banco Universal CA was intervened by the Bolivarian Government on May 3 while eleven senior executives were detained by the Public Ministry of that country. The charge: breach of obligated subjects; that is to say, according to the government, there was responsibility of the top management of the banking entity to 'facilitate or cover up the attacks against the Venezuelan currency'.

But how was the Venezuelan currency 'attacked' exactly? Lenny Durán, Venezuelan reporter specializing in economic issues, helps us understand it.

OPERATION OF PAPER HANDS

The Venezuelan Government, together with the nation's security forces, began Operation Hands of Paper to dismantle the criminal gangs that have carried out the extraction and theft of the monetary cone, as well as the imposition of criminal rates of the speculative dollar. The action resulted in the discovery of 1,133 bank accounts in 19 national banks that, according to the Venezuelan government, used a 'transnational network of organized crime' to extract paper money and purchase cash to the Colombian-Venezuelan border.

Of the total bank accounts raided, 959 belonged to Banesco; that is, 90%, which is why the Attorney General, Tareck William Saab, linked the management of Banesco Venezuela with the plot and gave rise to the intervention of the financial institution for ninety days.

BACKGROUND

Durán recalled that the government has said on other occasions that international mafias take out the country's notes (mainly towards Cúcuta), to make fake dollars or to acquire subsidized goods sold in Colombia.

The reporter explained to La Estrella de Panama that this argument was used by President Nicolás Maduro in December 2016 to take out of circulation the 100 bolívares ticket, which at that time was the highest denomination, in a period of 72 hours, without that the 500 bolivars bill that was going to replace it had still reached the banks. That generated chaos because that (the Bs.100) was the ticket with which people could buy their goods, without having to load so much cash, in a country where the rates of insecurity are eleven times higher than the world average. , according to Amnesty International.

On the border with Colombia, the 'mafias', in which according to the communicator also participate Venezuelan national guards, people connected with the government and citizens of the neighboring country, bought the tickets for a price less than their value. "In the end that measure only created a terrible shortage of cash, since people had to make long lines in the banks in an attempt to get rid of the bills that would lose their value in 72 hours. There were even elderly people who burned them or threw them out because of the frustration of not being able to change them, "Durán explained.

Maduro retracted and postponed the measure "benefiting the mafias he said he was fighting." He has already tried thirteen times to remove the 100 bolivars bill from circulation and it has not yet been done; supposedly next May 20 is the last term, now under a new monetary cone, said the editor of informative portals.

Regarding the accusation of currency speculation, Durán recalled that in Venezuela there has been exchange control for many years; that is, there is a dollar price set by the government and a real price. At one point there were up to seven exchange rates, one of which was preferential for supposedly importing medicines and basic necessities, but only those people connected to the government through their companies had access to these currencies.

At present, the common citizen does not have the facility to obtain dollars at the official price, because there is little supply, except for the auctions that he carries out.eventually the government and to which only people with high purchasing power and close to the government have access. The only way for people 'to walk' to acquire foreign currency is to buy them on the black market, which is known as the parallel market, which in many cases has the price closest to the dollar with respect to the bolivar, although it also lends itself to speculation.

The Operation Hands of Paper was born to detect those mafias that, says the Government, 'try to establish a parallel financial system with speculative dollar rates'.

INTERVENTION

Banesco is the only bank in Venezuela through which people living abroad can send remittances to their families, they sell the dollars and thus have cash in bolivars to buy basic necessities. Many Venezuelans consulted indicated that it is "the only reliable bank at the moment", while economists, analysts and opposition sectors point out that the Maduro government wants to control those currencies that are entering Banesco through the remittances that are sent.

According to a report by the firm Datos, about $ 1,500 million of remittances come into the country each year. The report also notes that 14% of Venezuela's adult population (approximately three million people) receives money, food and medicine from abroad. And of that 14%, 11% receive foreign currency (euros or dollars) and the other 3% get medicines, food and also foreign currency.

The communicator deduces that the idea of ??the government is that these remittances do not reach directly to their recipients, but that the Central Bank of Venezuela manages them and gives the family the official equivalent price in bolivars for them to keep the foreign currency.

One dollar in Venezuela, in the parallel market (black) is equivalent to Bs.710,845.12 (until May 11), while the Dicom price (official rate) is in Bs.70,000 (until May 11). To have an idea, a dozen eggs cost Bs. 2 million according to consulted sources, and every day reflects an increase (see graph).

Last January, Chavez leader Diosdado Cabello commented in a radio program that they were in negotiations for the purchase of Banesco, as he said then, for 3.5 million dollars, "Banesco put it on sale for us cheap, really cheap," he said in statements replicated in international media; same as at that time refuted Juan Carlos Escotet, president of Banesco, to deny in their social networks that the bank was for sale. 'Today more than ever, my bet is for Venezuela,' the executive posted on his Twitter account.

BANESCO PANAMA, OUT OF THE EQUATION

Banesco was established in Panama in 1993 to operate under an international license as a subsidiary of Banesco Holding CA, of Venezuelan capital, although the opening was made in dollars because it is the circulation currency in Panama. Subsequently, in 2007 they entered the local market with a general license, which is what they currently maintain.

The Banking Superintendency of Panama clarified in a statement that the Banesco group (including its Abanca brand in Europe) is structured legally and organizationally in four main parallel markets: Venezuela, the United States, Europe and Panama, so they have a "management of their banking business separately and independently 'and stressed that Banesco, SA (Panama)' has no relationship with the banking business in Venezuela. "Fitch Ratings sees this primarily as a correction to an overly sanguine view on the U.S. interest-rate outlook rather than signaling any serious threat of a sharp economic slowdown," he says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

They explains this by saying that asset managers and insurers that have reduced their bund holdings due to low yield levels over recent years might return to the market and compete increasingly with the European System of Central Banks--the ECB and national central banks. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0906 ET - The eurozone's four largest issuers--Italy (up to EUR7.75 billion), Germany (EUR1.5 billion), France (up to EUR10 billion in nominal and inflation-linked bonds) and Spain (estimated EUR4.5 billion)--, plus Portugal (up to EUR1.25 billion) have scheduled government bond auctions for next week, aiming to sell up to around EUR25 billion in a test for investor appetite in the current market turmoil. Duration, however, "will be manageable," said Antoine Bouvet, rates strategist at Mizuho, as maturities stretch across the curve and five issuers. With supply significantly exceeding coupon payments, there will be positive net supply. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0907 ET - Canada's latest jobs report suggests an earlier surge in employment creation may have been too good to be true, said Avery Shenfeld, chief economist at CIBC World Markets. Canada dropped 88,000 jobs in January, giving back roughly half of the significant gains that were registered late in 2017. "Market participants are getting schooled in the ways of Canada's employment numbers, and the lesson seems to be that when they're too good to be true, they might not be," Shenfeld wrote. (kim.mackrael@wsj.com; @kimmackrael)

title: Omar Barboza: The petro is not constitutional
text:
The president of the National Assembly Omar Barboza, indicated that the petro "is not constitutional", after having been approved the nullity of the cryptocurrency in the session that took place this Wednesday, January 10, the parliament.

"It is not constitutional, according to article 12, oil, natural resources, can not be given in guarantees ... Article 318 of the Constitution says that the monetary unit of Venezuela is the bolivar, and that only through international agreements , that currencies are agreed between several countries, we ask to have a means of exchange different from the bolivar as a monetary unit, "he said in an interview with Venevisión.

He also noted that "The hydrocarbons law in its third article prohibits giving oil as collateral," assuring that this economic measure is a form in which the government "evades its obligations."

"This is a way of evading the fulfillment of obligations again. If the government needs some solutions to the economic and debt issue, it simply has to do one thing so that it has our support ... if it is not approved by the National Assembly, it is null, "he added.

Concerning what in his opinion is a humanitarian crisis and the possible international intervention of Venezuela, he stated: "The Venezuelan people have to live at the cost of a parallel dollar that already goes above 140 thousand bolivars ... while those of the government have dollar to 10 (...) ".

In addition, he explained that money circulation "has to correspond to international reserves and national production" and that the Central Bank of Venezuela is "a banknote factory without backup."

"In 2014, in the month of April, the national monetary circulation was around one trillion bolivars, today it is over 12 trillion bolivars," he said on the subject.

After the approval of the national humanitarian alliance by the National Assembly, he explained that they will visit institutions to coordinate aid to the most needy: "We are going to visit many institutions, highly qualified and credible in the country, that can help tell all Venezuelans, let us put our hands in our hearts and we will help our compatriots who are suffering, who do not have how to satisfy their basic needs, and who help us, a bread flour, two kilos of rice, a clothing that it does not work for us. "

"We will ask the Episcopal Conference to assume this activity, in function that they can be recipients of the aids, so that they can fairly and transparently reach those in need," he said.

"We are going to go out and promote that alliance (...) It's not a political issue, it's a human issue," he stressed.

As for the legislative initiatives of the Assembly added: "We are of the criterion, that political change is a precondition to solve the underlying problems that Venezuelans are suffering ... that is why we are going to build, we are going to promote ... to rebuild the unity democratic as an alternative ... our call is that we can not give up fighting for Venezuela without trying to find a democratic alternative. "

title: Global  Forex  and Fixed Income Roundup: Market Talk
text:
11:36 ET - Venezuela President Maduro's decision to rewrite the constitution is pushing the country's political crisis to the brink "into an all-or-nothing stand-off, from which a stable transition or exit looks increasingly difficult," Teneo Intelligence says. The consultancy boils Maduro's strategy down into three main points: to avoid elections, divide the opposition, and try to weaken international resolve to intervene in Venezuela. "This is a hazardous strategy," Teneo notes because it will radicalize the anti-government protest movement, increasing the risk of serious violent disorder. (kejal.vyas@wsj.com; @kejalvyas)

11:35 ET - Foreign investors bought a net $20.6B in emerging-market assets in April, a slowdown from inflows of about $30B in both February and March, IIF data shows. Investors have poured into emerging-market currencies, stocks and bonds this year, as worries over higher US interest rates diminished and growth in developing economies picked up. Last month, appetite for riskier assets was dented by the French election and escalating geopolitical tensions with North Korea. Still, flows into EM assets have been positive for five straight months. Developing Asian economies received roughly 80% of April's inflows, IIF data shows. Foreign investors bought a net $13.8B in debt and only $6.8B in equities. (chelsey.dulaney@wsj.com)

11:21 ET - With Venezuela's opposition pledging to ramp up anti-government demonstrations, there is a risk of the protest movement reaching a breaking point, overcoming the capacity of security forces to contain them for several consecutive weeks, says risk consultancy IHS Markit. So far, Venezuela's armed forces has provided almost unconditional support to President Maduro, but IHS warns that that loyalty could wither in the face of wider spread looting and an increasing death toll. Another scenario, IHS says, is that the military convinces Maduro to step down and call for elections later this year instead of 2018, something that the leader has thus far ruled out. (kejal.vyas@wsj.com)

1515 GMT - Greek economic sentiment grew to 94.9 points in April, from 93.4 in March and 90.7 points a year ago, Greek think-tank IOBE said in its monthly report. Business expectations improved in the services and commerce sectors were stable in manufacturing but deteriorated in the construction sector. Greek consumer confidence remained at very low levels, but ended a three-month decline, due to expectations for a swift conclusion of the a second bailout review. (nektaria.stamouli@wsj.com)

11:11 ET - Venezuela's opposition begins what it says is a new, intensified wave of street demonstrations against President Nicolas Maduro after the leftist leader's decree to rewrite the country's constitution. His rivals call Maduro's move a nuclear option to cling onto power in the oil-rich country and avoid elections that polls show his ruling Socialist Party would easily lose. Protesters are blocking traffic in the capital Caracas and major cities around Venezuela, facing tear gas and National Guard armored vehicles. At least 29 people have died in violent clashes over a month of protests but the opposition says it will remain on the streets until Maduro allows for general elections and the chance to vote on the presidency. (kejal.vyas@wsj.com)

"This week's [Fed] announcement should be fairly sleepy, lacking in pomp with no press conference, no updated dot plots or new growth forecast," Lascelles says. A "slightly softer" statement is likely, given recent macro data showing lower inflation, a lower index of US manufacturing activity, weak 1Q GDP growth and soft March payroll numbers, he says. title: Venezuela to Use Diamonds to Boost International Reserves
text:
CARACAS--Venezuela, facing default fears amid an economic crisis and falling oil prices, will use diamonds as well as other precious stones and metals stored in its central-bank vaults to boost international reserves, the central bank said Thursday.

It will also incorporate easy-to-convert foreign currencies into its reserves, the bank said in a statement explaining changes to a law regulating its activities. Venezuela's international reserves have dropped 28% in the last three years to $21.7 billion.

The country is likely to start holding some reserves in Chinese Yuan, a central bank official familiar with the matter said.

It is the latest effort by President Nicolás Maduro--whose approval rating hit a record low of 24.5%, according to a poll released this week--to try and salvage the oil-rich, but cash-poor economy. The country is facing crippling dollar shortages and scarcity of imported food and consumer goods. Its local currency, the bolívar, is in free fall, reaching new lows almost daily.

But analysts said the new accounting methods for international reserves would do little to build trust among investors, who currently charge Venezuela one of the highest borrowing rates in the developing world.

"It looks like a cosmetic boost to the reserves which doesn't improve investor confidence and doesn't improve reserve liquidity," said Siobhan Morden, head of Latin America strategy at Jefferies in New York. "This is a strategy of counting pennies to see how long they have."

Venezuela holds more than 70% of its reserves in gold bullion. Having a small portion of the reserves in cash has been a concern for investors who worry about the country's ability to honor debt payments. Venezuela's benchmark 2027 sovereign bond offered a yield of more than 19% Thursday.

Mr. Maduro this week authorized a 20% cut in government spending in light of the more than 30% drop in the price of oil, which Venezuela relies on for 96% of its dollar income. Finance Minister Rodolfo Marco is in China this week seeking financing and will next head to allied countries like Russia and Iran, Mr. Maduro said.

Last month, Venezuela used a $4 billion loan from China, funds that are typically earmarked for infrastructure investments, to beef up its reserves. But reserves since have declined again by $1.8 billion.

"We have a special plan to strengthen our reserves," the president said in a speech Tuesday. "They're going to rise further in the upcoming weeks and beginning in January and February," he said, promising to open up the country's access to "freely convertible currencies."

But those measures will only buy Venezuela time without changes to its heavily interventionist economy and simplifying rigid currency controls that maintain three different exchange rates for the dollar and deter investment, analysts said.

Barclays estimates that Venezuela's economy will be an outlier in the region this year, shrinking by 4.4%, followed by contractions of 6.2% and 1.5% in 2015 and 2016, respectively.

Write to Kejal Vyas at kejal.vyas@wsj.com

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  firms, Venezuelan bonds jump after primary
text:
* Brazil real hits 3-1/2 mo high, intervention eyed

* Venezuela bonds gain on opposition leaders strong showing

* Brazil currency gains 0.71 pct, Mexico's strengthens 0.76 pct

(Updates prices)

By Rachel Uranga and Daniel Bases

MEXICO CITY/NEW YORK, Feb 13 (Reuters) - Brazil's real firmed to a 3-1/2 month high on Monday, raising concerns of interevention, while Venezuelan bonds gained after the opposition rallied behind a candidate to battle socialist president Hugo Chavez.

Greece's parliament approved tough austerity measures needed for a new bailout, which lifted appetite for riskier assets around the world and helped Brazil's real and Mexico's peso

bounce back from their sharpest weekly losses in two months

last week.

Mexico's peso strengthened 0.76 percent to 12.6955

per dollar , recovering much of its slump last week,

while Brazil's real bid 0.71 percent stronger at 1.7145 per dollar, its strongest close since the end of October.

"Most of the so-called risk currencies are doing better in the wake of the Greek austerity package being passed," said Clyde Wardle, emerging markets FX strategist with HSBC in New York.

Despite Monday's parliamentary approval, the Greek government remained under pressure to convince a skeptical euro zone that it would abide by the terms of a multi-billion-euro rescue package. European finance ministers meet on Wednesday to discuss the bailout package.

Analysts said gains in riskier assets may be limited after a huge rally at the start of the year. Further milstones need to be met in the coming weeks to ease concerns of a chaotic default by Greece. "I don't think there's huge enthusiasm that we are out of the woods by any stretch," Wardle said.

Concerns about Greece last week ate into a surge in Latin American currencies this year made on the back of

improved economic data in China and the United States, along with hopes the euro zone's debt crisis would ease.

Investors are also looking forward to another round of cheap bank funding from the ECB later this month, while some are betting on another round of asset purchases by the U.S. Federal Reserve could further support demand for higher yielding assets.

Last month the Fed said it envisions exceptionally low interest rates through late 2014. Low interest rates in major economies drive investors to seek higher yields in emerging markets.

The sharp gains are pressuring the margins of Latin American exporters, since stronger local currencies make the region's manufacturers less competitive against cheaper imports while also making their exports more expensive.

Brazil intervened in its spot market for the first time last week since September, and traders said they were expecting the central bank to take further measures to curb the recent appreciation of the real.

Venezuela's bonds outperformed their emerging market peers after opposition presidential candidate Henrique Capriles'

strong showing in his party's primary stirred hopes that the center-left former governor could unseat Chavez.

Venezuela's benchmark 2027 Global bond bid up a point in price to 80.75, pushing its yield down 17 basis points to 12.124 percent, its lowest since late April 2010.

Sovereign U.S. dollar denominated bond yields spread over comparable U.S. Treasuries narrowed roughly 32 basis points compared to 9 basis points of tightening for the overall benchmark JPMorgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Plus.

Venezuela, by far the country with the largest yield spread on the EMBI+, is trading 996 basis points over U.S. Treasuries versus 335 basis points for the index itself.

Chile's peso bid 0.25 percent weaker at 479.90

per dollar, pulling back from a five-month high last week as the price for copper, the country's top export, slipped.

title: Venezuela's Bolivar Weakens To VEF6.6 Against Dollar
text:
CARACAS (Dow Jones)--The bolivar continued to weaken against the dollar in unregulated trading Wednesday, falling to its lowest level in two weeks as a dearth of dollars sold by the government continues to spawn demand in the parallel currency market.

The bolivar traded at VEF6.6 against the dollar, weakening from the previous rate of VEF6.55. The central bank, which has become a major player in Venezuela's parallel currency market, hasn't intervened in the market as it stopped selling its 90-day, zero-coupon dollar-denominated bonds.

The central bank previously sold $260 million through the bonds, which serve as a backdoor tool for Venezuelans to get their hands on dollars and sidestep currency controls. The issues haven't helped strengthen the bolivar and local news reports have indicated that Finance Minister Jorge Giordani is questioning the central bank bond sales as a device to prop up the bolivar.

Giordani said last Friday that the bond sales weren't geared at boosting the bolivar, a statement that seemed to contradict other government officials. President Hugo Chavez vowed in January to bring down the so-called black market rate to VEF4.3, the same level as the official rate.

Local daily El Mundo reported Tuesday that Giordani had halted the sale of a bond issued by the central bank that could top $750 million.

   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

CARACAS (Dow Jones)--Venezuela plans to battle the country's currency black market with "heavy intervention," President Hugo Chavez said Saturday, one day after he announced a devaluation of the bolivar's official rate.

"We're going to attack the parallel market with heavy intervention," Chavez said during a televised address.

In announcing the devaluation Friday, Chavez indicated the government would intervene in the thriving and legally murky black market, but provided few details.

The black-market bolivar rate currently stands at about VEF6.25 for $1. On Friday night, Chavez announced he was cutting in half the official value of the bolivar against the dollar, to VEF4.3 per dollar from VEF2.15 previously.

Following the devaluation, receiving the official rate will still require government approval that has been hard to obtain, so it is doubtful the black market will disappear overnight.

Government intervention in the black market could entail flooding it with dollars to weaken the greenback and bring down the rate, perhaps until it reaches the official VEF4.3 per dollar level. That could lessen the black market's relevance, and in the meantime would allow the government to get more bolivars for its dollars than it would get at the official rate.

The president of this oil-rich nation also on Saturday cited a "weak" U.S. dollar against international currencies as one of the reasons for his decision to devalue.

"Every day our barrel of oil is worth less because of the weak dollar, because oil is priced in dollars," Chavez said.

The devaluation will help offset this, Chavez said, because now every time state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela, or PdVSA, goes to the Central Bank to change its dollars for bolivars, it will get VEF4.3 per dollar rather than VEF2.15.

"This will have a huge impact on the national fiscal situation, and will strengthen our oil industry," Chavez said.

He also said the devaluation will spur national production and reduce imports. "We've been selling dollars cheaply for too long."

In addition to the VEF4.3 official rate, another, secondary rate of VEF2.60 will be available, with authorization, for those buying key "necessary" imports such as basic foods and medicine that Venezuela doesn't produce enough of.

title: Moody's concludes review of Venezuelan bank ratings; downgrades deposit ratings; confirms Banvenez BFSR
text:
Moody's Investors Service downgraded both the long term local currency deposit rating of Mercantil, C.A., Banco Universal (Mercantil) to Ba3, from Ba2, and that of Banco de Venezuela (Banvenez) to Ba2, from Ba1. The outlook is stable for both these ratings. At the same time, Moody's confirmed Banvenez's bank financial strength rating at D-, with a negative outlook.

The downgrade of the local currency deposit ratings is driven by the rating agency's reassessment of a government's ability to support its banks during a protracted, systemic event, such as during the ongoing global crisis. The likelihood of such support is an important part of Moody's credit analysis, and it provides uplift to deposit ratings above the floor implied by a banks' own financial strength. The local currency deposit rating downgrades bring both banks' ratings closer in line with that of the Venezuelan government's own B1 local currency bond rating. These rating actions conclude the review for possible downgrade of the deposit ratings initiated on July 1, 2009.

Moody's noted that the rating action on Mercantil's deposits does not reflect a change in the bank's intrinsic financial strength. In fact, on July 1, 2009, Moody's had affirmed Mercantil's D- bank financial strength rating and its Ba3 unsupported baseline credit assessment to reflect the adequacy of the bank's balance sheet. The bank financial strength rating measures a bank's intrinsic safety and soundness and, as such, excludes external credit-support elements. Mercantil's Ba3 deposit local currency rating benefits from no uplift due to systemic support.

The confirmation of Banvenez's D- bank financial strength rating reflects Moody's view of its potentially enhanced importance in the system, which could result from its intended role as a consolidator of other Venezuelan public sector banks, under the newly created Corporación de la Banca Pública.

However, Moody's believes Banvenez's new role is also likely to result in changes in the bank's risk management and thus its asset allocation, as greater emphasis is placed on executing public policy at the expense of risk-adjusted returns. Over the medium term Bavenez's new public policy role may have a negative effect on the bank's financial metrics, Moody's said - particularly asset quality, profitability and capitalization - which it assesses in its analysis of a bank's intrinsic financial strength. The rating agency therefore has assigned a negative outlook to Banvenez's financial strength rating, indicating that it would monitor the bank's financial fundamentals closely during the next several quarters.

Banvenez's new Ba2 deposit rating reflects full systemic support for the bank's local currency obligations as a government-owned bank, which adds one notch of uplift to the bank's unsupported baseline credit assessment.

Deposit Rating Changes Reflect Revised Approach to Systemic Support

Moody's has refined its assessment to better reflect the capacity of governments to support their banking systems as a whole in the event of a systemic crisis. Moody's continues to believe that most governments are likely to support their banking systems during a crisis to avoid a meltdown of the local payment system.

Nevertheless, the agency also views the capacity of a country and its central bank to support the nation's banks to be more closely aligned with the government's own creditworthiness, especially in times of crisis like these. (The revised approach to systemic support is outlined in the special report entitled "Financial Crisis More Closely Aligns Bank Credit Risk and Government Ratings in Non-Aaa Countries," published in May 2009.)

Moody's said that the new systemic support indicator for Venezuela has been established at Ba2, thus replacing the current Baa1 local currency deposit ceiling. Despite the downgrade, the Ba2 systemic support indicator remains two notches above the government's B1 local currency bond rating.

The two-notch differential reflects Moody's assessment of the Venezuelan government's high willingness and ability to support its banking system. This attitude is demonstrated by the following: (i) a history of no local currency deposit defaults in the past 20 years; (ii) the small size of the banking system in relation to GDP - a very modest 19%; (iii) the virtual lack of foreign currency obligations by banks, given that foreign currency lending or deposit-taking is not allowed in Venezuela; and iv) a very high level of central government intervention in the bank industry, which suggests a high likelihood that the government will continue to support the banking system as a whole.

Moody's also pointed out that Venezuelan banks have for some time successfully managed their operations in a highly unpredictable legal, political, and economic environment. Continued high inflation, coupled with negative economic growth, will cause lower business volumes and declining asset quality, thus continuing to stress the banking system's performance.

Previous Rating Actions and Principal Methodologies

Moody's last rating action on Mercantil and Banvenez was on July 1, 2009. At this time, Moody's placed the local currency deposit ratings of both banks on review for possible downgrade. At the same time, Moody's affirmed Mercantil's D- bank financial strength rating with a stable outlook and placed Banvenez's D- bank financial strength rating on review for possible downgrade.

The principal methodologies used in rating these banks were "Bank Financial Strength Ratings: Global Methodology" (February 2007) and "Incorporation of Joint-Default Analysis into Moody's Bank Ratings: A Refined Methodology" (March 2007) and available on www.moodys.com in the Rating Methodologies sub-directory under the Research & Ratings tab. Other methodologies and factors that may have been considered in the process of rating this issuer can also be found in the Rating Methodologies sub-directory on Moody's website.

The following ratings were affected:

Mercantil, C.A., Banco Universal

Local currency deposit rating downgraded to Ba3, from Ba2

Banco de Venezuela

Local currency deposit rating downgraded to Ba2, from Ba1

Bank financial strength rating of D-, confirmed with a negative outlook

title: =DJ Venezuela Law May Push  Central Bank  To Play Bond,  Forex  Mkts
text:
CARACAS (Dow Jones)--The Venezuelan central bank may be gearing up to become a major player in the market for government-backed dollar-denominated bonds.

The institution could become an enforcer for the government's plans to tame a booming unofficial market for U.S. currency while allowing the administration of President Hugo Chavez to continue its massive debt issues next year.

A new law approved by the National Assembly allows the central bank to buy and sell bonds issued by state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela, or PdVSA, in the primary or secondary market, giving it a new weapon to influence the price of Venezuelan bonds and the unofficial currency rate.

The new rules come as the government is ramping up the sale of dollar-denominated bonds to plug its budget, which is hurting from a decline in oil revenue, and to manipulate the country's unofficial rate for U.S. currency. It recently sold a total of $11.26 billion, including debt sold by PdVSA.

The bond issues help quench Venezuelans' thirst for dollars. The securities are bought with bolivars and can then be sold abroad for U.S. currency, providing a backdoor alternative to the official currency-exchange mechanisms.

Now the central bank would be able to buy those bonds back from overseas investors and sell them again to Venezuelans to mop up more bolivars.

If this is the case, the central bank "could buy around $6 billion in PdVSA paper," said Alejandro Grisanti, an analyst with Barclays Capital. Purchases by the central bank could help increase demand for the bonds.

Although the final text hasn't yet been published, it seems the bill wouldn't allow the central bank to tally the dollar-linked bonds as part of its international reserves.

The changes "create a potential time-bomb within the central bank," said Russ Dallen, head trader at Caracas-based brokerage firm BBO Financial Services. The new law "could create a huge liquidity crunch at the central bank if and when an economic downturn occurs," he added.

Central bank President Nelson Merentes didn't returns calls seeking comment. In an interview published Monday with a local newspaper El Nacional, he said the new law expands the ability of the central bank to intervene in the primary and secondary debt markets.

Venezuela pegs its currency at a rate of VEF2.15 and residents or companies that can't buy dollars at that rate must turn to the unofficial market.

Merentes said the government's goal is to bridge the gap between the peg and the unofficial rate to 60%, meaning that a dollar should fetch no more than VEF3.55 in the parallel market. The sale of dollar-denominated bonds has already helped the government to lower the parallel rate by 35%, Merentes said in the report.

The unofficial rate on Tuesday weakened against the dollar to VEF5.35 as many investors await the chance to examine the details of the new law and discover the true scope of the central bank's new role.

Purchases by the central bank in the secondary market could also help the performance of the bonds, which have been pummeled by what analysts see as a supply glut by the increased bond sales.

"This will have an effect on prices" for Venezuelan bonds, said Asdrubal Oliveros, a director at Caracas-based economic research firm Ecoanalitica. "They want to influence the parallel rate," he said. Purchases by the central bank could help increase demand for the bonds, he said.

The state-run oil company has issued $6.2 billion this year and may issue as much as $5 billion more before the end of the year, according to Barclays. On Tuesday, Oil Minister Rafael Ramirez told reporters that PdVSA was considering selling debt in the short term.

The bond sales are expected to continue next year. Barclay's Grisanti expects PdVSA to sell $6 billion next year, while the central government could issue as much as $10 billion.

For PdVSA, the bond sales not only allow the oil company to satisfy pent-up demand for U.S. currency, but also to squeeze more bolivars from every dollar of oil revenue. PdVSA by law has to sell its dollar income to the central bank at the official rate while selling debt allows it to receive a higher rate.

"The government is looking to maximize its oil income without devaluing the bolivar," said Andreas Faust, an economist with Caracas-based Banco Mercantil. For PdVSA, which faces mounting debts with service providers, selling dollars to the central bank at the official rate "doesn't make much business sense," he added.

title: Venezuela's Increasingly Statist Economy Starts To Sputter
text:
CARACAS (Dow Jones)--A sharp slowing in Venezuela's economy in the first quarter suggests that output could become sluggish throughout the year and even worsen in 2009.

Despite sky-high oil prices, economists blame the government's highly interventionist policies for the petroleum-rich country's flagging growth.

Venezuela's gross domestic product, the broadest measure of overall economic activity, increased an annualized 4.8% in January through March. It was the lowest figure after four years of double-digit growth.

Forecasts from four private sector economists now have the economy growing anywhere from 4% to 5.5% this year, less than the government's 6% target. And all of them see it cooling off even more next year.

"We're in for a sharp slowdown," said Orlando Ochoa, an economist with Andres Bello University in Caracas.

Stifling bureaucracy and fast-expanding regulatory regimes, including a gamut of price, interest rate and foreign exchange controls constrain private enterprise, which has been badly shaken by nationalizations in the energy, telecommunications, power and mining sectors. President Hugo Chavez's harsh anti-market rhetoric also hasn't helped.

The restrictions on the local currency, which is pegged to the U.S. dollar at 2.15 bolivars, make it difficult for companies to obtain the greenbacks for their operations. Price controls on several food items mean that some farmers aren't covering their production costs, leading to shortages.

Chavez's socialist rhetoric has scared off foreign investment. Foreign direct investment receded by $475 million, "despite the vast opportunities in the oil and gas sector," wrote Goldman Sachs' economist Alberto Ramos. "In the meantime, FDI flows into Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Peru are booming," he noted.

Some key sectors like manufacturing and construction almost came to a standstill in the first quarter after posting double-digit growth last year.

More alarming than that, said Pedro Palma, an economist with local research firm Metroeconomia, was the 12.6% contraction in the car-making industry, despite government imposed quotas on car imports that seek to boost domestic production.

The Venezuelan mining industry has also failed to take advantage of the worldwide commodities boom, retreating an eye-popping 20.5% in the quarter.

Economists have long warned that extremely loose monetary and fiscal policies would likely be less effective this year than in previous years, given that they have fueled a boom in consumption, but not investment - due to the administration's statist bent.

The government has been streaming record oil windfalls into social programs, said Andreas Faust, an economist with Caracas-based Banco Mercantil. "We're seeing higher consumption with very little investment," he added.

The result has been the highest official inflation in the region: April's level stood at 29.3% on year. "This is the Achilles' heel of the Venezuelan economy," said Andres Bello University's Ochoa.

Inflation could accelerate even more in coming months as the Chavez administration is likely to ramp up government spending ahead of regional elections in November.

The GDP figures released Tuesday by the central bank are also somewhat of an embarrassment for the government's economic team.

Planning Minister Haiman El-Troudi, an electric engineer who has inked a handful of socialist treatises, on several occasions publicly boasted that growth for the first quarter would surpass 6%. El-Troudi is the head of Chavez's economic team and also sits on the central bank's board of directors.

"The government was clearly surprised by this," said Mercantil's Faust, who added that he was baffled by El-Troudi's public predictions considering that he had access to detailed and updated economic growth data.

title: New Chavez Rival Blames Govt For Venezuela's Economic Woes
text:
CARACAS (Dow Jones)--Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez's most formidable political opponent hasn't talked much about the country's economy, which is struggling with double-digit inflation and food shortages.   

But retired general Raul Baduel, Chavez's former armed forces commander, says one thing is clear: "A severe economic crisis is looming in Venezuela, and it has been brought about by state intervention."   

Baduel, a close, long-time Chavez ally, defended the president during a brief coup in 2002, enabling Chavez's quick return to power. But in recent months Baduel has become a vocal critic, calling Chavez's failed bid in December to overhaul the Constitution through a referendum a coup of its own.   

The general blasted the proposed reform and caused a political storm as he became one of the most high-profile Chavez allies to turn around and condemn the administration. In a country devoid of popular opposition leaders, Baduel was transformed into a rallying figure for traditional Chavez detractors.   

His credentials also split the Chavez ranks and his denouncements were seen as a major force behind the referendum's defeat, Chavez's first electoral setback since he took office in early 1999.   

After the Dec. 2 vote, Baduel has kept his distance from the traditional political parties, and vowed to stay away from the races in regional elections slated for November. Instead, he has engaged in what seems like a quixotic bid to call for a constitutional assembly and fine-tune the current charter.   

Baduel admits he hasn't been able to garner much support, but says drafting the reforms let him "clear his head" on such thorny subjects as the Venezuelan economy.   

In a recent interview with Dow Jones Newswires, Baduel said after studying Venezuela's economic problems, he remains "a pragmatist."   

Most of his ideas, however, seem to be a direct indictment of Chavez's socialist-inspired economic policies, which he blames for "wasting the revenue of a historic oil bonanza."   

Propelled by high government spending, inflation, which has run rampant in recent years, "can only be fixed with traditional weapons like well-coordinated fiscal discipline and monetary policy," Baduel said.   

The central bank has effectively become subordinate to the executive branch, with the result that real interest rates are now deeply negative.   

Baduel sees the erosion of central bank independence as one of most grievous mistakes by the current administration. "The overwhelming evidence in the world shows that the greater the autonomy of the central bank, the lower the inflation figures," he said.   

Baduel, who said he has several economic advisers but was unwilling to disclose their names, noted that the officials in charge of monetary policy must be "shielded against populist demagoguery," and their professional advancement be uncoupled from national politics.   

The general also denounced what he called "the waste of billions" of dollars that have been funneled directly by the president to social programs that "have done little to change the plight of the poor."   

"If the government has the resources, it should spend them (wisely). But in Venezuela it's completely discretionary and depends on the president's whims," he said.   

Baduel's proposal - which is still being drafted - to reform the Constitution will include provisions to guarantee that social spending won't depend on the president, but will be regulated through pre-established mechanisms.   

Baduel said he still espouses the social equality ideals that brought him close to Chavez in their early days in the military, when together with two other young officers they pledged never to rest until they had "broken the chains of the powerful that oppress us."   

That oath, taken under a tree where 19th century South American Independence hero Simon Bolivar once rested, still stands, he says. "The state has a responsibility to the disenfranchised, but what we have seen lately is a rise in consumerism while the poor remain poor."   

His most scathing criticism was kept for currency controls, which he blames for spawning a black market for dollars and causing distortions throughout the economy.   

Venezuela pegs the bolivar currency to the dollar at a rate of VEB2.15, but the dollar often fetches double that amount in the parallel market. "Keeping those controls over a long period of time only creates economic problems," said Baduel.   

The general says he is not shy about running for office but argues that it's too soon to talk about a possible presidential bid. "I'm still sorting some ideas out in my mind," he said.

title: Argentina Pres: Venezuela, Argentina To Jointly Issue Bond
text:
CARACAS (Dow Jones)--Venezuela and Argentina plan to jointly offer a bond to Venezuelan investors, another step in the economic cooperation between both nations, Argentine President Nestor Kirchner said Tuesday.  

During a televised address in Venezuela, Kirchner said both nations seek to create a "bond of the South" in 60 to 90 days.  

Kirchner's announcement confirms rumors vented in the Argentine press that both neighbors seek to offer a "bi-national" bond, or that Venezuela could offer a guarantee for Argentine debt.  

A Venezuelan lawmaker confirmed the plans as well.  

Officials from both countries "are putting the final touches on a regional bond that would give investors exposure to risk from both Argentina and Venezuela," said Rodrigo Cabezas, head of the congressional finance commission.  

Cabezas couldn't provide many details about how the instrument would work or how much of it would be sold. He did say he expects the government to sell the dollar-denominated bonds to local investors in exchange for bolivars.  

It is unclear how much of the proceeds from the bond sale would go to Argentina.  

By selling a new bond to domestic buyers, the government of Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez would create a new way to impact the price of the dollar in the local black market for the U.S. currency without increasing domestic debt.  

Venezuela's government regularly intervenes in the unofficial market for the dollar by selling public debt denominated in dollars in exchange for bolivars.  

Investors buy these bonds and sell them overseas for much-needed U.S. currency.  

Chavez imposed strict capital controls in early 2003 and has forced businesses and ordinary Venezuelans to seek government permission to buy dollars for various needs.  

The controls have spawned a black market for the dollar that Venezuelans follow closely to determine future costs and set prices for their products.  

His administration, however, has left a window open for investors to obtain the U.S. currency by using complex stock and bond transactions.  

Chavez has made it a priority to keep inflation under control, especially this year as he seeks reelection in December.  

As of early March, Venezuela had purchased $2.5 billion in Argentine debt and sold off $1.1 billion of that amount to local banks.  

It is unclear whether the government has helped reduce liquidity by recycling the debt of its South American neighbor.  

In the fight against inflation, Chavez's government has faced difficulties keeping excess liquidity out of the economy in recent months.  

A hamstrung central bank continues to issue a costly amount of short-term debt to soak up the bolivars in circulation resulting from heavy government spending.  

The central bank and the Finance Ministry are looking for new ways to limit the amount of cash in circulation without hurting the central bank's bottom line.  

Chavez has vowed to gradually move the Venezuelan economy away from capitalism and adopt a new socialist system for the 21st Century.  

-By Raul Gallegos, Dow Jones Newswires; 58-212-564-1339; raul.gallegos@dowjones.com

title: Venezuelan GDP Sprints As Oil Income Pumped Into Economy
text:
CARACAS (Dow Jones)--Booming oil revenues are fueling Venezuela's high economic growth, but heavy government intervention in the economy make some critics doubt whether the good times can last over the long run.  

Planning Minister Jorge Giordani Wednesday touted the country's 9.4% annualized gross domestic product growth in the first quarter, and said more is to come.  

"Venezuela is now experiencing sustainable economic growth and has been for the last 10 quarters," he said in televised remarks from Libya, where he accompanied President Hugo Chavez on a state visit. Growth this year will exceed the 6% rise originally forecast, he added.  

Chavez himself took credit during his televised remarks, declaring, "Venezuela is experiencing solid and sustainable growth."  

Analysts don't doubt that Venezuela's economy will expand beyond 6% in 2006, given a high tide of oil revenues, aggressive government spending and loose monetary policy. Capital controls that trap liquidity in the country and interest rate controls ensure that interest rates remain low. Authorities also require banks to allocate about a third of their lending to favored sectors at sweet-heart rates.  

All the liquidity made for a broad-based economic expansion in the non-oil sector, even as Chavez focused much of his government's effort on redistributing wealth to the poor. He is seeking another six-year term in December elections.  

Fueled largely by government spending and consumption, household incomes have benefitted. Private consumption rose 19.3% year over year and government consumption was up 9.2% during the same period. Construction was also up sharply.  

Chavez's subsidies and social spending programs have given the poor more spending power, the central bank noted. Through off-budget programs called "missions," the Chavez administration provides health, education and subsidized food products, among other services.  

To counter the enormous inflationary pressures from the huge economic stimulus, the government has imposed price controls on scores of goods. Under Chavez the way inflation is measured has also been adjusted to include subsidized prices at the state-owned grocery chain Mercal--resulting in artificially lower readings.  

Despite the price controls, Venezuela suffers double-digit inflation.  

"Significantly loose fiscal and monetary policies are contributing decisively to leverage the non-oil economy up, although through mechanisms that are inherently unsustainable," Goldman Sachs said in a Wednesday report. "The large wealth transfer from abroad (oil revenues) through terms of trade gains has been recycled back into the economy via profligate fiscal spending."  

Venezuela has a history of boom and bust cycles dependent on oil, with little saving and varied populist measures. Detractors claim Chavez is more of the same, and will face tough times in a few years when the fortunes of the oil market turn.  

Moreover, as social spending has increased in recent years, investment in the oil sector has dwindled.  

Oil activity declined 0.2% year on year during the first quarter, central bank data show. Government oil production declined 0.3% during the quarter while private production was down 4.5%, according to a UBS Investment Research report. Analysts pointed out that first-quarter foreign direct investment numbers showed a $1.6 billion outflow, reflecting private capital outflows given the government's continual, unilateral contract changes in its quest to garner more rent from oil companies.  

Some observers caution that the lack of investment and saving could hurt the country's economic viability in the long run. But others point out oil prices will likely stay high for years.  

"This government has a considerable degree of freedom. Stress scenarios show government spending is sustainable for another three to four years at least," said Luis Zambrano Sequin, an economics professor for the Andres Bello Catholic University.  

Zambrano points out the government can easily continue to tap local banks for cash when needed, and can also resort to weakening the currency occasionally so it can convert dollars from oil sales into more bolivars.  

Chavez has said he will continue to spend heavily in hopes of creating a new socialism for the 21st Century in Venezuela. He has vowed to remain in politics until 2030.  

-By Raul Gallegos, Dow Jones Newswires; 58-212-564-1339; raul.gallegos@dowjones.com [ 18-05-06 1819GMT ]

title: Venezuelan Politics, Econ Controls Slam Economy In 2003
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Political turmoil and heavy-handed state intervention took a huge toll on Venezuela's economy in 2003.  

In a preliminary estimate, the central bank reported Tuesday the country's economy dove 9.2% last year, surpassing the previous year's 8.9% contraction.  

In dollar terms, gross domestic product withered to $83 billion in 2003 from $126 billion in 2001, said Alberto Ramos, Andean economist at Goldman Sachs in New York. "It's more than a recession; it's a collapse," he said.  

The monetary authority placed a great deal of blame for the shrinkage in 2003 on a two-month nationwide general strike that brought the critical oil industry to a virtual halt. The strike was lifted last February, but year-old, government-imposed capital and price controls remain firmly in place. The currency was also pegged to the dollar.  

After firing nearly half the workforce in the state-owned oil giant PdVSA in retaliation for going on strike, the Chavez administration was mostly successful in reestablishing oil production. For the year as a whole, though, oil production fell 10.7%.  

Despite improved administrative procedures in the second half for obtaining foreign exchange, "the restrictions translated into transactional costs that affected the results of the principal macroeconomic variables," the central bank noted in its statement to the National Assembly.  

The monetary authority pointed out that it had approved a total of $14.3 billion from March through the end of December for foreign exchange transactions, but a currency exchange panel created to oversee domestic dollar sales only released $5.24 billion.  

"It's very clear part of the economic contraction was due to all the controls," Ramos said. While economically deleterious, politically they can be used to reward the administration's friends and punish its enemies, he added.  

The opposition staged the strike to force Chavez to resign or call early elections. They feared his self-proclaimed revolution is steering the country toward Cuban-style communism. Chavez denies it, and says his "oligarch" opponents just want their privileges restored.  

The opposition is now trying to advance a legal recall referendum on Chavez's mandate, though the outlook for the plebiscite remains unclear.  

The economic impact of the political uncertainty and the state interventions into the economy are also evident in the 8% shrinkage in non-oil output. The construction sector - significant for its multiplier effect - was the hardest hit, crumbling 37% last year.  

Balance of payments data also reflected the extent of the economic distortions. Thanks to the capital controls, international reserves ballooned $8.66 billion to $20.67 billion last year.  

Along with the economic freefall, the controls took a heavy toll on the trade account, badly affecting a country that imports more than 60% of all it consumes. Imports plunged more than 21%, while exports dropped 3.4%. The current account ended 2003 with a $9.62 billion surplus.  

The capital account, meanwhile, registered a $3.17 billion deficit, and the "errors and omissions" category showed a $1.01 billion outflow.  

Despite the price controls and economic depression, inflation still ran at 27% last year.  

Investment plummeted 39%, notwithstanding a marked fall in lending rates, a product of the increased liquidity wrought by the capital controls.  

The government tried to compensate for the drop in investment by jacking up spending, and sourcing a good portion of its funds from internal debt issuance.  

A 20% rise in domestic public debt - raising its total outstanding to 17.1% of GDP - likely spurred a recovery in the last months of the year, though that was also helped by a low base comparison. The sharp increase in liquidity was clear in the monetary base, which expanded more than 46% in 2003, making the central bank dramatically increase its own monetary sterilization operations.  

But the monetary authority hasn't yet released fourth quarter data, which central bank director Domingo Maza Zavala's office told Dow Jones Newswires Wednesday was still being compiled and should be made public by the end of the month.  

Analysts are awaiting fourth quarter results and any revisions to data in previous quarters to draw firmer conclusions about current trends in Venezuela's economy.  

Some Wall Street houses expressed surprise by the central bank's full year 9.2% contraction estimate, which would imply a major recovery in the fourth quarter after preliminary estimates of a 7.1% contraction in the third quarter, a 9.4% shrinkage in the second and a 27.7% nosedive in the first.  

In a Wednesday research note, Credit Suisse First Boston said it thinks "the central bank's estimate underestimates the economy's actual contraction." CSFB noted that the monetary authority's full-year figures imply a 26.7% real increase in fourth quarter oil-sector GDP from the third quarter, compared with CSFB's own 4.0% estimated decline.  

On non-oil fourth-quarter GDP, CSFB expects a 0.8% rise from the third quarter, considerably less than the central bank's 5.9% advance.  

CSFB reckons Venezuela's economy dropped 11.9% last year from 2002, nearly three percentage points more than the central bank's own estimate.  

Ramos, the Goldman Sachs economist, estimated the country's GDP lost about 10% last year.  

-By Charles Roth, Dow Jones Newswires; 201 938 2226; charles.roth@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-Venezuela eyes controls on commercial bank rates.
text:
CARACAS, Venezuela, Feb 16 (Reuters) - Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez on Sunday proposed introducing controls on commercial bank lending rates for the first time in seven years as the embattled leader looked to tighten his grip on the private sector. 

 The proposal, if approved by the Central Bank, would follow the government's creation of new currency and price controls in the past month. Those controls have closed foreign exchange markets and forced retailers to sell everything from tomatoes to funeral services at government-set levels. 

 Explaining the need to intervene in commercial rates, Chavez complained Venezuela's poor were not offered affordable credit. He said commercial bank lending rates should fall by about 10 percentage points and be set at 30 percent or less. 

 "I would fix lending rates at a maximum of 30 percent," Chavez said. 

 "I want rates to be fixed. I want interest rates to be cut and I want the BCV (Venezuelan Central Bank) to fix interest rates," Chavez said during his state-sponsored Sunday television program "Alo Presidente." 

 Venezuela's economy is suffocating under a grueling strike by oil workers against Chavez's government. Oil shipments from the world's fifth largest exporting nation have fallen dramatically since the strike began in December. 

 Commercial banks angered the populist president in December by slashing operating hours to support the strike meant to force Chavez from power. Most of the private sector has reopened. But the strike continues in Venezuela's vital oil industry, strangling an economy already reeling from a 8.9 percent contraction last year. 

 Any decision on fixing rates would have to come from the Central Bank, which is largely independent but has supported Chavez's recent initiatives - including the currency and price controls which are strongly opposed by the private sector. 

 Opponents warned that the new price controls would further damage shopkeepers, many of whom shuttered their businesses for nearly two months as part of the general strike abandoned earlier in February. 

 The currency controls have also hurt the private sector, starving businesses of the much-needed U.S. currency in a nation that imports more than 60 percent of its goods. 

 Venezuela has allowed commercial banks to set their own lending rates since 1996, after seven years of government rate-setting programs.

title: Venezuela  Mkts: Bolivar Flat Although Ctrl Bk  Intervenes
text:
CARACAS -(Dow Jones)- The Venezuelan central bank posted the bolivar's close at VEB1467.25 Monday, a bit weaker than Friday's VEB1467, despite efforts to boost the local currency, traders said. 

 The institution put in up to $25 million more than its preset daily $51 million buying bolivars, but steady demand for dollars prevented the local currency from strengthening, a currency dealer at a local bank said. 

 The institution reported that it bought bolivars at rates ranging from VEB1482.33 in the first of its three daily auctions to VEB1442 during the last. 

 Comments by President Hugo Chavez during the weekend increased dollar demand, the currency dealer said. 

 Chavez said Venezuelans should "punish" private banks by transferring their money to state-run banks, because, he said, private banks are conspiring against the government by not buying public debt to help the government out of a cash crunch. 

 Bankers have said they can't risk exposure to Venezuela's deepening economic crisis, highlighted by a 7.1% contraction in the first half. 

 Analysts said Chavez's comments can't be taken seriously. 

 "People with money in the bank want Chavez out of office ... they aren't going to move money to government banks," said one local analyst who asked not to be quoted by name. 

 Indeed, Chavez's growing opposition - some 70% want him out of the presidency, according to local polls - have launched several separate efforts to oust him from office. 

 The president's primary support base consists of Venezuela's poor, most of whom reportedly have barely enough money to pay for their monthly needs, given annualized inflation of about 25%. 

 Local stocks ended mostly unchanged, with the IBC General Stock Index closed 86 points, or about 1.1%, higher at 7274 points. Of the IBC's 16 stocks, four gained, two closed lower, and 10 were unchanged. 

 Just 1.9 million shares valued at VEB293 million changed hands, compared with 1.3 million shares valued at VEB151 million Friday. 

 Telephone giant CA Nacional Telefonos de Venezuela lost VEB25.00 to end at VEB2350.00 while its American Depositary Receipts, worth seven common shares apiece, ended at $11.36, down 41 cents on the New York Stock Exchange. 

 There were no public debt auctions Monday.

title: Venezuela  Bolivar Ends Up; Ctrl Bk  Intervenes
text:
CARACAS -(Dow Jones)- The Venezuelan central bank reported the bolivar's official close Wednesday at VEB1373.88 per dollar, after the central bank took advantage of a slow session to bolster the local currency, traders said. 

 Wednesday's close was stronger than VEB1383.38 Tuesday because the central bank intervened with about $10 million more than its standard daily $45 million, buying the bolivar at rates ranging from VEB1388.57 down to VEB1361.92. 

 Trading was slow because most investors have adopted a "wait and see attitude" about a critical Supreme Court ruling expected to be announced later in the day, a currency dealer at a local bank said. 

 But dollar demand is still generally high given increased political uncertainty which has already resulted in street gun battles and general violence, the dealer said. 

 The Supreme Court is expected to announce whether four military commanders will be charged in connection with  President Hugo Chavez's brief ouster in April. 

 Analysts have said a decision to not charge the officers will likely be seen as positive for markets because it would be detrimental to the left-leaning Chavez's presidency. 

 However, the bolivar is expected to continue devaluing beyond VEB1500 against the dollar by the end of this year because it would help the government meet its obligations. 

 Given that more than half the government's income is in dollars, a weaker bolivar will give officials more money in the local currency to cover this year's financing needs equal to about 9% of the country's $100 billion gross domestic product.

title: Venezuela  Ctrl Bk/Bolivar -2: Only  Intervenes  Modestly
text:
CARACAS -(Dow Jones)- Venezuela's Central Bank Director Domingo Maza Zavala said Wednesday that the bank won't any longer burn its foreign reserves to keep the bolivar afloat against the dollar. 

 "The bank won't sacrifice its reserves to keep defending the bolivar and that policy is a fundamental difference from the past week," Maza told the Globovision network in a televised interview. 

 However, Maza said that the bank won't stay completely on the sidelines if the bolivar keeps on falling at the same rate as it is doing now. "...in that case the bank would consider the possibility of the convenience to intervene in the market and ease the fluctuation," Maza said, who added that the currency turmoil is likely to ease down after a couple of days. 

 Currently, the bolivar is collapsing after the government decided to scrap the currency band system and implement a free-float exchange rate. 

 Around 1450 GMT (9:50 a.m. EST), the bolivar sank to VEB909 a dollar traded in the over-the-counter market, according to traders in Caracas, who added that the central bank intervened "mildly" at VEB820. 

 According to another currency trader, the central bank isn't intervening with hefty dollar sales. In the announcement Tuesday, it wasn't clear to what amount the bank would keep supplying dollars to the market. 

 On Friday, the last time it was traded, the bolivar closed at VEB792.50 to the dollar. The market was closed Monday and Tuesday for the Carnival holiday. 

 After spending several years trading in a band, Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez announced late Tuesday that the bolivar would freely float. He also announced a major overhaul of the $34.34 billion budget and vowed to cut government spending for 2002 by 7%. Analysts, however, have said the program lacks credibility. 

 Low oil prices and assorted fiscal pressures had made the band - the central parity of which the bolivar was allowed to move within a 7.5% range - untenable. 

 Capital flight was estimated at $9 billion to $10 billion last year, and was rapidly eroding central bank reserves this year. Reserves now stand at $10.34 billion, not including a $6.24 billion windfall oil-revenue fund. 

 -By Fred Pals, Dow Jones Newswires; 58212-5641339; fred.pals@dowjones.com

 Dollar outflows have increased in recent weeks after President Hugo Chavez said he may declare a state of emergency to better fight crime and corruption.

 Pablo Medina, a leftist politician recently readmitted to Chavez's inner circle, said last week the government may impose a tax on foreign exchange transactions.

title: REPEAT: Latin America  Forex : Mexico Peso Slightly Firmer
text:
NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- The Mexican peso ended slightly firmer against the dollar Tuesday. It staged a brief rally after the U.S. Federal Reserve decided to keep interest rates steady, while maintaining a neutral bias. 

 In Mexico City on 48-hour spot dollar markets, banking leader Banamex quoted the peso (MXN) closing at a midrate of MXN9.3120 per dollar, stronger from its open of MXN9.3150 and stronger from its close of MXN9.3190 Monday. 

 As reported, the Federal Open Market Committee Tuesday afternoon announced it had left interest rates unchanged, while surprising financial markets by maintaining its neutral stance on monetary policy. 

 The central bank's policy-making panel held the federal funds rate at 5.50%. 

 One trader said that highly illiquid market conditions and the absence of investors ahead of the holiday season prevented the Mexican peso from strengthening substantially on the FOMC news. 

 But another trader attributed the lack of enthusiasm to an underlying hawkishness in the FOMC statement. 

 In the statement, the FOMC said it remained "concerned with the possibility that over time increases in demand will continue to exceed the growth in potential supply." 

 "What you got here is a neutral directive with a non-neutral text," the second trader said.

title: Caracas shares lose 0.28 pct, bolivar weaker.
text:
CARACAS, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Caracas stocks slipped for a second day Tuesday, losing 0.28 percent, as investors continued to avoid the market ahead of a December 15 referendum on a controversial new constitution. 


The bolivar currency	  also weakened as the Central Bank trimmed its sales of dollars despite steady demand from local businesses.
The IBC index	  of leading shares lost 15.14 points to close at 5,464.24 points, with 14 stocks stable, five rising and five falling.


 "I don't think there will be much interest in investing in the local market until the new constitution is approved," said Miguel Ortiz of the Patagon.com brokerage. 

 While populist President Hugo Chavez has staked his political future on the approval of the new charter, it has elicited strong criticism from business leaders and opposition politicians who say it is economically backward and interventionist. 

 National telephone company CANTV  , Venezuela's largest publicly traded company, lost 1.44 percent to close at 2,400 bolivars a share. Benchmark share Electricidad de Caracas  gained 0.93 percent to end at 223.05 bolivars each. 

 Meanwhile, the national currency closed 0.5 bolivar weaker at 635.75/636.75. 

 Traders said demand for the dollar was boosted because foreign currency bought Tuesday is payable one day later than usual due to Thursday's Thanksgiving national holiday in the United States. 

 The exchange rate will remain fixed Thursday at the previous day's close. 

Central Bank Director Armando Leon said Tuesday the bank had sold around 20 to 30 percent less foreign currency this year than in 1998 due to the deep recession gripping Venezuela.
