title: Venezuela  analysts blast  interventionist  proposals.
text:
CARACAS, July 13 (Reuters) - Venezuelan analysts and businessmen on Tuesday blasted President Hugo Chavez's plans to boost the flagging economy through major public investment schemes and a forced reduction of interest rates. 

 Chavez has come under heavy criticism recently for failing to act on Venezuela's worsening economic plight, concentrating instead on his controversial programme of political reforms. 

 But his recent announcement of a $934 million job creation programme and calls for the Central Bank to set lower interest rates were greeted as a worrying sign of renewed state intervention in the oil-based economy. 

 "It's the typical Keynesian investment plan which boosts the non-transferable sector of the economy, construction and generates employment, but also boosts inflation," said private economist Maxim Ross of the job-creation scheme. 

 The Venezuelan economy, ravaged by a slump in oil prices earlier in the year, is currently undergoing its worst recession this decade and is forecast to contract by at least 3 percent this year, according to government officials. 

 Unemployment has surged to 15 percent from 11 percent at the start of the year. Chavez took office in February. 

 In announcing the job creation plan Monday, Chavez reiterated his rejection of the "extreme, savage neo-liberal model" and insisted that "the state has an obligation... to orient the country, to be a motor that drives the economy." 

 Chavez, a 44-year-old former paratrooper, also warned Tuesday that interest rates might be unilaterally lowered to allow small businesses greater access to credit. 

 "What's lacking here is, if banks do not agree to lower interest rates, then the Central Bank should set rates which are more reasonable," he said at a news conference in the western city Maracaibo. 

 Annualized bank lending rates currently average about 33 percent even though inflation over the next 12 months is forecast to be less than 20 percent. 

 But bankers and analysts said setting rates would bring more problems than benefits. 

 "In the past, when there have been interest rate controls, it hasn't led to a growth in lending nor has it boosted the economy," said financial analyst Jose Grasso. 

 Banking Council President Hector Mantellini, meanwhile, warned that a forced reduction in interest rates could have the effect of reducing the incentive for saving and thus spark a run on the local bolivar currency. 

 ((-Silene Ramirez and Ana Isabel Martinez, Caracas newsroom 582 505 2600, fax 582 861 3621, caracas.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Venezuelan Bolivar Closes Weaker Despite  Intervention
text:
CARACAS (Dow Jones)--The bolivar closed weaker against the dollar Thurssday in heavy trading despite heavy intervention by the Central Bank of Venezuela as people stocked up on dollars ahead of the Dec. 6 presidential election,traders said. 

 The bolivar closed at a midrate of 574.50 bolivars per dollar, down from Wednesday's close of 573.75. 

 The average bank spread was 574.00/575.00 bolivars. 

 Traders said the general public, such as small savers and investors, were snapping up dollars Thursday in anticipation of the election as well as out of concern that the bolivar's recent weakness may be precusor to worse times ahead. 

 After rallying 1.9% between Sept. 25 and Nov. 19, the bolivar has weakened 1% in the last two weeks. 

 Meanwhile, corporations and banks continued their week-long movement into dollars, traders added. 

 Though some of the demand is seasonal, such as people planning vacations abroad and retailers paying for Christmas imports, the bulk appears to be being purchased out of concern about the election and the bolivar's outlook, according to traders. 

 In an effort to relieve pressure on the bolivar, the central bankintervened Thursday, dumping dollars onto the market, traders said. 

 Traders estimated that the central bank sold roughly $100 milion during the course of the day. 

 The last time the central bank sold this many dollars was on Aug. 24, when it was at the end of an aggressive defense of the local currency amidst a speculative attack. 

 The central bank, which by law must buy most of the dollars earned by state-owned oil monopoly Petroleos de Venezuela SA, is the biggest supplier of dollars to the market. It sells roughly $30 million to the market in a typical day.

title: Venezuelan Bolivar Weaker Vs Dollar At Midday
text:
CARACAS (Dow Jones)--The bolivar was weaker against the dollar at midday Thursday in heavy trading as devaluation fears spurred strong dollar-buying, traders said. 

 At around 1510 GMT, the bolivar was quoted at a midrate of 574.00 bolivars per dollar, down from Wednesday's close of 573.25. 

 The average bank spread was 573.50/574.00. 

 Traders said the local currency market remained spooked after AFP-Extel News Ltd., or AFX, reported early Wednesday afternoon that an unnamed presidential spokesman had said that the government could devalue the bolivar by 17%-20%. 

 Though the report was later categorically denied by Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff and Finance Minister Maritza Izaguirre, the financial market remains wary about this possibility, causing many to increase their dollar positions. 

 "It's mostly a defensive position by clients. Most don't believe that a devaluation is going to happen soon, but they also don't want to take the chance," a trader said. 

 With dollar-demand up sharply, the Central Bank of Venezuela swung into action and intervened to meet the strong wave of dollar-buying, according to traders. 

 Traders estimated that the central bank sold roughly $70 million to $80 million to the currency market by the late morning. On a typical day, the central bank would only sell roughly $30 million to the market. 

 The central bank, which by law must buy most of the dollars earned by state-owned oil monopoly Petroleos de Venezuela SA (PDVSA), is the biggest supplier of dollars to the market. 

 Despite the strong dollar-buying, traders don't expect the dollar to push much further beyond 574.00 bolivars during the rest of the session. 

 "It looks like the central bank is willing to support the bolivar until devaluation fears ebb," another trader said.

title: Emerging debt languishes on Russian uncertainty.
text:
NEW YORK, July 9 (Reuters) - Trading in emerging debt was slow and directionless Thursday as investors looked to events in Russia but found little in the way of news to push the market one way or the other, traders and analysts said. 

 Sentiment improved, but not by much, on news that Russian Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Khristenko said talks with the International Monetary Fund are going well and deals on new credits from both the IMF and the World Bank should be reached this week. 

 Market reaction was similarly muted when President Boris Yeltsin said Russia would not devalue the rouble, despite a crisis draining its reserves. 

 "Every headline moves the market a half point to one point up or down," one New York-based emerging sovereign debt trader said. 

 "We've seen these headlines before - that the IMF negotiations are going fine," the trader said. "This keeps the market from falling father but it does not bring confidence." 

 In order to take direction, the market needs concrete news about the size of Russia's IMF package and the conditions the IMF will impose as part of the deal, traders said. 


Russia PRIN bonds		  were up 1/2 to bid 45 and her IAN debt 	    was up 5/8 to bid 52-1/2.
Benchmark Brazil C bonds		  were flat on the day at a bid of 74-7/8 and Argentina PAR bonds		 were flat at a bid of 75-1/2.



Elsewhere, the dollar rose against the yen on Thursday amid growing scepticism that Japan's government would take sufficient measures to stimulate its economy, despite pledges of tax reform, foreign exchange dealers said.



"All the fundamental economic information coming out of Asia right now is very negative," said Devi Aurora, Asia analyst at Standard & Poor's DRI. "A whole lot more needs to be done in terms of government policy in Japan before sentiment is turned around."



Until then, emerging market debt will continue to suffer - and the U.S. Treasury market will continue to benefit - from a flight to quality, she said.



The benchmark U.S. Treasury bond was up 9/32 at 107-12/32 late Thursday.



But Luis R. Luis, head of emerging market bond research at Scudder Kemper Investments, said the yen, while weak, seems to have found a stable trading range. This, he said, accounts for the fact that the bonds of Asian countries have held their own in recent days.



One of the worst Brady bond performers of the day was Venezuela, whose GLB27 paper		 slipped 1 to bid 71.



Duff & Phelps Credit Rating Co. on Thursday said it lowered its rating on Venezuela's bolivar-denominated public national debt (DPN) to CCC from BB because of a reported missed payment on principal and interest last week.



The move was important, analysts said, because it downgraded Venezuelan local currency debt to default status.



"There are two ways for the Venezuelan government to defend the bolivar, direct intervention by selling dollars or issuing Treasury and central bank paper," said Siobhan Manning, Latin American debt analyst at Paine Webber.



"If the latter is compromised by this downgrade, the government will bleed down reserves as it intervenes by spending dollars on bolivars," she said.


Venezuela had announced plans to sell $500 million in a global bond issue, to be priced when oil prices improve and spreads narrow. The downgrade can only hurt that effort, Manning said.



(( Emerging Markets Unit, 212-859-1728 )).

title: Venezuela  Central Bank  may tweak monetary policy.
text:
CARACAS, April 17 (Reuter) - Venezuela's Central Bank may tweak its monetary policy in light of higher government spending forecast for the year, but will hang tight with its current foreign exchange policy, a Central Bank director said. 

 Exchange rate policy will continue to "promote a fall in inflation while also allowing a reasonable degree of flexibility that avoids market distortions and negative effects," Bank director Carlos Hernandez Delfino told Reuters. 

 Venezuelan inflation has steadily fallen since prices and exchange rate controls were liberalized last April -- but at the expense of an increasingly overvalued bolivar. 

 Although the bolivar floats freely between gently depreciating bands, its has only slipped some three percent against the dollar in the past year -- even as inflation has topped 70 percent. 

 Reducing inflation further -- March's 1.6 monthly rate was the lowest in five year -- remains a high government priority. Yet official inflation targets for the year have been upped to 35 percent, largely after a 70 percent public sector wage increase was agreed in February. 

 Hernandez said monetary policy would be determined by the state of Venezuelan fiscal accounts -- seen deteriorating from last year's one percent central government surplus due to the wage hike. 

 "Changes in these (fiscal) accounts will lead to some adjustments in the Bank's approach to monetary policy," Hernandez said. He details, except that the changes "are still being studied." 

 "Reducing inflation requires a high degree of financial, fiscal and monetary discipline, which also requires a high degree of institutional coordination between the Finance Ministry, PdVSA and the Bank," he added. 

 PdVSA is Venezuela's state-owned oil industry. 

 Other than intervention in the exchange markets, Central Bank monetary tools are currently limited to open market operations with Bank-backed paper, called TEMs, in weekly auctions. Primarily used to soak-up excess liquidity, the TEMs are also taken as benchmark for wider interest rates.

text:
